At the cap pause_for raises PauseCapacityError instead of deleting a live entry, so a granted pause holds until its TTL or an explicit resume, and the failure lands on the caller making the request rather than on a session that could not see it. Rejected the sketch's second branch (surface the eviction on the write that outlived it): telling the evictor is not actionable for them, and telling the victim needs a tombstone map whose own bounded eviction would be silent in the same way — the defect one level down. PauseCapacityError subclasses ValueError so it rides the channel do_pause_persistence already turns into {ok:false, error}. Decay runs before the cap check, so the cap counts live pauses and a full map recovers on its own; re-arming a key already in the map is never refused. The denial a full map now produces is loud, where the revocation it replaces was silent — the safe direction of the same failure.
issues.note: Deferred from the 2.5.8 review; picked up in the 2.5.9 line. Reaching the cap needs that many distinct declared keys live in one process, which no measured deployment approaches — the fix changes the direction of the failure, not its likelihood, and deliberately leaves the cap itself alone.

issues.summary: (LOW) The queue's task-to-session attribution is documented as never outliving its row ("every delete/complete path drops its entry"), and three paths delete queue rows without touching the map: agent-data deletion, a move-mode merge, and the stale-queue repair. The entries leak until the cap evicts them. No wrong pause decision follows — a reused row id is always overwritten before it is read — so the cost is cap pressure and an occasional early eviction, but the docstring and the design note both state a stronger invariant than the code holds. The test named for the invariant exercises only the completion and self-pause paths, so its name is broader than its body.
issues.note: Deferred from the 2.5.8 review; picked up in the 2.5.9 line. No wrong pause decision was possible either before or after: an enqueue always writes or clears the entry for its row id before that id is read, so a reused row id cannot inherit a stale key. The cost was cap pressure and early eviction of a live entry.
issues.fix_note: Took neither branch of the fix_sketch literally. Dropping the attribution on the three row-deleting paths would be correct only until a fourth deleter is written, and would have a health probe and two admin handlers reach into in-process queue state to do it; narrowing the claim would leave the leak in place. The queue instead ends every drain pass by reconciling the map against the rows that still exist, which covers any path that deletes a row, including ones not yet written. The query asks only about the ids the map holds, so it is bounded by the attribution cap rather than by the queue, and the ids are snapshotted before it runs so a row attributed concurrently cannot be forgotten by it. It is called where the pass ends rather than in a finally: a reconcile that raised inside one would turn a drain that succeeded into a drain that aborted, and an aborted pass is re-armed anyway. The docstring and the design note now describe that mechanism, and the test named for the invariant gained the out-of-band case it always claimed — asserted through the handler that really deletes the rows. Mutation M13 covers the reconcile call.

issues.summary: (LOW) A keyless pause now reports `scope: "process"` with a docstring calling that "the widest honest answer", but since the pause became per-session the keyless bucket no longer reaches a declared session's writes. The word is no longer the widest radius, only the widest of the buckets — a caller that pauses keylessly for a benchmark can still be contaminated by a concurrent declared session's writes, which could not happen before. The tool description states this correctly; only the one-word `scope` value and the docstring behind it overstate.
issues.note: Deferred from the 2.5.8 review; picked up in the 2.5.9 line. The behaviour is as designed; the finding was about the accuracy of one word.
issues.fix_note: Corrected the docstring and left the reported value alone, as the fix_sketch reasoned: consumers branch on the two strings, so changing what is reported is a contract change with its own decision to make. The docstring now says what `process` names — the widest bucket, not the widest radius — and states the loss explicitly: before the pause was per-session the two were the same thing, and a keyless pause no longer reaches a declared session's writes. The tool description already stated the radius correctly and is the surface a caller reads, so it needed nothing.

issues.summary: (LOW) One handler tests the raw `session_key` argument for truthiness instead of resolving it, so a whitespace-only value counts as declared and the response omits the shared-identity flag that every other surface would add. The resolver strips exactly so that a client template rendering an absent value cannot produce a bucket of its own; this call site bypasses that rule and is the only remaining place that does.
issues.note: Deferred from the 2.5.8 review; picked up in the 2.5.9 line. Predated the stage 2 work and became the sole deviation once that work made the seam canonical.
issues.fix_note: Resolved the argument through the session seam and branched on the resolved `declared` flag, matching every other handler. Two truthy strings were slipping through, not one: whitespace-only, which the resolver strips so a client template rendering an unset variable cannot mint a bucket, and the literal TRANSPORT_KEY, which names the bucket every keyless caller already shares — the raw test let either silence the honesty flag while landing in exactly the bucket the flag reports. Rejected the narrower repair of stripping the argument in place: it fixes the whitespace half and leaves the sentinel half, and it re-implements a decision the seam is the one owner of. The claim that this was the last raw call site was re-counted rather than inherited: three sites compare `session_key` without the resolver, and the other two are correct by contract (tasks.py takes an already-resolved key whose default is the sentinel, session.py compares inside the seam).

issues.summary: (LOW) The pause-seam structural gate exempts its own module by base name rather than by path, so a `session.py` added inside a future sub-package would drop out of the scan silently. The companion test that checks the gate's reach asserts only that the top-level module is absent, so it would not notice.
issues.note: Deferred from the 2.5.8 review; picked up in the 2.5.9 line. Same class as the Gate 10b finding earlier in the line — an exemption applies to paths, and a gate's green means only what its own patterns reach.
issues.fix_note: Both exemptions in `_pause_seam_files` now compare the path relative to the package root, so only `cpersona/session.py` is the seam and a `session.py` inside a future sub-package is scanned like any other module. Widening the exemption alone would have been half a fix: the companion reach test asserted the same bare name against a set of relative posix paths, so it agreed with the defect and would have kept agreeing. It gets a new case that walks a synthetic tree containing `sub/session.py` — asserted synthetically on purpose, because the real package has no such file, which is why the defect was invisible in-tree and would have stayed invisible until someone added one. Mutation-checked: restoring the base-name exemption fails that one test and no other.

issues.summary: (HIGH) The NULL-embedding prefetch reported a failing backend to the health breaker only from an `except` that the most likely failure never reaches: the embedding call reports an unreachable endpoint by returning no embeddings rather than by raising. A re-embed pass with the backend down zipped against an empty sequence, wrote nothing, told health nothing, and reported success. The evidence it did pass on the rare raising path was a constant that named neither the mode nor the endpoint.
issues.fix_note: The prefetch reads the outcome the embedding call now carries and reports `outcome.error`, so an unreachable endpoint promotes the breaker and reaches the advisory with the failing call's own evidence. Recovery deliberately stays on the recall path: clearing health from a maintenance run would erase a fault a user's recall had just latched. Regressions: test_prefetch_health_feedback.py (four cases; two mutations were run — dropping the report kills three of them and dropping only the outcome read kills the two that cover it, so the cases are differentiated rather than all-or-nothing). Test doubles that offered `embed` but not `embed_with_outcome` were aligned with the client contract; one of them had been masking this class by raising where the real client does not.
issues.note: Found while wiring the failure evidence through, not by a failing check. bug-129 recorded this feed as part of its fix and was marked fixed; see the note added there.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) A failure that never reached the backend is reported as an unreachable backend, on both surfaces that report one. `EmbedOutcome` carries `attempted`, and bug-248 gated the success side on it, but the failure side is ungated: `vector.py` calls `health.observe_failure()` for any falsy embed, and `checks.py` treats a probe that returned no dimension as a backend that did not answer. An invalid `CPERSONA_EMBEDDING_MODE` produces exactly that shape — `attempted=False, ok=False, error='mode=<x> is not a supported embedding mode'` — because the mode string is never validated: config reads it from the environment unchecked and the server only tests it against 'none' before constructing a client with it. Measured with mode='openai': two recalls latch FAULT with reason 'embedding endpoint unreachable; recall fell back to keyword/FTS-only' and a runbook whose four investigation steps are all network-layer (is the process alive, is the port reachable, curl the URL, was the model downloaded) and whose repair names the URL environment variables; check_health returns type 'embedding_backend_unreachable' with hint 'the configured embedding backend did not answer'. Nothing was contacted. The evidence string does name the real cause on both surfaces, so the operator is misdirected rather than left blind, and semantic recall genuinely is degraded, so raising an advisory at all is correct — what is wrong is the classification and the repair it points at.
issues.note: Found by the v2.5.8..v2.5.9a2 release-gate audit and reproduced end to end before filing. Same class as bug-248 (a cache hit is not an observation) but on the failure side: that fix asked whether a call reached the backend before believing a success, and this one did not ask before believing a failure. Both mutations were checked to kill only their own targets.
issues.fix_note: Both halves, because either alone leaves the other's failure mode. (1) The classification follows attempted the way the success side has since bug-248: observe_failure takes it, latches a fault_kind of misconfigured when nothing was contacted, and both surfaces read that — the advisory picks a runbook that names CPERSONA_EMBEDDING_MODE and drops the four network-layer steps, and check_embedding_backend emits embedding_backend_misconfigured instead of _unreachable. fault_kind is kept beside the state rather than made a state of its own: recall is degraded identically either way, and the states are what decide whether an advisory fires at all. The advisory is NOT suppressed. (2) The mode is validated once at startup, before the client is built. It raises rather than falling back to 'none', because 'none' is a supported configuration that disables semantic recall deliberately — silently substituting it would give a misconfigured server the same shape as a correct one, which is the silence this area keeps being repaired for. Nothing in _vendored_mcp_common was touched: that is the cross-consumer axis (common bump + re-vendor), a different cost class, and the classification belongs to the reporting surfaces rather than to the client.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The vector index's promise that it always falls back to the scan does not hold for every way it can fail, because only one of its failure modes is funnelled into IndexUnusable. `_index_backed_candidates` wraps `cached_index()` in `try/except IndexUnusable` and then calls `vector_index.select()` OUTSIDE that guard, so an exception raised while selecting escapes into recall instead of returning None. One such exception is reachable through data rather than corruption: `select()` filters by source with `v.startswith(source_id)` over values taken from `json_extract(source, '$.id')`, and SQLite returns a JSON number as a Python int, so a memory whose source id was written as a number raises AttributeError. The scan path this index replaces does not share the defect — it filters in SQL with LIKE, which coerces the integer to text and matches (measured: json_extract returns int 123; `LIKE '1%'` returns 1; `.startswith` raises). A derived, optional artifact whose whole design claim is 'the scan stays correct and is still the fallback' can therefore take down the query it was meant to accelerate.
issues.note: Found by the v2.5.8..v2.5.9a2 release-gate audit (index area, external finder). The entry recorded that reachability of the int source id was NOT established; fixing it established more than the entry claimed — the builder raises on such a row before any query runs, so the exposure was never confined to the read path. The index remains operator-opt-in in this release: no shipped code path builds it.
issues.fix_note: Both moves from the sketch, plus one the sketch did not have. (1) Selection moved inside the guard, and a broad except added beside the IndexUnusable branch — the backstop, not the fix, because the claim to hold is 'recall survives a broken index' and that cannot rest on having enumerated every way a mapped file and a numpy filter can fail; the scan below is always correct, so falling back costs latency only. (2) The sibling header read now raises IndexUnusable instead of KeyError/ValueError. (3) NOT in the sketch: the numeric source id breaks the BUILDER before it ever reaches select() — _intern sorts the string table and int < str raises TypeError, measured. So the normalisation belongs at the boundary where the column is read, which also makes the table match what the scan's LIKE compares against; it is computed once and used for both the table and the per-row codes, since two spellings of one normalisation is how one of them looks a value up under a key the other never wrote. select() keeps its str() anyway and is tested: an older build only raised when it had to sort ints AGAINST strings, so a corpus of entirely numeric source ids sorted fine and produced a table of ints, and such a file is still format 2 and still loaded.

issues.summary: (LOW) The queue's attribution reconciliation is reached only when a drain pass ends by finding the queue empty, so a pass that raises leaves the map holding entries whose rows are gone — the state bug-270 was fixed to prevent. The fix placed the reconcile at the `task is None` branch and justified skipping a `finally` on the grounds that an aborted pass is re-armed and the next one reconciles anyway. That justification misreads the word: `_loop` catches the exception, logs 'drain aborted, re-arming', and returns to `await self._event.wait()`. Re-arming means the loop survived, not that another drain was scheduled — with no subsequent enqueue the event is never set and no later pass runs. A queue that is never started never reconciles at all. Measured on a throwaway database: enqueue under a declared key, delete the row out of band, make _fetch_next raise once, and the vanished id is still in the map after the pass.
issues.note: Found by the v2.5.8..v2.5.9a2 release-gate audit and reproduced before filing. Same class as bug-270 itself: a claim stated more strongly than the code holds it. The consequence is unchanged from bug-270 — cap pressure and an early eviction of a live entry, no wrong pause decision — which is why this is LOW despite being a recurrence. The audit found it by being handed the registry's known-issue list for these files and told to name any id it saw recurring, which is what it did.
issues.fix_note: Moved the reconcile into a finally that swallows and logs its own exception, which is the one shape that satisfies both constraints: it is reached however a pass ends, and it cannot turn a drain that succeeded into a drain that aborted — the thing the original placement was right about. The justification that replaced it misread 're-arming': _loop catches, logs and returns to awaiting the event, so the loop survived but no further pass was scheduled, and with no later enqueue none ever runs. Reconciling at the top of the next pass was the other candidate and was not taken: it has the same hole for a queue whose loop never runs again, and it delays the cleanup by one pass for no gain. The test aborts a pass and asserts the map is clean, which is the claim the design note makes, rather than asserting a call site was reached; a third case pins that the ordinary pass still reconciles, since a finally that never ran would otherwise satisfy the other two.

issues.summary: (HIGH) A memory whose embedding is filled in after the index was built becomes unreachable through the index path, while the scan still returns it — the silent withholding the watermark exists to make impossible. The builder collects `embedding IS NOT NULL AND id <= watermark`, so a row that was NULL at build time enters neither the index nor excluded_ids (that list is for non-canonical created_at, not for missing embeddings). Its id is at or below the watermark, so the tail, which reads `id > watermark` plus the excluded holes, does not read it either. Filling the embedding leaves the row in no set the index path consults. Measured on a two-row corpus: build with row 1 embedded and row 2 NULL (built count=1, watermark=2, excluded=0), then set row 2's embedding; the scan considers ids [1,2], the index path reaches [1], the tail reads nothing, and id 2 is returned by one path and not the other. The trigger is routine maintenance, not an exotic edit: prefetch_null_embeddings under check_health(fix=True) is what fills NULL embeddings. CONTIGUOUS_INDEX_DESIGN accepts staleness for deletes, for re-tagging and for rebuild cadence, and §5 states there is no window in which a new memory is invisible; this row is invisible until the next manual rebuild, and no accepted case covers it.
issues.note: Found by the v2.5.8..v2.5.9a2 release-gate audit and reproduced end to end before filing. Reachability is bounded by the index being operator-opt-in in this release: nothing in the shipped server builds it (build_index has callers only in the module's CLI entry point and in tests), so only an operator who built one is exposed — but that operator is also the one who runs check_health(fix=True). Severity is HIGH rather than MEDIUM because the failure is silent and subtractive: recall answers successfully with fewer memories, which is the outcome the design document names as worse than being slow. The reverse direction was measured while fixing this and is filed separately as bug-279: an indexed row whose embedding is later set to NULL stays in the matrix, and the hydrate does not filter on the embedding, so the index can return a row the scan excludes.
issues.fix_note: Took the fix_sketch's second hole set. The builder now records the ids at or below the watermark that it skipped for a NULL embedding, in unembedded_ids beside excluded_ids, and the tail reads both through the one IN clause it already had. The tail stays exact and the watermark keeps answering the only question it can answer. FORMAT_VERSION went to 2 because a sidecar written by the old builder has no record of what it skipped: a new reader cannot repair it, only reject it, and rejection is already spelled IndexUnusable, which the query path answers with the scan. The cap is on the sum of the two lists rather than one each, because they are bound into the same statement; a corpus that exceeds it declines to build, which is the answer a mixed-width corpus already gets. Rejected: lowering the watermark to the smallest NULL id (the tail then scans everything after it) and rebuilding on every re-embed (that puts correctness back into rebuild cadence, which the design is written to keep out). Mutation-checked: dropping unembedded_ids from the tail's holes fails the new equivalence test and nothing else (1 failed, 1553 passed).

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The mirror of bug-278: a row that is indexed and later loses its embedding stays in the index matrix, so the index path can return a row the scan excludes, ranked by a vector that no longer exists. Two maintenance repairs blank an embedding in place — the content sanitiser rewrites the text and nulls the vector in the same statement, and the dimension repair nulls mismatched vectors — both under check_health(fix=True). After either, the scan drops the row (every scan phase filters embedding IS NOT NULL) while the index still holds its bytes; the by-id hydrate selects id, msg_id, content, source and timestamp with no embedding predicate, so the row is returned. In the sanitiser's case the ranking reflects text that no longer exists in the row being shown. Measured: build over two embedded rows, null one, and the index path reaches both while the scan reaches one.
issues.note: Found while fixing bug-278 and deliberately not folded into it: the one-line repair that looks right is the one that breaks keyword-only recall, and that deserves its own change and its own test rather than riding along. Reachability is bounded the same way as bug-278 — the index is operator-opt-in in this release, nothing in the shipped server builds it — but the trigger is the same routine maintenance run.
issues.fix_note: The index path now asks, in one bounded existence probe over the ids it selected, whether any of them has lost its embedding, and hands the query back to the scan when one has. The sketch's other branch — filter those positions out and continue — was rejected after working it through: the scan's window is the newest scan_limit rows THAT HAVE an embedding, so dropping k rows from a saturated selection leaves the index short by k rows the scan reaches. That divergence is invisible on any corpus smaller than the window, which is exactly where a test would look, so the repair would have shipped with a green equivalence test and the bug intact. Falling back is exact at every window size and is what the same function already does for the other condition it cannot reproduce. The probe is LIMIT 1 and bounded by the selection rather than the corpus. The hydrate was left alone as the sketch instructed, and a test pins that a row with no embedding still comes back through it — the one-line repair that looks right there is the one that breaks keyword-only recall.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The advisory mutation lane bounds the number of mutants it will run but not the time they take, so a run that fits the cap can still be killed by the job's ceiling — and because the lane is continue-on-error, that death is silent. The cap is a count (default 60) and cosmic-ray runs the test command once per mutant; the command carries -x, so a killed mutant returns early while a surviving one pays for the whole suite. At the suite's measured size a worst case inside the cap is roughly 46 minutes against a 20-minute ceiling. Measured on 2026-09-01: a run started at 22:17:21 was cancelled at 22:37:36, exactly at the ceiling, having written no report. On the pull request the outcome was indistinguishable from a lane that ran and found nothing, which is the failure that matters — the lane exists to measure, and an unmeasured commit that reads as a measured one is worse than no lane.
issues.fix_note: Two halves, and neither is sufficient alone. The bound is now priced rather than guessed: the run times one unmutated suite, converts a wall-clock budget (default 900s, under the 20-minute ceiling) into a number of mutants it can afford, and refuses as 'capped' with the price stated when the diff needs more. Pricing off the worst case is deliberate — a mutant that dies early is cheap, so an estimate assuming early death stops bounding exactly when the diff is weakly tested, which is when the lane has something to say. A baseline that does not pass yields 'unpriced' rather than a number, because timing a broken suite prices nothing. The second half removes the silence: a step that runs even when the previous one was cancelled writes 'did-not-complete — treat it as unmeasured, not as clean' into the job summary when no report exists. The lane stays advisory; continue-on-error was never the defect, and gating on it would institutionalise a number nobody has validated yet.
issues.note: Found by being blocked by it: a HIGH fix (bug-278) sat waiting on a lane that had already stopped measuring. Validated before shipping — the pricing helper was exercised against fast, slow and failing commands, and the workflow step's body was extracted verbatim and run under bash in both branches (report present, report absent). The variable in that step was renamed off `status` because it is read-only in some shells; the step runs under bash, where it would have worked, but the rename costs nothing.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Three recipes in the shipped skill cannot be followed as written, and the worst of them fails silently. The backup instruction is `sqlite3 "$DB" ".backup 'b.db'"`, but `$DB` is defined nowhere in the skill or the docs — the variable a reader who followed setup actually has is CPERSONA_DB_PATH. With DB unset the command expands to `sqlite3 ""`, which opens an empty transient database and backs that up, so the reader is told their memory is backed up and it is not. Separately, both from-source recipes clone a repository and never enter it: CPersona's says clone, create a venv, `pip install .`, which installs whatever is in the directory the reader started in, and CEmbedding's says clone then `pip install ".[onnx]"` with the same defect. The CEmbedding from-source line also drops the two things its own PATH recipe two lines above keeps — the model download and EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=onnx_jina_v5_nano — so a reader who follows it starts a server that ignores the model it just downloaded.
issues.pattern: substitute the path you set as
issues.note: Found by the v2.5.8..v2.5.9a2 release-gate audit, which was asked to verify every command, path, flag and environment variable in the skill against the tree rather than reason about them. The finder also reported that the PATH recipe omits EMBEDDING_PROVIDER; that half is wrong — it is present — and only the from-source line drops it. Verified by reading both recipes. The corrected form was checked the same way the defect was found: no backup line in the skill now expands a shell variable.
issues.fix_note: Both clone recipes gained the `cd` they were missing, and the CEmbedding source line gained the model download and EMBEDDING_PROVIDER its own PATH recipe two lines above already had, with a sentence saying why they are not optional. The backup command took the longer repair. Renaming $DB to $CPERSONA_DB_PATH was drafted first and rejected on measurement: that name is set in the MCP client's config JSON, not exported into the reader's shell, so the substitution would have reproduced the same silent `sqlite3 ""` under a more convincing name. Both call sites now show a literal path and say where its value comes from. The lesson is the one the finding is an instance of: an instruction is verified by asking whether the reader's environment actually holds what it references, not by whether the name is spelled correctly.

issues.summary: (LOW) The repair reference calls a recall the read-only liveness test and states there is no side effect on stored data, without naming the configuration in which that is false. With CPERSONA_CONFIDENCE_ENABLED=true a successful non-deep recall that is not gate-fallback and not paused updates recall_count and last_recalled_at for the rows it returned. The flag ships off, so the sentence is true for a default install and false for one that turned confidence on — which the production instance has. The page's own purpose makes the omission matter: it is the page a reader consults while diagnosing, and it recommends running the test repeatedly.
issues.note: Found by the release-gate audit and confirmed by reading the gate in do_recall: the write is guarded by `not deep and not gate_fallback and recall_counts and not session.is_paused_for(...)`, and recall_counts is populated only under the confidence flag.
issues.fix_note: Stated the condition rather than weakening the sentence: the recall writes recall_count and last_recalled_at when confidence is enabled, does not when it is off, and does not while the session is paused — that last clause kept deliberately, because it is what makes the test safe during a no-persist window. The code was not changed to match the doc; the bump is deliberate and its own comment explains why making it unconditional was rejected. The pattern now anchors on the env name the page had to gain, which the widened docs-facts gate (bug-282) also checks is a real one.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The documentation gate that verifies environment-variable names against the source only reads Markdown table rows, so a name written inline — as a bullet or in a code fence — is unchecked. The reference page shipped in this release writes its setup variables inline, which puts every one of them outside the gate. Measured by mutation: renaming CPERSONA_EMBEDDING_URL to CPERSONA_EMBEDDING_URl in that page's inline bullet leaves check-docs-facts at exit 0, although no such name exists anywhere in the source. The gate's guarantee is that a documented variable is a real one; for this page it guarantees nothing, and the page is the one a reader with a broken install is sent to.
issues.note: Found by the release-gate audit and reproduced before filing. Same class as the pause-seam exemption (bug-273) and Gate 10b: a gate is green only over the surface its own pattern reaches, and the surface here is narrower than the docs it is trusted for.
issues.fix_note: Widened the reading rather than the exemption list: a new check_env_names scans every CPERSONA_* token in the tracked pages, and check_env_tables keeps the table-row reading untouched because the two answer different questions (is this name real, versus is this table complete). The one construct the widening surfaced was `CPERSONA_CALIBRATE_*`, a family named in prose; it is satisfied by requiring a real member with that prefix rather than by an allowlist entry, so a typo in the prefix itself still fails — allowlisting the token would have given that up, and narrowing is how the gate got here. The scan is split into env_name_violations(text, known) so the repair is proved on a page's text with the mutation applied, without writing a mutated page to disk.

issues.summary: (LOW) The mutation harness refuses to run against a dirty tree so that its results describe the release candidate, but the check reads only unstaged changes: `git diff --name-only` with no --cached. A staged edit to a target file with a clean working tree passes the guard, so the harness can apply its mutants on top of code that is not the candidate and report that every seam is pinned for a tree nobody is shipping. The failure is quiet in the direction that matters — the run goes green.
issues.note: Found by the release-gate audit while reviewing the gate scripts, and confirmed by reading tree_is_clean. Not reproduced by staging a file, because doing so in this working tree would have disturbed the release branch.
issues.fix_note: tree_is_clean now asks git for the staged set as well as the unstaged one. The end-of-run `git diff --quiet` check was deliberately left alone: a mutant left on disk is by construction an unstaged write, and widening that one would trip on staged work the run never touched. The test pins the query and not only the verdict — a guard that refused everything would satisfy a verdict-only assertion while measuring nothing — and it runs against a stubbed git rather than staging a file in the real tree.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The lost-embedding probe that guards the contiguous index binds one SQL parameter per selected row, so a scan window above SQLite's variable limit turns the index from an accelerator into a hard failure. `_index_rows_lost_embedding` builds `IN (?, ?, ...)` with one placeholder per id in the selection, and the selection is the scan window. SQLite's default SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER is 32,766 (3.32+); the probe raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: too many SQL variables` at any window above it, and the call sits outside the `IndexUnusable` guard in `_index_phase1`, so the error escapes `_search_vector` and the recall fails instead of falling back to the scan. Reproduced on macOS Python 3.11 (SQLite 3.50.4, limit 32,766) with CPERSONA_MAX_MEMORIES=40000 and an index built over 40,000 rows: every recall raised. The reference measurement machine's build allows 250,000 variables, which is why the 100,000-row window measured there ran at all. The same probe is also 72 ms of a 212 ms arm at that window — cost and correctness share a cause, the parameter list scaling with the selection.
issues.fix_sketch: Bound the probe by the selection's shape rather than by its size: for the common all-index case the selected ids are one contiguous id range, so `WHERE id BETWEEN ? AND ? AND embedding IS NULL LIMIT 1` asks the same question with two parameters; for a scattered selection, chunk the ids at a fixed size well under the smallest limit a supported build ships with. Whichever shape is used, the probe must stay inside a guard that degrades to the scan on an operational error — a derived, optional artifact must never turn a query into a failure. Add a test that runs the index path at a window above 32,766 against `sqlite3.connect(...).getlimit(SQLITE_LIMIT_VARIABLE_NUMBER)` lowered via `setlimit`, so the failure is reproducible on every build rather than only on ones that ship the default.
issues.note: Found by the segment profile taken after the contiguous-view change (benchmarks/measurements/results-contiguous-index.md), which showed the probe as the second-largest term, and confirmed as a failure rather than a cost by running the measurement script on a build with the default limit. Registered open: the view change it was found under does not touch the probe, and the fix changes what the function promises (its bound) rather than only its speed.
issues.fix_note: The probe is now bounded by the selection's shape. A contiguous run of ids (the ordinary all-index selection: the span of the ids equals their count, and ids are unique) is asked with BETWEEN and two parameters, whatever the window; a scattered selection is asked in fixed chunks of 500, under the 999 that every SQLite before 3.32.0 compiled in, so the statement fits the smallest build a supported Python links against. The call moved inside a fail-open guard of its own, so whatever the probe raises degrades to the scan instead of escaping into recall — the same claim bug-276 pinned for selection, extended to the one statement the index path issues against the database. Both statement forms carry the agent predicate — it cannot exclude a selected row and it keeps the probe inside the isolation gate every agent-scoped read is held to — written as `+agent_id` so the planner does not constrain the isolation index with it: measured at 100,000 rows, the plain predicate made the planner walk every row of the agent per statement (43 ms for the range form instead of 25, 3.0 s for the chunked form instead of 41 ms). A test pins the plan on the id term. Re-profiled at 100,000 / 100,000 the probe fell from 72.5 ms to 36.5 ms; what remains is SQLite walking the rows in the range to test the column, which a partial index would remove and which is recorded as a schema decision, not made. The tests lower SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER with setlimit on the live connection so the failure reproduces on every build, and each part of the repair is pinned by the test that goes red without it: the range form (limit below the selection size, cleared embedding still detected), the chunking (scattered selection, cleared row in the last chunk), and the guard (a raising probe still returns the scan's answer). The ids for the probe are taken as one numpy slice rather than one scalar conversion per row.

issues.summary: (LOW) The confidence span orders timestamps as TEXT, so a scope holding more than one UTC offset can report a span whose ends are not its oldest and newest rows. `scope_stats.get_span` returns MIN/MAX over the `timestamp` column, which SQLite compares byte by byte. An ISO-8601 stamp's byte order equals its chronological order only while every stamp compared carries the same offset: '2026-05-31T15:00:30+09:00' is 06:00:30Z but sorts after '2026-05-31T11:05:00+00:00'. The `datetime(timestamp) IS NOT NULL` guard does not cover this — it excludes unparseable strings, and these parse fine. Measured on a live 2,977-row corpus carrying '+00:00' (2,456 rows), 'Z' (503) and '+09:00' (10): seven places where the byte order runs backwards in time, and one real 237-row scope whose reported MIN is 0.16 h later than its actual oldest row. The consequence is a scoring input, not a wrong row: the span scales the confidence time axis and anchors undated rows (bug-107 / bug-207), so a wrong span shifts how rows are ranked against each other and never which rows exist. The error is bounded by the largest offset difference inside one scope — up to 26 h between -12:00 and +14:00 — and is silent at every size.
issues.fix_sketch: Order by the instant rather than by the text. Aggregating `datetime(timestamp)` is correct and gives up the index seek, which is what the current shape was built to get — so the candidates that keep both are a stored normalised column written at store time, or a generated column, either one indexed in place of the raw column. Both are schema changes and both alter what a scope's span is, so the change has to be made where scoring semantics are decided rather than alongside a cost fix. Whichever is taken, the test needs a scope holding at least two offsets whose byte order and chronological order disagree — a single-offset fixture cannot fail.
issues.note: Found while measuring the span statement for the covering index, by asking what the production corpus's timestamps actually look like before assuming they were uniform. The census is the evidence: five distinct spellings in one corpus, and the offsets are what break the ordering. Registered open rather than repaired in that change, which moves no scoring input; the split into two statements landing at the same time preserves this behaviour exactly rather than introducing or worsening it. bug-287 is the same mistake at a second seam and was repaired separately, which is the split worth explaining: there, the ordering is done in Python over a list already in memory, so reading the instant costs a parse per row and changes the order of what a caller is handed. Here it is done by SQLite over an indexed column, so reading the instant gives up the index seek on a statement in the recall path, and it changes a scoring input rather than a returned row. Same reasoning, two prices an order of magnitude apart -- fixing them together would have priced the cheap one at the expensive one's cost, and would have put a schema change in front of a correction that needed none.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) recall_with_context ordered its merged conversation by the raw timestamp string, so a message spelled in a different UTC offset was placed at the position its bytes sorted to rather than the instant it names. An ISO-8601 stamp's byte order equals its chronological order only while every stamp compared carries the same offset, and this is the surface where that stops holding: the tool merges rows the database wrote with entries a caller supplied, and nothing makes the two sides agree on a spelling. '2026-01-01T09:00:03+09:00' is 00:00:03Z but sorted after every '...T00:00:0NZ' row, because '9' > '0' in column 11; a '+00:00' stamp sorted before the same instant spelled with 'Z'; a naive stamp SQLite wrote with datetime('now') sorted into its own neighbourhood ahead of every offset-bearing one. The caller renders this list as a conversation, so a misplaced row did not read as an error -- it read as a turn that happened at a different time. A stamp that did not parse was worse than unplaced: its position followed its first byte, so 'zzz' sorted last (where last reads as most recent) and a stamp beginning with an early digit sorted into the middle of the chronology, posing as a dated turn at a specific point in the conversation.
issues.note: Found by an external audit of the boundary and time-semantics surfaces, and confirmed by reading the sort key rather than by a report from the field. Recorded in the behaviour matrix before being repaired: the two scenarios whose fixtures are built so that byte order and instant order disagree are the two whose recordings moved, and the other 79 did not, which is what said the change reached only the seam it was aimed at. A fixture whose two orders agree cannot tell a byte sort from an instant sort, so it would have stayed green through both the defect and the fix; the fixture asserts its own disagreement to keep that from being edited away.
issues.fix_note: The key is now the parsed instant. _parse_timestamp_utc settles the naive case by the bug-114 invariant, so a database row and a caller's entry become comparable instead of sorting into separate byte neighbourhoods. A stamp that names no instant cannot be placed in the chronology, only somewhere fixed, and the key's leading flag puts every one of them ahead of every dated message: it is where a missing stamp already sat (the case that actually occurs), it is not the end of the list where an unknown would read as the most recent turn, and it does not depend on the first byte, so no unreadable stamp can imitate a position. list.sort is stable, so messages naming the same instant keep the order they were merged in -- recall's ranked rows first, then the caller's entries as given. Pinned by mutation M14 (restoring the string key), which kills five unit tests and both golden scenarios.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The container path could not be followed as written, and nothing ever ran it. The Dockerfile shipped unchanged from the repository's first commit and was referenced by no document, no workflow and no test. Every claim it made was wrong in a way that only running it reveals. `CMD ["python", "server.py"]` starts the transport CPERSONA_TRANSPORT names, which defaults to stdio, so the container bound no socket while `EXPOSE 8400` advertised a port the server does not use either (the HTTP default is 8402). Had the HTTP transport been selected, CPERSONA_HTTP_HOST defaults to 127.0.0.1 — the container's own loopback — so a published port would forward to a socket nothing was listening on. CPERSONA_DB_PATH pointed at /data with no VOLUME, so the database of a persistent-memory server lived and died with one container. `COPY . .` with no .dockerignore put the git history, the built documentation site, node_modules and a local virtualenv inside the image, which then also installed the package and ran the source tree beside it. The process ran as root.
issues.note: Found by an external audit, which reported the file as verbatim from its own example. The audit was right about the cause and understated the effect: this is the same class as bug-280 (a shipped recipe that cannot be followed), and the reason both survived is identical — a recipe nobody executes has no failing state. Five months and one initial commit is what that looks like on a Dockerfile.
issues.fix_note: The image is built in two stages and installs the wheel, so it runs the artifact a PyPI user runs rather than a second copy of the tree; .dockerignore is an allowlist of the wheel's inputs, because a denylist admits whatever is added later. CPERSONA_HTTP_HOST is set to 0.0.0.0 — the one value a container must override, and safe here for the reason the server's own guard states, that the bind address decides nothing and the token does. /data is a volume owned by an unprivileged uid, and a HEALTHCHECK asks whether the port answers HTTP rather than whether the process exists. None of that is the durable part: the `container` job in ci.yml builds the image and asks it the questions a user would — it refuses without a token, it answers through a published port, and a row written through the API is read back by a DIFFERENT container from the same volume. A corrected Dockerfile with no gate is the same file with a later date on it.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Every file the server created took its mode from the ambient umask, so the corpus shipped world-readable on a default host. Seven of eight write paths called open(path, "w") or os.makedirs with no mode; only the alias ledger asked, via fchmod after tempfile.mkstemp. Under the default umask 022 that is 0644 for the database, an export (the whole corpus as plain-text JSONL), the contiguous embedding index, the calibration sidecar and its backups, and 0755 for any directory the server created for them. SQLite widens it further by inheritance: it copies the database file's mode onto the -wal and -shm files it derives, and the -wal holds recently written rows that have not been checkpointed yet. Measured on the reference deployment before the fix: cpersona.db, cpersona.db-wal and cpersona.db-shm were all 0644 inside a 0755 directory under a 0755 home, and a 3.9 MB export sat beside them at 0644 — readable by every local account on a host running four other services. The mode was never a property of the data; it was a property of whichever shell started the process, so nothing in the deployment could be inspected to predict it.
issues.note: Found by an external audit of the boundary surfaces, which named database.py and the export and was right about both; reading the package for the whole class found five more (the embedding index, the calibration sidecar, its backups, the update-check cache, and every directory). The one path that was already correct is what makes this a seam problem rather than a memory problem: the rule was known and written down in aliases.py, and seven later writers did not know it. Confidence off, remote transports, none of it matters here — this is reachable by anyone with a shell on the host, which is a different boundary from the ones the audit's other findings sit on.
issues.fix_note: cpersona/fileperms.py is now the only place the package brings a path into existence, and tests/test_structural_gates.py fails on any open(..., 'w') / os.open / os.makedirs / Path.write_* outside it — the seam-ownership pattern the write lock and the vector packer already use, chosen because remembering a mode is exactly what seven call sites did not do. The database is pre-created with O_EXCL at 0600 rather than chmod-ed after connecting, for two reasons: SQLite then gives -wal and -shm the same mode (measured on 3.40.1 and 3.53.1, and asserted as a test so the premise fails loudly if it ever stops holding), and there is no window in which the corpus exists world-readable. The fchmod inside open_private is not redundant with the creation mode: three write paths write <dest>.tmp and os.replace it, so a temp file left by a killed run is REOPENED at its old mode and that mode is then installed over the destination. An existing file is never re-chmod-ed — its mode is the operator's — which is also the limit of this fix: an install that upgrades keeps the 0644 files it already has, and only new ones are private. Every helper degrades rather than raises when the platform has no fchmod (Windows, which the package supports) or the filesystem refuses it (FAT/CIFS): a refused chmod must cost the mode, never the write.

issues.summary: (HIGH) The HTTP transport had no bound on a request body before the body was parsed. Every payload cap in the package — MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH, the metadata and source caps — is applied by a tool handler, and a handler is the sixth thing that happens to a request: TCP, ASGI body, json.loads, MCP validation, dispatch, and only then the cap. So the caps bound what is stored and bound nothing about what it costs to arrive. Measured on this transport before the fix, a 64 MiB POST reached the tool surface with all 67,108,864 bytes intact, and it made no difference whether it declared a Content-Length of 64 MiB, a Content-Length of 10, or none at all, because nothing was counting. The SDK buffers the whole body (`await request.body()`) before parsing it, which cost a further 3.25x on a body of conversation turns (1 MiB body -> 3.25 MiB peak, 32 MiB -> 104 MiB), so the process cost is several times the payload and proportional to it without limit. exclude_contents and external_context carry no maxItems and their strings no maxLength, so the JSON-RPC arguments themselves are unbounded too.
issues.note: Found by an external audit of the boundary surfaces, which was right about the cause and specific about what must not count as a fix: a handler-side truncation, a Content-Length check, a len() after parsing, or a reverse proxy. The reason all four are wrong is the same one — each of them reads a number somebody else supplied, or reads it after the cost has already been paid. The baseline above was measured rather than assumed, including the two misdeclaration cases, because 'no limit' and 'a limit nobody reached' are the same picture from outside.
issues.fix_note: RequestBodyBudgetMiddleware sums bytes over ASGI receive() events, so a chunked body and a lying Content-Length are both measured by what arrived. It is mounted inside CORS (a 413 has to carry the headers that let a browser read it) and outside authentication (so it covers everything below it); the position deliberately does not shield an unauthenticated flood, which is refused by the credential check before any body is pulled, and a test pins that a 401 is not turned into a 413. The shipped mode is `warn`: the body is delivered whole and the crossing is logged at the 1st, 10th and 100th occurrence. That is the 2.5.x half of this on purpose — a cap that refuses before anyone has measured an operator's real payload distribution is a cap set by guessing, and warning first makes a wrong number cost a log line instead of an outage. `reject` (413, stops reading) is written, mounted and tested now so the release that turns it on changes a default rather than adding a code path. The 4 MiB default is measured, not chosen: the largest possible single store is 144 KB and a recall_with_context of 200 turns x 2000 chars is 407 KB. Tests drive the assembled app rather than the class (a middleware never mounted is indistinguishable from one never written) and 8 mutations are caught, each by its own test; the eighth was added after a survivor showed the fixture, not the assertion, was blind — with 1 KiB chunks, deleting the abort after the 413 changes nothing, and only a single oversized chunk separates 'the application never sees it' from 'the application receives and parses it'. Not fixed here and left to the line that may break the tool contract: maxItems / maxLength on exclude_contents and external_context, which would refuse payloads accepted today.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) A non-string value on a declared external_context field was fatal for `timestamp` and silently wrong for `name` and `user_id`. `do_recall_with_context` read all three with a bare `entry.get(...)`, so whatever the caller sent went straight on: a `timestamp` that was not a string reached `_parse_timestamp_utc`, which calls `.replace` on its argument and catches only ValueError and OSError, so an epoch integer raised AttributeError out of the entire call — the recall hits and every well-formed entry beside it were lost to one malformed neighbour. `name` and `user_id` reached the response verbatim, so `source.name` could be a dict and `source.id` could be the f-string interpolation of one (`discord:{'a': 1}`), an identity the caller never sent. An explicit JSON null on `timestamp` was emitted as `null` where every other message carries a string. This is the third instance of the class bug-035 settled for `content` and bug-163 for `role`; these three fields were never revisited because the schema did not admit they were read (bug-292).
issues.note: Found by measuring the fields an external audit reported as undeclared, rather than by reading the declaration against the handler. The declaration mismatch was the reported finding; the crash was underneath it and is the more expensive half. Recorded before the fix as the behaviour scenarios `rwc-untyped-timestamp-aborts` (raised: AttributeError, result: null) and `rwc-untyped-identity-fields`, so the change is reviewed as a diff against a measured baseline.
issues.fix_note: `_ctx_string` reads a declared field and falls back to that field's own default when the value is present but not a string — the same answer `_ctx_content` gives for a non-string `content`, and the same value an absent key already produced, so the malformed case lands where the missing case sat. Deliberately not `str()` coercion, which is what `_ctx_role` does: that coercion exists so the C13 disclosure can name the bad role, whereas these three are consumed — coercing invents an identity for `source.id` and a position in the chronology for `timestamp`. The report in `context_field_issues` names the field instead of guessing the value.

issues.summary: (LOW) The `external_context` item schema declared `role` and `content` while the handler read `name`, `user_id` and `timestamp` as well. The three were named only in the array's free-text description, which no client validates against and no generated type carries, so a caller working from the schema had no statement that a timestamp was consulted at all — and an entry sent without one merges into the undated group ahead of every dated message, which reads as a turn that happened first. bug-163 had already closed the same gap for `role` and `content` after the item shape was advertised in prose only; the other three were left behind.
issues.pattern: Every declared field is a string
issues.note: Reported by an external audit of the boundary surfaces. `additionalProperties: false` is deliberately NOT part of the fix: closing the object would refuse payloads that work today, which is a break the declaration gap does not justify. Callers do send their own bookkeeping alongside these fields, and the scenario `rwc-untyped-identity-fields` records an undeclared key being accepted so that stays an assertion rather than an assumption.
issues.fix_note: The three fields are declared with their types and their meaning, including what an entry without a timestamp does. Enforcement of the declared shape ships in the same release but off: CPERSONA_EXTERNAL_CONTEXT_MODE is `warn` by default (report and read the field as absent) with `reject` written, mounted and tested beside it, so turning it on is a change of default rather than a code path written under release pressure.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) A caller-supplied `timestamp` was stored verbatim with no policy on how far ahead of the server's clock it could be, and the confidence curve reads `max(0.0, now - timestamp)` — so a stamp in the future was scored as the age of a row written this instant, and it could not decay, because tomorrow it was still ahead. The larger half is what one such row does to its neighbours: the corpus span is MIN/MAX over the column and it scales the decay RATE, so a single row stamped 2099 widens the span and flattens the time axis for the whole scope. Measured on a four-row corpus of honestly dated rows, the quality gate admitted one; adding one row stamped 2099 admitted all five, including the three-week-old row that had not previously made the gate. Reachable from client clock skew, an import with a wrong century, a timezone applied twice, or any caller that names its own time.
issues.note: Reported by an external audit of the boundary surfaces. The shipping default is the face that matters and it is not the same face: CPERSONA_CONFIDENCE_ENABLED is false by default and scope_stats issues the MIN/MAX span only when it is true, so on a default install a future stamp reaches no scoring arithmetic at all. Both faces were recorded in the behaviour golden BEFORE the change (corpus-future-*), because a face nobody looks at passes by not being looked at. The allowance is a range rather than an instant because a caller's clock is not this one: the stamp is generated on another host and arrives after a network hop. 300 seconds was chosen from measurement, not from what sounds safe — on this project's deployment no row of 3,228 is ahead of the clock at all, and the observed skew between a writing host and the server is 0.12s including the round trip.
issues.fix_note: Detection is one function, `utils.future_timestamp_issue`, with `utils.future_timestamp_boundary` for callers that must compare in SQL; a structural gate keeps the allowance readable in one module so no seam grows its own copy. Enforcement ships in the same release but off: CPERSONA_FUTURE_TIMESTAMP_MODE is `warn` by default (store the row, report it in the log and in the write's own answer) with `reject` written, mounted and tested beside it, so turning it on changes a default rather than adding a code path. `import_memories` reports and imports in every mode — an export must come back exactly as it left, and refusing there would make the round trip lossy for the rows most worth inspecting. For rows already stored, the `future_timestamp` health check reports them and `fix=true` restores each from its own `created_at`, the insertion time the row still carries honestly, leaving locked rows and rows whose created_at is itself ahead untouched. The boundary is computed in Python and passed into the SQL rather than taken from `datetime('now')`, because SQL's clock is a second clock that no caller can inject: a predicate written against it answers differently in December than in January for the same rows and the same code.

issues.summary: (LOW) `_compute_confidence` still clamps a future timestamp's age to zero — `age_hours = max(0.0, (now - parsed).total_seconds() / 3600)` — so a row already stored with a stamp ahead of the clock is scored as one written this instant for as long as it stays there. bug-293 stops new ones at the write seam and gives `check_health` a way to find and repair the ones already stored, but the scoring path itself still has no answer for a stamp it is handed. `episodes.start_time` reaches the same arithmetic through `utils.episode_timestamp`, and `_derive_episode_row` takes it as `min()` over the caller's history stamps, so an episode whose whole history is ahead of the clock lands there too.
issues.note: Deferred deliberately, and not because it is hard. Changing what age a future stamp is scored at is a change to the scoring semantics, which is the axis the pre-release ladder is meant to keep readable: a soak cannot tell 'the behaviour changed' from 'the behaviour broke' while two scoring changes are in flight. The same reasoning already holds bug-247 for the 2.6 scoring line, and this belongs beside it. It is also the smaller half now: on a default install the clamp is unreachable (confidence off means the span is never computed), the write seam refuses new rows once the mode is flipped, and the health check names and repairs the rows already stored. What remains uncovered is a row an operator chooses not to repair, and an episode start_time — for which there is no check yet.

issues.summary: (LOW) Nothing in the package normalises Unicode, so identity is byte equality after `strip().lower()`: a Japanese string written precomposed and the same string written with a combining dakuten are two different memories. They are two rows (the dedup UNIQUE index sees different bytes), two FTS entries — measured, not assumed: FTS5's `unicode61` tokenizer performs no canonical composition, so a composed query returns zero hits against a decomposed row — and an `exclude_contents` entry in one spelling excludes neither the other. The reachable sources are the ones a published package has no control over: a macOS client, an IME, a paste, an import.
issues.note: Reported by an external audit of the boundary surfaces, and the ruling was to measure the production corpus before designing anything — which changed the answer. Measured 2026-09-05: all 3,234 memories, all 3,234 msg_ids, all 657 episode summaries and all 657 keyword rows are ALREADY NFC, and no dedup key would newly collide under NFC, NFD, NFKC or NFKD. The defect is latent, not live. For contrast on the same corpus, NFKC would move 478 rows (14.8%) — fullwidth parentheses, circled digits, the ellipsis, the micro sign — which is why NFKC is not the canonical-identity question: it folds characters an author chose. A separate axis, casefold() vs lower(), differs on 12 rows and all of them for U+00B5 alone, changing no dedup key.
issues.fix_note: PARTIAL, deliberately. 2.5.x ships the detector only: `deep_unnormalized_content` is a report-only deep check that counts rows not in NFC across memories and episodes, names the codepoints composition would remove, and reports `complete: false` past its scan cap. It repairs nothing, because a repair would rewrite stored text and the canonical form has to live BESIDE the original — that is a column, and this line preserves the schema. The canonical_identity column, and with it dedup and exclude comparing on it, belongs to the release that can take a migration. The identity rule as it stands is recorded in the behaviour golden first (store-canonically-equivalent-pair, corpus-unnormalized-*), so the release that changes it has a baseline that was not written after the fact.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Nothing reported a file the package placed earlier and left group/world-readable. bug-289 made every NEW path owner-only and deliberately did not chmod the ones already on disk -- an existing file's mode belongs to the operator who set it -- so an install that upgraded keeps its 0644 corpus, which is the state the reference deployment was measured in. The only thing that said so was a boot warning over the database alone: one path, once per start, into a log. The -wal beside it holds the rows not yet checkpointed, the calibration sidecar decides recall breadth, the alias ledger decides whose memory space a caller reaches, and the contiguous index holds an embedding of every row; none of them was read by anything. That same warning also had no platform guard, so on a target where the mode is not the access control it would fire on every boot of every install and advise a chmod that changes nothing.
issues.note: The residual of bug-289, registered separately because the ruling that creates it is deliberate: not touching an existing mode is correct, and the gap is that nothing SAYS what those modes are. Found while closing that gap, not by a new report. Two things the work measured rather than assumed: every path the package places lands at 0600/0700 under umask 000, 022, 077 and 002, so a check reading them cannot record the runner's umask; and an export goes to a path its CALLER chooses, so it stays out of reach of any list the package can build -- named in owned_paths' docstring rather than left as a silent hole.
issues.fix_note: fileperms.owned_paths() names every path the package places, asked of the module that places each one so moving a file moves the list with it, and checks.check_file_permissions reports the ones a local account can reach. warn, fix_capable: fix narrows a file to 0600 and never widens one, which is consistent with the bug-289 ruling because that ruling is about what a version bump does unasked, and this runs because an operator asked for repairs -- said on every finding's hint. Directories are reported and never chmod-ed: a 0600 file inside a 0755 directory is still unreadable, and the directory can hold files the package did not place. A directory-only finding declares repairable 0, so the registry's de-escalation rule stops it gating. The whole check, and the boot warning, decline where fileperms.mode_bits_are_enforced() is false. Golden recorded the blind answer first (perms-corpus-private / perms-corpus-group-world-readable were identical before the check existed); five mutations were run against the detector and all five were caught, one of which first exposed that the platform test crashed pytest's reporting instead of failing.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The OAuth metadata and key-set fetches cap the document they accept, not the bytes they receive. _http_get returns response.content, so httpx has already buffered the whole body by the time the MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES check runs on len(body) -- the cap decides what is parsed and trusted, and the allocation it was meant to bound has already happened. The size is chosen by whoever answers at the configured issuer or JWKS URI, which is precisely the party OAuth verification exists to survive. Bounded in practice by three things worth naming so the severity is judgeable: the origin is operator-configured rather than caller-supplied, a refetch is floored at JWKS_MIN_REFETCH_SECONDS (60s), and the request carries a timeout.
issues.fix_sketch: Stream the response (client.stream) and accumulate with an early abort once the running total passes MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES, so the refusal happens before the allocation rather than after it. The declared Content-Length can be refused first on the server's own word, but it cannot be relied on alone -- it may be absent or false, which is the same reasoning the HTTP request-body budget already uses on the inbound side.
issues.note: The inbound mirror of this is already solved: RequestBodyBudgetMiddleware counts bytes at the ASGI receive() events rather than trusting a header. This entry is the outbound direction, which that work did not cover. Related: the embedding client has the same shape on its own receive path (bug-298).
issues.fix_note: _http_get reads the body through client.stream and stops once the running total passes MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES, so the bound moved from what the fetch agrees to PARSE to what it agrees to RECEIVE. It stops one byte past the cap rather than at it: the caller refuses on len(body) > MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES, and a read that halted exactly at the cap would hand that check a silently truncated document to pass and json.loads to reject as a parse error -- the wrong diagnosis for an oversized answer. Declared Content-Length is not consulted; it may be absent or untrue, which is the same reasoning the inbound request-body budget already uses. The test drives the real seam against a transport streaming eight times the cap and asserts on the bytes the generator was ASKED for, not on the returned length: a buffered read that trims afterwards returns the same length having received all of it. Reverting to response.content was measured and fails that test.

issues.summary: (LOW) The embedding client's response budget bounds parsing, not receiving. _parse_within_budget refuses an oversized body before json() turns it into a much larger Python object graph, and it checks the received length as well as the declared one -- but httpx has already buffered the body by the time it runs, so max_response_bytes cannot bound the receive-side allocation. The limit is documented in the function's own docstring rather than tracked, which is why it is recorded here: an accepted limit that lives only in a docstring is indistinguishable from one nobody noticed.
issues.pattern: httpx has already buffered the body
issues.fix_sketch: Streaming the response bounds the receive side, but it changes the request path, which the docstring already states as the reason it was not done. Decide rather than patch: the backend is an operator-configured service and the default budget is 64 MiB, so the question is whether that origin is in the threat model at all.
issues.note: This file is vendored. A change here is not local: it needs the canonical package bumped, re-vendoring here, and the other consumers carried along, so the cost is a different class from a fix inside this package. Same shape as bug-297, which is local by comparison.

issues.summary: (LOW) archive_episode lost the whole episode when `history` mixed timestamp types. The span was computed as min()/max() over `msg.get('timestamp')` with no normalisation, so one epoch int or dict beside one ISO string raised TypeError out of the entire call -- and it raised BEFORE the embed and the INSERT, so nothing was written. The write-side sibling of bug-291, which fixed the same shape on the read side (recall_with_context) and left this one standing. Homogeneous non-string stamps did not raise, which is worse in its own way: they were stored as an int in a column every other row fills with an ISO string, producing a span that cannot be compared with its neighbours.
issues.note: Adjudicated CONFIRMED-mech / LOW in the 2026-07-29 audit as rega-1 and left unregistered. Re-measured at the b1 branch point: half of it was gone (bug-291 closed the recall side in 2.5.12a3) and this half reproduced live, so only the surviving half is filed.
issues.fix_note: `_ctx_string` reads a non-string stamp as absent, which is the ruling bug-291 already made for the read side -- a value that is not a string names no instant, and coercing one invents a position in the chronology. Deliberately NOT reported in the response the way recall_with_context reports context_field_issues: that would be a new response field, which a fix release does not add. MEASURED DELTA, per input class, against the shipped pre-release rather than reasoned about -- because one of the three classes changes rather than restores, and that is worth stating before anyone is surprised by it. (1) A history whose stamps are all ISO strings, the declared and documented use, is BYTE-IDENTICAL: the span is the same two values. (2) A history mixing an epoch int with an ISO string used to raise TypeError out of the whole call, before the embed and the INSERT, losing the episode; it now answers, and the span comes from the stamps that name an instant. That half is the restoration. (3) A history whose stamps are ALL epoch ints used to store the digits verbatim -- start_time '1772000000' -- and now stores NULL. That half is a change, not a restoration, and it would not be freeze-eligible under a frozen line. It was accepted on three grounds: the field has been declared a string since bug-292, so an int is outside the published contract; what it stored was digits in a column every other row fills with an ISO stamp, and SQLite compares that column byte by byte, so the value sorted wrongly against every neighbour it was compared with -- the defect class bug-286 records; and the release this lands in is feature-bearing on other grounds, so the line does not need this change to be restoration-only. The narrower alternative -- stop the TypeError and keep storing the digits -- was considered and declined, because it means deliberately continuing to ship a value known to sort incorrectly.

issues.summary: (LOW) The cosine backfill checked a stored blob's WIDTH and not its values, so a correctly sized embedding holding a NaN multiplied through to `_cosine = nan`, and from there into match_reason and confidence as a bare NaN -- a token RFC 8259 does not admit as a number, emitted by the one branch that exists to give these rows a real similarity signal. 2.5.12a2 added a write-seam guard (pack_for_storage refuses a non-finite embedding) and a health check that reports the ones already stored, but neither reaches the READ side, which is where a blob written by an older version or by import_memories' embedding_b64 arrives.
issues.note: Adjudicated CONFIRMED-mech / LOW in the 2026-07-29 audit as hotpath-3. Re-measured live at the b1 branch point rather than read off the report -- a same-width NaN blob was inserted and the backfill driven, producing `_cosine = nan` that json.dumps(allow_nan=False) rejects.
issues.fix_note: The width filter also asks vector.stored_blob_is_finite -- the same helper the health check asks, deliberately, so the read side and the maintenance side cannot come to disagree about what finite means. A row that fails it keeps _cosine=None alongside the others this backfill cannot serve (no blob, foreign width, profile sentinel), which is the branch it already sat on before b2 introduced the backfill. The test carries a finite control row, so the None is evidence about the guard rather than about a backfill that did nothing.

issues.summary: (LOW) The cosine backfill's id lookup built one `IN (...)` of whatever length the result set happened to be, while its sibling vector._fetch_rows_by_id splits the same kind of query at _ID_FETCH_CHUNK. Both read the same two tables by id on the same recall, so the bound belongs to the pair; the one without it was bounded only by how many rows a caller asked for, which the library layer lets reach RECALL_LIBRARY_MAX_LIMIT. Measured rather than assumed: the bound-variable ceiling is 250000 on the deployed host and 32766 locally, so this is an asymmetry between two functions rather than a reachable crash.
issues.note: Adjudicated CONFIRMED-mech / LOW in the 2026-07-29 audit as V-in-unchunked. The severity rests on a measurement, so it is written down here: at the default limits no SQLite this ships against refuses the statement, and the entry exists because two functions doing the same thing disagreed about their own bound.
issues.fix_note: The chunk width is imported from vector._ID_FETCH_CHUNK rather than chosen again, so the pair cannot drift apart the way they already had. The test drives 2 * _ID_FETCH_CHUNK + 1 ids and asserts both the statement count and that no row lost its cosine -- chunking that silently drops the tail would otherwise pass a count-only check.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The mutation-waiver verifier never checked a waiver against itself. verify() called neither fingerprint() nor survivor_fingerprint(), and _code_present only asserted that SOME line in the declared file still hashed to the declared code_context_hash -- so a `fingerprint` copied from another survivor, hand-edited, or left behind when the location was retargeted was accepted with zero problems reported. The fingerprint is what the runner matches a LIVE survivor against, so a wrong one silently suppresses a survivor other than the one the entry documents and a human approved: the registry's whole promise is that it does not silently rot.
issues.note: Adjudicated CONFIRMED-mech / LOW in the 2026-07-29 audit as rel-7 and filed here at MEDIUM instead: what the mechanism defeats is an approval gate, and an approval that attaches to the wrong subject is not a small version of an approval. Reproduced live before fixing -- the shipped waiver's fingerprint was replaced with one belonging to a different line and verify() returned [].
issues.fix_note: _code_present is now a thin wrapper over _waived_line, which returns the matched line TEXT; verify() recomputes the fingerprint that this waiver's own declared file / definition / operator and that line produce, and reports a hard fingerprint_mismatch when the declared value differs. Every input was already on the waiver, so the check needs nothing the registry does not carry. A waiver whose code has moved on has no line to recompute from, so it gets the one finding that is true (code_changed) and not a second, misleading one -- asserted as its own test so the guard cannot be satisfied by reporting everything.

issues.summary: (LOW) mutation-diff.py's docstring and the CI job's comment both asserted the script ALWAYS exits 0, and it does not: two SystemExit sites abort non-zero on a config the script cannot honour (a git-filter branch it cannot rewrite, a config with no test-command). Failing loud there is correct -- diffing against the wrong ref would publish a number that looks measured and is not -- so the false half was the claim. What actually keeps the lane non-blocking is the job's continue-on-error, and an invariant asserted only in a docstring is the kind a reader trusts and a maintainer then quietly breaks.
issues.pattern: ALWAYS exits 0, and it does not
issues.note: Adjudicated CONFIRMED-mech / LOW in the 2026-07-29 audit as rel-2, which paired the false claim with a second half -- a crash produced neither a report nor a signal. Re-measured at the b1 branch point: that half is CLOSED (the workflow gained a step that writes did-not-complete to the summary when no report exists), so only the claim is filed.
issues.fix_note: Both places now say what is true and name what actually buys the non-blocking property, so the two are not conflated again. No behaviour changed: making the claim true instead would have meant swallowing the two aborts, which is the outcome the aborts exist to prevent.

issues.summary: (LOW) A bulk remote index push reported partial synchronisation as success. remote_index_upsert returns None, sent each 128-item chunk in a try/except that routed every exception to logger.debug -- off in any normal deployment -- and never read the response status at all, so a service answering HTTP 500 to half the chunks counted as a full push. import_memories returns ok:true either way, which is correct (a failed index is not a failed import) and is exactly why the log was the only place the shortfall could appear: rows that are in the database and not in the index answer recalls with silence, and silence is the one symptom that does not look like a fault.
issues.note: Adjudicated CONFIRMED-mech / LOW in the 2026-07-29 audit as schema-1, a sibling of bug-146/159. Scope was deliberately narrowed when it was fixed: reporting the shortfall in the import_memories RESPONSE would add a response field, which a fix release in a frozen line does not do. It stays a log-level change.
issues.fix_note: Non-2xx is counted as a failure alongside the exception path, every chunk is still attempted, and the shortfall is said once at WARNING naming the namespace, the chunk and item counts, and the consequence. Both failure modes are tested (status and exception) and so is the silent case, so the warning means something when it appears; the test also asserts a failing chunk does not stop the ones after it.

issues.summary: (LOW) do_update_memory's copy of the local-blob write gate was unexercised. do_store's gate is pinned (bug-192) but admin_handlers has its own binding of VECTOR_SEARCH_MODE / STORE_BLOB and its own call, and nothing drove it: pinning STORE_BLOB to a literal there -- local_blobs_stored(VECTOR_SEARCH_MODE, True), the exact shape of the historical defect bug-182 -- was measured to leave the whole suite green. The only test that caught the cruder mutation of deleting the call was a source-inspection gate, which reads the module text and not the behaviour.
issues.note: Adjudicated CONFIRMED-mech / LOW in the 2026-07-29 audit as teeth-4. Filed on the test file rather than the source, because the defect IS the missing detector and an entry anchored to the unchanged production line would never go stale.
