issues.fix_note: Two tests drive the real do_update_memory under remote/STORE_BLOB=false and remote/STORE_BLOB=true. The row is seeded WITH a blob first, so the NULL is not inherited from a row that never had one, and the positive counterpart proves the same fixture writes a blob when the policy allows it -- without which the negative assertion would also pass against a broken embedder. Checked against the literal-pinning mutation that motivated it: with these present it fails.

issues.summary: (LOW) The gate on pause_persistence's description checks that it is COMPLETE and says so in its own comment -- every handler consulting is_paused() must be named -- but nothing checked that it is TRUE. Inverting the blast-radius sentence, so the text claims a keyless pause reaches nobody else when in fact every keyless caller shares one bucket, left the whole suite green: the tool names were untouched, so the completeness gate had nothing to say. A tool description is the only contract an MCP caller reads, and this one tells an operator what a no-persist window actually covers.
issues.note: Adjudicated CONFIRMED-mech / LOW in the 2026-07-29 audit as rega-4. Truth is not mechanically checkable in general, which is what the original gate's comment says; this particular claim is, because the two scope strings it names are decided by session._scope and can be read back.
issues.fix_note: The new gate pairs each scope value with the key that produces it: both must appear in the description, the 'Omit it and ...' sentence must name the keyless one, and must NOT name the keyed one. Pairing is what an inversion breaks while leaving both words present, and both halves are asserted so the swap is caught in either direction. It also asserts the two scopes still differ, so the gate fails loudly rather than passing vacuously if the implementation stops distinguishing them.

issues.summary: (LOW) store's `content` schema description states the refusal contract -- empty or sanitizes-to-empty content is refused with ok:false, result:'rejected' -- and nothing pinned it to the handler that decides whether that is true. The wording was corrected once (bug-162, when the guard was reading the raw value) and then left unguarded: rewriting it to say the opposite, that empty content is accepted and stored as an empty row, was measured against the full suite and passed. A false tool description is not a documentation problem; it is the published behaviour disagreeing with the real one, discovered by the caller.
issues.note: Adjudicated CONFIRMED-mech / LOW in the 2026-07-29 audit as rega-5.
issues.fix_note: The gate drives do_store with whitespace-only content, asserts the refusal it actually gets, and then asserts the description names the two tokens a caller branches on (ok:false and result:'rejected'). Driving the handler first is what makes it a check of agreement rather than a spelling test: if the handler stops refusing, the gate fails on that instead of quietly describing something else.

issues.summary: (LOW) The operating-context gate's refusal shape in do_archive_episode_boundary was untested. bug-169 fixed the line -- every other archive_episode failure carries episode_id, and utils.error_response names it as the archetypal field a failure still owes its caller, but the gate refusal dropped it, so a caller reading resp['episode_id'] hit a KeyError on exactly one path -- and the fix was never pinned. Deleting the `"episode_id": None` half of the returned dict was measured against the full suite and passed, which puts the KeyError back with nothing red.
issues.note: Adjudicated CONFIRMED-mech / LOW in the 2026-07-29 audit as rega-6.
issues.fix_note: The test forces the gate to refuse, asserts the underlying handler never ran, and asserts both that the key is PRESENT and that its value is None -- a caller branching on membership and one branching on truthiness both have to survive the refusal, and only the membership half fails when the key is dropped.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) verify-issues.sh reported success on a registry it could not read. Malformed JSON already aborted, but a file that PARSES with the wrong shape did not: data.get('issues', []) returned the same empty list for a missing key, a mistyped key and a wrong type, and the run printed a no-issues summary and exited 0. A registry of 298 entries silently becoming 0 is the shape of a truncated or half-written file, and this script is named by RELEASE_LIFECYCLE_STANDARD as part of the release gate -- so the whole freeze-to-certification path rests on it being honest about what it could not check.
issues.note: Raised as a proposal and approved before implementation, since the script is read-only infrastructure. The reported reproduction -- broken JSON exits 0 -- did NOT reproduce at the b1 branch point: json.load raises and the assignment runs under set -e. Re-measuring found the real shape underneath it, which is the structurally-wrong-but-valid registry, and that is what is filed here.
issues.fix_note: The emitter refuses a non-object root, a missing issues key and a non-list issues, each with its own message, and a registry that parses to zero records is an error rather than a clean bill of health. The counterpart is asserted too: --filter selecting none of a registry that WAS read stays a pass, and its message now names which question got the empty answer -- without that test the fix would make --filter open fail the day the last open issue closes. Six malformed shapes are parametrised on the exit code, because the message is for a human and the exit code is what CI reads.

issues.summary: (HIGH) check_health(fix=true) is authorised against a single agent_id but repairs rows belonging to every agent. The ACL demand for the health tools is one pattern taken from the call's own argument -- `required = PERM_WRITE if args.get("fix") else PERM_READ` (cpersona/acl.py:424-427) -- while one registered repair resolves msg_id collisions under `isolation_where(agent_id=None)`, a deliberate whole-table UPDATE (cpersona/checks.py:1237-1250), and the tool description advertises the repair as agent-scoped (cpersona/server.py:1582). Measured through the guarded handler on a database missing idx_memories_dedup_msg_id: a client granted read-write on exactly one agent had a call naming a second agent refused with permission_denied (so the guard was live and the grant narrow), then called fix=true on the agent it did hold, and the second agent's older duplicate row came back with msg_id blanked. Only the older duplicates of a colliding key lose their id -- the UPDATE keeps the MAX(id) row -- but they are rows the caller holds no grant on at any level, and those callers' later stores no longer dedup on the ids they supplied.
issues.fix_sketch: Either demand the whole table when the requested checks include a cross-agent repair (a wildcard write demand, refused unless the principal holds it everywhere), or scope that repair to the requested agent and leave the remaining collisions to an operator-run pass that is authorised globally. The tool description must then match whichever is chosen.
issues.note: The same call shape from a per_subject tenant using agent_id='@me' was read in source (the boundary at cpersona/acl.py:815-846 admits it because the pattern equals the caller's own alias) and not exercised, so that half is unmeasured.
issues.fix_note: The guard now sizes the fix=true demand to the reach of the write: a selected check whose repair writes rows under every agent (dedup_msg_id_index, declared by Check.cross_agent_fix and derived into CROSS_AGENT_FIX_CHECKS) adds a read-write demand on '*'. checks=[...] that excludes it keeps the narrow agent demand, so an agent-scoped repair still needs only that agent. deep_check was split onto its own _deep_demands and is deliberately NOT escalated -- it reads a different registry whose two fix-capable checks both scope their UPDATE with WHERE agent_id = ?. The tool description now names the exception instead of calling every repair agent-scoped.

issues.summary: (HIGH) verify_token turns two legal token shapes into an unhandled 500 on the unauthenticated path. Only jwt.decode is wrapped (cpersona/oauth.py:216-231); the AccessToken construction at cpersona/oauth.py:266-274 is not, so `scopes=(claims.get("scope") or "").split()` raises AttributeError when an issuer emits `scope` as a JSON array, and `expires_at=claims["exp"]` raises a pydantic ValidationError on the fractional NumericDate that RFC 7519 permits. Both were reproduced against the shipped verifier with real RS256 keys, and the array-scope token was also driven through the assembled ASGI app with the client provisioned in the ACL file: the exception escaped, no http.response.start was ever sent, and the tool mount was never entered -- neither the bearer middleware nor the principal resolver catches it. This contradicts the method's own stated contract, that every rejection returns None because the only correct answers on an unauthenticated request are a verified identity or a 401. A missing scope claim is handled correctly, so the fault is the claim type and not the claim's absence.
issues.fix_sketch: Normalise before constructing: accept a list of strings for `scope` as well as the space-delimited string, coerce a numeric `exp` through int(), and put the construction inside the same guard as the decode so any remaining surprise becomes None (a 401) rather than a traceback.
issues.fix_note: AccessToken construction is inside the try that already governed jwt.decode, so any claim shape the SDK model refuses is a refusal (None) rather than an exception escaping onto the unauthenticated path. The two shapes RFC permits are folded rather than refused: _normalized_scopes reads scope as either the space-delimited string or a JSON array, and _numeric_date_seconds truncates a fractional NumericDate to whole seconds (never later, so it cannot extend a token's life).

issues.summary: (HIGH) Threshold calibration admits a stored blob on width alone, so one non-finite embedding yields a NaN threshold that is reported as success and persisted. `_safe_frombuffer` gates only on `len(blob) % 4` (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:697-711), the NaN propagates through `vecs @ vecs.T` (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:1302), and `round(max(raw, floor), 4)` returns NaN because `floor > nan` is False. Measured with eleven finite vectors plus one all-NaN blob: do_calibrate_threshold answered ok:true, sidecar_persisted:true, null_admit_rate:0.0 and new_threshold NaN, the in-process threshold map held NaN, and the sidecar on disk read `"agent_thresholds": {"probe-nan": NaN}` (json.dump allows NaN by default), so it survives restart. Downstream the NaN floor is not merely strict but inconsistent: the chunked and episode arms filter with `sim_val >= effective_min_sim` and admit nothing, while the streaming arm filters with `sim_val < effective_min_sim` and admits everything. The precondition is a non-finite blob, which the current write seam refuses, so it needs data written by an older version or arriving through import.
issues.fix_sketch: Ask the same finiteness helper the write seam and the health check already use before a blob enters the sample, and refuse to persist or apply a threshold that is not finite -- an ok:false naming the offending rows is more useful than a silently poisoned floor.
issues.note: Neighbouring but distinct from the read-side backfill guard (bug-300, fixed): this is the calibration sample, which decides the floor for every later recall rather than one row's reported cosine. bug-384 is the same missing guard in the deep near-duplicate check.
issues.fix_note: _safe_frombuffer now gates on values as well as width: a right-width blob whose elements are not finite is skipped like a corrupt one, which is what its own contract ('skip the poison row') already said. Both callers are calibration paths (_temporal_adjacency_sims, _sample_embeddings), so the NaN can no longer reach vecs @ vecs.T, the threshold, the in-process map or the sidecar. Verified by mutation: reverting admin_handlers.py alone turns both probe assertions red.

issues.summary: (HIGH) The calibration sample ceiling bounds an allocation an order of magnitude smaller than the one the default method makes. `_separation_threshold` broadcasts the whole null population against 256 candidate thresholds in one array -- `fpr = (null[None, :] >= candidates[:, None]).mean(axis=1)` (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:656-658) -- on top of the similarity matrix and its upper triangle, and the default method is separation. Measured with tracemalloc around the shipped handler on 700 rows: peak 71.0 MB for 244,650 null pairs, i.e. 290 bytes per pair, against the 21-26 bytes per pair the ceiling's own justification was sized with. At the clamped ceiling of 5,000 samples (12,497,500 pairs) that measured rate is 3.6 GB in one call, which is the OOM the sample clamp exists to prevent, reachable from a published tool argument that carries no maximum. The OOM itself was not triggered -- that needs a corpus of that size and several GB to lose -- but the per-pair identity that predicts it is measured rather than read off the code.
issues.fix_sketch: Compute the two rates by sorting the populations once and searching the candidate grid (np.searchsorted), which is O(n log n) time and O(n) memory instead of a 256 x pairs boolean array; then re-derive the sample ceiling from a measurement of the method that actually runs by default.
issues.note: The existing gates on this path only assert the constant stays under 10,000, which cannot see the allocation the constant is supposed to bound.
issues.fix_note: The candidate sweep computes the identical numbers from one sort instead of a (256, len(pop)) boolean broadcast: the count of x >= c on a sorted array is its tail, and NaN is excluded from the search but kept in the denominator so the result matches the comparison for every input (400 randomised trials over duplicates, NaN and +/-inf, 0 mismatches). Measured whole-call peak fell from 290 to 29.0 bytes per null pair, flat from n=700 to n=10,000, so the n=5,000 ceiling now bounds 363 MB rather than 3.6 GB. config.py's ceiling justification was restamped with those measured figures -- the earlier 52/266/982 MB covered the product only, not the triangle and sweep the ceiling also has to bound.

issues.summary: (HIGH) A report-only health run holds the database write lock on the shared read connection, so concurrent writers fail with "database is locked". The FTS integrity probe is spelled as an INSERT into the virtual table (cpersona/checks.py:881); sqlite3 opens an implicit transaction before a statement it classifies as DML and SQLite takes the write lock, and the fix=False path wraps the whole registry in `async with connection()` (cpersona/maintenance_handlers.py:121), whose transaction is only ended at scope exit. Reproduced by pausing the run after that check: both a raw transaction() write and the background queue's enqueue -- the shipped drain entry point -- waited out the 5 s busy_timeout and raised sqlite3.OperationalError, while the health run itself reported status healthy. The window is bounded: it lasts from that check to the end of the run, so it hits writers arriving in that interval rather than unconditionally, and a writer that happens to open a read scope first is spared only because that scope's exit rolls back the health run's transaction.
issues.fix_sketch: Commit or roll back immediately after the FTS integrity probe so the implicit write transaction does not outlive the one check that needed it, rather than widening the scope's lifetime rules; the same probe on the fix=True path is already inside a transaction that ends promptly.
issues.fix_note: The FTS integrity probe writes nothing, so on the report-only path it now hands the implicit transaction back as soon as it has its answer instead of pinning the write lock until the whole run ends. The rollback itself lives in database.py (release_read_probe_transaction) because that module owns the commit/rollback boundary on the shared connection -- routing it through the owner rather than taking a seam waiver, which tests/test_structural_gates.py::test_db_boundary_owned_by_seam caught on the first attempt. Guarded on fix=False: under fix this runs inside transaction(), which is holding real repairs.

issues.summary: (HIGH) check_vector_index measures staleness only as rows past the index watermark, so a deleted indexed row is invisible and the index path returns a short answer. The check counts `id > ? AND embedding IS NOT NULL` and reports nothing when that tail is small (cpersona/checks.py:2319-2335), while the lost-embedding probe it relies on tests only `embedding IS NULL` (cpersona/vector.py:659-675) and therefore cannot see a row that no longer exists. Measured on a 12-row corpus: deleting one indexed row through the shipped delete handler left the health check answering with no findings, and with a saturated window the index path returned 9 rows where the same query with the index file moved aside returned 10 -- the index still scores the deleted id, hydration drops the missing row (cpersona/vector.py:1339-1343), and nothing backfills the tenth. The divergence is permanent until the index is rebuilt.
issues.fix_sketch: Count indexed ids that no longer resolve to a live row, alongside the tail, and let the delete path mark the index stale the way the embedding-clearing path does; hydration already knows which candidates vanished, so it can also over-fetch to refill the window.
issues.note: The deletion counterpart of bug-278 and bug-279, which cover a row gaining and losing its embedding after the build. Distinct seam: those rows still exist and can be probed by predicate, this one cannot.
issues.fix_note: Two halves. Detection: check_vector_index now also counts how many rows the index holds that the database still has, and reports vector_index_rows_missing when that shrank -- the tail count only ever saw staleness that GREW. Correctness: rather than make the recall hot path ask a more expensive question (an early attempt rewrote the lost-embedding probe as a COUNT and broke the partial-index plan tests/test_bug285_probe_bound.py pins), the index path falls back to the scan when hydration returns fewer rows than the index promised -- the branch this design already has for an index that cannot promise the same rows, at the cost of one length comparison on the healthy path. Applied to the episode path too, which had the same shape.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The index's exact tail read encodes each row's created_at as ASCII to compare it against a fixed-width column -- `t_created = tail[j][1].encode("ascii")` (cpersona/vector.py:960) -- and the rows the tail exists to serve are exactly the ones the index could not spell, so a non-ASCII created_at is guaranteed to arrive there and raise. Both the tail read and the merge sit outside every guard in the phase (cpersona/vector.py:632, 645), which end at line 610, so the UnicodeEncodeError escapes into recall rather than falling back to the live scan the module's own contract promises. Reproduced with three canonical rows plus one whose stamp ends in a non-ASCII byte: the index built and excluded that row as expected, then a search raised UnicodeEncodeError out of the merge, and every recall for that agent fails identically for as long as the index file exists. Reachability is import-only -- the import path binds a caller-supplied created_at verbatim -- and that half was read in source rather than driven, which is why this is MEDIUM and not HIGH.
issues.fix_sketch: Encode with a total codec (errors are not exceptional here, the value is a sort key) and extend the guard that already wraps the lost-embedding probe over the tail read and the merge, so any surprise on this path degrades to the live scan instead of failing the call.
issues.fix_note: The sort key is encoded with a total codec, and the tail read and merge now sit inside the same fallback guard as the rest of the phase. utf-8 agrees with ASCII on every byte of a canonical stamp so no row already served moves, and a surprise on the one path that reads the rows the index deliberately excluded degrades to the live scan the module promises instead of escaping into recall.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The contiguous index resolves the source axis case-sensitively -- `str(v).startswith(source_id)` (cpersona/vector_index.py:686) -- while every SQL path it stands in for filters with `json_extract(source, '$.id') LIKE ?`, and SQLite's LIKE is ASCII case-insensitive by default. That inverts the one-directional obligation the module and the design doc both state, that the index may offer more than the authority admits but never less. Measured with two rows whose source ids differ only in case: the SQL predicate admitted both, select() offered one, and the containment assertion failed. The split is visible inside a single answer, because the tail read carries the case-insensitive clause, so rows written after the build are returned while identical rows written before it are not. The designated inclusion check cannot catch this: its corpus and its probes are all lowercase, so the case axis has no variance and containment holds vacuously on the broken code.
issues.fix_sketch: Fold both sides for the ASCII range before comparing, matching what LIKE does, and give the inclusion check variance on the case axis so it can fail; the containment direction means over-offering is safe, so folding is the conservative choice.
issues.note: Read-side sibling of bug-336, which is the same case-folding divergence on the SQL LIKE used for per-user source filtering; this entry is the index's mirror of that predicate, not the predicate itself.
issues.fix_note: Settled on the case-sensitive side rather than by folding both: the permissive half was the SQL authority, and folding would have kept a recall scoped to one principal returning another's rows. See bug-336 for the predicate. The second half of this entry is closed here: the designated inclusion check had no variance on the case axis, so containment held vacuously on the broken code. Its corpus now carries both spellings, and reverting the predicate to the folding form makes it red -- measured.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The recall-count read binds one host parameter per result id with no chunk bound: `SELECT id, recall_count, last_recalled_at FROM memories WHERE id IN ({placeholders})` (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:1174-1179), and its width comes from the fused result list before truncation, not from the caller's limit. Its sibling on the same pass was chunked at the shared id-fetch bound on the stated ground that a statement's width must not track how many rows a caller asked for; this one was left. Measured with a recording proxy: 1001 results produced one statement binding 1001 parameters, and driven against real SQLite the same call with 32776 results raised OperationalError: too many SQL variables out of a code path that sits inside no guard, aborting the whole recall. On any SQLite older than 3.32 the ceiling is 999 and ordinary library limits reach it. One sub-claim of the report is wrong and is not carried here: the recall-count UPDATE binds at most `limit`, because truncation happens before its id list is built, and it is guarded, so it degrades to a silent stop of the recall-count feedback rather than an error.
issues.pattern: for start in range\(0, len\(mem_ids\), vector\._ID_FETCH_CHUNK\)
issues.fix_sketch: Loop the read at the same id-fetch chunk its sibling uses and merge the partial rows, so both statements on this pass carry the bound the pair shares.
issues.fix_note: The recall-count read is chunked at vector._ID_FETCH_CHUNK, the width its sibling on the same pass already used; the partial rows are merged. Its width came from the fused result list before truncation, so it tracked how many rows a caller asked for rather than a bound anyone reasoned about. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py records the host-parameter count of every statement the scoring pass issues and pins both the per-statement bound and that the chunks cover every id.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The per-scope statistics cache is a process-global dict keyed by the caller-supplied agent/project/channel triple with no cap and no eviction (cpersona/scope_stats.py:86, 225). Expiry is a freshness test at read time, so a stale entry is recomputed and re-stamped under the same key rather than removed, and the clear() helper has no caller outside tests -- while every recall reaches this map unconditionally (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:1357). Measured: 500 calls with distinct caller-supplied project and channel values left 500 entries, and 2000 distinct triples traced 788,744 bytes, about 394 bytes each. The three sibling per-process maps keyed the same way are all bounded at 256 for precisely this reason, each with a comment saying the key space is client-supplied. In a single-process streamable deployment a client that varies channel per conversation grows this for the life of the process, with no cap, no eviction and no operator-visible signal.
issues.pattern: _cache: dict\[tuple\[str \| None, str \| None, str \| None\], _Entry\] = \{\}
issues.fix_sketch: Bound it like its siblings -- an LRU capped at the same order of magnitude, evicting on insert -- since a scope that has not been asked about recently is exactly the entry whose recomputation costs least.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The JWKS TTL bounds refetching but not acceptance, so a revoked signing key keeps verifying tokens for as long as the provider is unreachable. `_signing_key` computes freshness (cpersona/oauth.py:309) and uses it only to decide whether to attempt a refresh; after a failed refresh it falls through to `return entry.keys.get(kid)` (cpersona/oauth.py:319-320) whatever the age of the entry, and a failed refresh leaves both the keys and their fetch time untouched. The refresh helper's own docstring promises the opposite, that the keys already held keep working until they age out, and nothing ages them out. Measured with an injected clock and real RSA-signed tokens: with the key set and the metadata endpoint both answering 503, a key removed upstream was still accepted at simulated cache ages of 2, 24 and 168 hours against a one-hour TTL, while a successful-refresh control correctly rejected it. Only the cache clock was advanced -- token expiry is still checked against real time, so this is stale-key acceptance and not acceptance of expired tokens.
issues.pattern: if not entry\.keys or \(self\._now\(\) - entry\.fetched_at\) >= JWKS_TTL_SECONDS:
issues.fix_sketch: Apply the freshness bound to the answer as well as to the fetch: past some multiple of the TTL, refuse rather than serve a key set that could not be revalidated. The grace window has to be a deliberate number, because refusing at exactly the TTL turns a brief provider hiccup into an outage.
issues.note: The existing outage test advances the clock only past the minimum refetch interval, so nothing pins behaviour beyond the TTL.
issues.fix_note: The freshness bound now governs the answer as well as the fetch: after the refresh attempt, a key set whose last successful fetch is older than JWKS_TTL_SECONDS is refused instead of served. That is the age-out the refresh helper docstring already promised and nothing implemented, so no new grace constant was introduced -- the horizon is the one the module already names for reuse. Pinned in tests/test_oauth_verification.py alongside the test that keys already held survive a short outage; removing the guard turns all three age parametrisations red. Re-anchored in the same series: the bug-338 lock restructure moved this guard into _from_cache, which is now the single place the cache is answered from, so the age-out applies both before a refresh is attempted and after it.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The recall precision setting is read from the environment with no trim and no membership check -- `os.environ.get("CPERSONA_RECALL_PRECISION", "balanced").lower()` (cpersona/config.py:597) -- and consumed through a dict lookup whose default silently returns the balanced weight. The module already owns a choice parser written for this exact shape, which trims, validates and warns, and uses it for the settings just above. Measured against real configuration: 'strict ' with a trailing space and the unrecognised 'high' both resolved to the balanced weight with no setting-specific warning, and the readback handler reported the precision as balanced because it re-derives the label from the applied weight -- so the response cannot distinguish an operator who asked for balanced from one whose strict setting was discarded. The same enum is refused loudly at the tool surface, which leaves the environment as the one door that accepts a bad value. The change in admitted matches on a real corpus was not measured.
issues.fix_sketch: Read it through the existing choice parser with the three legal values, so an unreadable setting falls back to the documented default and says so in the log.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The alias ledger writes its file with a bare os.fchmod (cpersona/aliases.py:184) instead of going through the permissions helper, which guards the identical call because the attribute does not exist on Windows and the package ships as OS-independent. Reproduced by removing the attribute: the first sign-in raised AttributeError rather than the module's own error type, so the `except OSError` rollback did not run, the in-memory alias stayed live, the descriptor and the temp file leaked, and the immediately following call was authorised under an alias that had never been written to disk. That inverts the contract the module states -- a persist failure at issuance must refuse the request, because an alias that authorised a write but was not durably recorded is re-rolled on restart and strands whatever the write stored. With the call failing as EPERM instead, which is what a filesystem that cannot honour the mode gives, both attempts refused and the alias was rolled back correctly, but two descriptors still leaked. The chmod is also redundant: a file created through mkstemp is already private by contract.
issues.fix_sketch: Call the permissions helper, which already returns quietly where the attribute is absent, and close the descriptor in a finally so neither failure mode leaks one.
issues.note: Native Windows was not exercised; the absence of the attribute was simulated. The non-OSError escape is shared with bug-348, which is the same handler seen from the caller's side.
issues.fix_note: The mode now goes through the package permissions helper, which returns quietly where os.fchmod does not exist (Windows) and logs a filesystem that cannot honour it; the helper lost its underscore because it has a second caller now. The descriptor is closed in a finally unless os.fdopen took ownership, and the temp-file cleanup catches BaseException rather than OSError, so neither failure mode leaks a descriptor or a file. Measured with the attribute removed: the issuance now succeeds and the ledger is readable by a fresh instance; with the helper made to raise, the refusal leaves no temp file behind.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Four remote-index side-effect posts discard the HTTP response entirely and log only at debug, the shape that was removed from the bulk push but not from its siblings. In do_delete_memory, do_update_memory, the agent purge and do_delete_episode (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:362-367, 444-452, 579-584, 2003-2008) none binds the return value of the post, so only an exception is noticed, and the debug line is off in any normal deployment. Measured against all four handlers with HTTP 500, HTTP 401 and a connection error: every call reached its endpoint, committed its local change, answered ok:true, and produced no warning in all twelve cases. The consequence is named in the code's own comment on one of these paths -- an orphaned remote vector keeps surfacing in remote-mode recall, spending top-K slots until the by-id rehydrate finds nothing -- and for the update path the index keeps serving pre-edit text against a post-edit row. Downstream recall degradation itself was not measured.
issues.fix_sketch: Give these the treatment the bulk push already has: read status_code, count a non-2xx as a failure alongside the exception, and say it once at WARNING naming the namespace and the row -- the local change stays committed either way, which is why the log is the only place the divergence can appear.
issues.note: The bulk push counterpart is bug-304 (fixed), whose scope was deliberately the bulk path in the vector module; these are the four single-row posts it did not cover.
issues.fix_note: All four side-effect posts (memory delete, memory update, agent purge, episode delete) now go through one helper that binds the response and says, once and at warning, when the index did not take the change. Still non-fatal by contract -- the local change is already committed and a failed index is not a failed delete -- but the state it leaves is the one that does not look like a fault, so it is no longer only visible at a log level that is off. The status is read defensively (getattr), because a client that answers something without a status must not turn a completed delete into an exception; the recording double in tests/test_252a2_i4.py was answering None and so had to start modelling a response for the check to be exercised at all.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) deep_check(fix=True) wraps the whole check registry in one transaction (cpersona/maintenance_handlers.py:288-294), so all eight deep checks run under the shared write lock although only two of them can write. Measured by recording the lock state inside each runner: with fix=True all eight -- including the stale-profile, orphaned-episode, calibration-staleness, near-duplicate, unnormalised-content and embedding-norm scans -- ran with the shared write lock held, and with fix=False none did. The report-only work under that lock includes a dense pairwise similarity matrix, thousands of row fetches per table, Unicode normalisation of row content, and a blocking read of the calibration sidecar, and every concurrent writer waits on all of it. The same class was fixed for the sibling health handler earlier in this file, on the stated ground that a scan which can never write has no business under the shared lock; the fix was not carried across. No corpus-scale timing or writer delay was measured, only the lock scope.
issues.fix_sketch: Split the loop the way the health handler does: run the report-only checks on the read seam and open the transaction only around the two that are declared fix-capable.
issues.fix_note: The deep runner now reads the declaration of which checks write, which already existed and is asserted against the AST, and opens the transaction only around those. The report-only scans run on the read seam, so a fix run no longer holds the shared write lock across the pairwise similarity matrix, the per-table row fetches, the Unicode normalisation and the blocking sidecar read. Serialisation still covers the half that can write, so the bug-042/043 property is unchanged. Results are assembled in the requested order rather than the order the two seams ran, so splitting the loop did not reorder the response; a test pins that.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) deep_check drops unrecognised check names and answers with a successful-looking empty envelope. The loop skips any name the registry does not know (cpersona/maintenance_handlers.py:289-292) and the schema enumerates the legal values in prose without declaring an enum, so nothing validates them. Measured: deep_check with a single mistyped name returned checks_run: [], results: {}, fixed: true -- which reads as a deep pass that ran, repaired and found nothing -- and a mixed list ran only the name it recognised while still answering fixed: true. The sibling health tool rejects the same input with ok:false and the list of valid names, so the two health tools now disagree on a documented point, in the opposite direction from the one the earlier fix recorded.
issues.fix_sketch: Validate the requested names against the registry before opening the run and refuse the call naming the unknown ones, the way the health handler already does; a caller who asked for a probe that did not exist has not learned anything from an empty result.
issues.fix_note: deep_check now refuses an unrecognised name the way check_health has since bug-230, with the same error_response fields (unknown_checks, valid_checks, checks_run: []), so the two health tools agree again on a point the documentation states. A mixed list is refused rather than partly run: the half that would have executed is what made the empty answer look plausible. Adds no field the sibling did not already have.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The FTS integrity check reports an absent full-text table as clean and never rebuilds it. Both integrity statements raise on a missing table and the second failure is swallowed by a bare continue (cpersona/checks.py:881-887), while the schema-object check inspects only indexes and triggers, so nothing notices. Reproduced by dropping the memories full-text table, which leaves its triggers in place: the report-only check returned no finding, the fix run left the table still absent, and a keyword recall then raised sqlite3.OperationalError: no such table from the unguarded join (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:2127-2141) instead of degrading to the LIKE fallback. Severity is bounded by reachability: an ordinary boot recreates and rebuilds the table, so the exposed states are a live process after the table went missing and the report-only maintenance CLI, which skips boot migrations.
issues.fix_sketch: Distinguish absent from unsupported: look the table up in sqlite_master first and report a finding (repairable by recreating and rebuilding it) when it is missing, keeping the silent continue only for a build whose integrity command genuinely does not exist.
issues.fix_note: check_fts_integrity now asks sqlite_master whether the index table exists before probing it, so an absent table is no longer indistinguishable from a build without the integrity command; the repair recreates it from FTS_TABLE_SQL (one statement, not executescript, which would commit the fix run transaction) and rebuilds. The read-path consequence named in the finding is closed too: the keyword FTS join in memory_handlers degrades to the documented LIKE fallback instead of raising. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py (four tests, incl. the probe assertion restated as an invariant).

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The all-agent deep sweep discovers agents from the memories table alone (cpersona/checkup.py:105-111), although two of the deep checks inspect profiles and episodes, so an agent represented only by those tables is never swept. Measured with a stale profile and an orphaned episode seeded for an agent holding zero memories: the deep handler called directly found each of them, while the CLI's own parser and runner with the deep sweep exited 0 and reported an empty deep section. The operator reads a clean run where two findings exist.
issues.fix_sketch: Union the distinct agent ids across the three tables the deep checks read, so the sweep's population matches what it is sweeping for.
issues.fix_note: The sweep now discovers its population from the three tables the deep checks read, so an agent represented only by a profile or an episode is visited. Measured: with a stale profile and an orphaned episode seeded for agents holding zero memories, the sweep returns both, and a named --agent still sweeps only that agent.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The short-content deep repair binds one host parameter per matching row with no chunking: it collects every short memory for the agent and deletes them in a single statement (cpersona/checks.py:2730-2745). Measured both ways -- with 33 rows against a lowered connection limit, and with 32767 rows at the native limit of 32766 -- the fix run recorded results.short_content.error 'too many SQL variables', deleted nothing, and still answered fixed: true, because the handler turns the exception into an error field. The read-only scan found every seeded row, so the check knows about them and only the repair fails. On any SQLite older than 3.32 the ceiling is 999.
issues.fix_sketch: Delete in chunks bounded by the same id-fetch constant the vector paths use, summing rowcount across chunks so the reported repair count stays honest; the locked-row exclusion is unaffected by the split.
issues.note: The reported fixed: true alongside a recorded error is a second, smaller defect on the same path -- an operator reading the envelope cannot tell a completed repair from an aborted one.
issues.fix_note: The repair deletes in chunks of _SHORT_CONTENT_DELETE_CHUNK (500, the width vector._ID_FETCH_CHUNK uses for a scattered IN list, under the 999 floor of every SQLite before 3.32), summing rowcount across chunks so the reported count stays honest; the locked exclusion is per-statement and unaffected by the split. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py drives the measured corpus (ceiling + 1 rows at the native limit) and pins the property that no single statement binds one parameter per matching row. The probe's other arm, which lowered SQLITE_LIMIT_VARIABLE_NUMBER on the live connection and required the repair to read it at run time, asserted a shape no chunked path here takes and was restated as that property.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The index phase returns a zero-copy view of the mapped file only when the selection is one ascending run with an empty tail; in every other shape it allocates the whole scan window as a matrix and fills it by fancy-index gather, which allocates a second array of the same size (cpersona/vector.py:915-923). The window is the caller's scan limit, so peak memory grows with both the memory cap and the reach -- the opposite of the design note's claim that memory on the index path is bounded by the index file and does not grow with the reach. Measured on a hermetic corpus: a single-agent no-tail control returned a view sharing the index storage, while a scattered two-agent selection and a selection with one row written after the build both returned owning arrays with no base, and traced peaks scaled linearly with the window at roughly 2.2x the window bytes. The fast path is lost whenever a second agent's rows interleave or one row has been stored since the build; a filtered recall is expected to lose it for the same reason but was not exercised, and no production out-of-memory event was reproduced.
issues.fix_sketch: Score the window in chunks on this path too, the way the SQL scan already does, so the accelerated path inherits the bound rather than re-introducing the peak the chunked scan exists to remove; the gather temporary disappears with it.
issues.note: Half fixed in 2.5.12b2, and left open deliberately. The gather temporary is gone: the block gather writes the same bytes into the same slots, measured bit-identical, and drops the traced peak from 2.00x the window to 1.10x. The other half -- scoring the window in chunks -- is NOT a fix-release change. _cosine_matrix states the invariant the equivalence gate's meaning rests on: every path reaches that one call with the same bytes in the same shape. Chunking changes the shape, so it re-decides the exactness the index path is built on, and belongs with whoever owns the scoring path. Until then the matrix itself is still window-sized, so the design note's claim that memory here does not grow with the reach still overstates this path.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The bulk remote index push names no deadline of its own, so each 128-item chunk inherits the embedding client's 30 s default. Every sibling remote call states its deadline deliberately -- the recall search at 5 s and the single-item index push to the same endpoint at 10 s, each with a comment saying it exists so as not to inherit the 30 s default -- and this loop passes no timeout at all (cpersona/vector.py:141-148). Measured with a transport that times out immediately: all three chunks of a 257-item push were attempted and every outgoing request carried connect, read, write and pool timeouts of 30 s, against the 10 s the sibling constant sets. Because the loop is serial and continues after failures by design, the delays add: an import of tens of thousands of rows spends 30 s per chunk against a service that accepts connections and stops answering, and the session-end archive path blocks 30 s per call. Two sub-claims of the report are corrected here: a client-level deadline does exist (it is just the wrong one), and this is not the only call omitting a timeout -- the single-row remote posts do too (bug-323). Real end-to-end latency was not measured.
issues.fix_sketch: Pass the same index timeout the single-item push uses, and consider a whole-loop budget as well, since a chunk count taken from the caller's row count multiplies whatever per-chunk deadline is chosen.
issues.note: The test double for this path accepts no timeout keyword, so it would raise if production started passing one -- worth updating in the same change, or the fix cannot be tested through it.
issues.fix_note: The bulk push states the same deadline the single-item push to the same endpoint already names, instead of inheriting the embedding client 30s default across every chunk of a serial loop. Two test doubles that refused the keyword were widened in the same change, and two recording assertions now pin the value rather than its presence.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The get_contents character budget counts only the content field, while the item it returns also carries the parsed source object, which is capped separately and much higher. Admission and charging both read `len(item["content"])` (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:1979-1982), so up to the per-call reference maximum of source blobs ride entirely outside the cap. Measured: 20 rows stored with roughly 7,850 characters of source each and trivial content came back as one response of about 159,000 characters against a 40,000-character budget, with neither a deferred list nor a budget field in the answer -- the budget never fired. That is precisely the coupling the constant was introduced to break, since it is documented as pinning the read blast radius so that relaxing a write bound cannot enlarge it; raising the metadata cap now multiplies this response instead. The pinning test cannot bite either, because it sums the same field the handler counts.
issues.fix_sketch: Charge the budget for the whole item the caller receives -- content plus the serialised source -- and change the pinning test to measure the response rather than the one field the handler happens to count.
issues.fix_note: Admission and charging count the whole item the caller receives, not the one field the loop held. Source carries its own much higher cap, so a budget over content alone was not a bound on the response: twenty rows of large source objects returned about four times the budget with neither a deferred list nor a budget field. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py measures the serialised response against the budget and asserts the batch defers.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) A failed remote index push on the store hot path is reported nowhere an operator can see it. The failure goes to a debug log that is off in any normal deployment (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:305-311), and the only response signal is `embedded`, which is the OR of the local and remote outcomes, so a written local blob makes it true regardless (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:313-318). Measured in remote mode with the index endpoint answering 500: store returned ok:true, result stored, embedded:true, emitted exactly one debug record and nothing at warning or above. The row is then in the database and not in the index, and remote-mode recall returns the service's answer verbatim while the search endpoint is healthy, so the memory is simply absent from every later recall with no signal in the response, the log, or the health advisory. The recall-side omission was read in source rather than driven.
issues.pattern: Remote index push failed for mem
issues.fix_sketch: Say it once at WARNING naming the row and namespace, as the bulk sibling now does, and report the two outcomes separately rather than OR-ing them into a single embedded flag -- non-fatal is not the same as unreported.
issues.note: The single-item counterpart of bug-304 (fixed), which was deliberately scoped to the bulk push; bug-323 is the same shortfall on the four admin side-effect posts. The existing test on this path uses a double whose embed returns an empty vector, so no local blob is written and the flag reflects the remote push alone -- an isolation that does not exist with a real backend.
issues.fix_note: The failed push is reported once at WARNING naming the row and the namespace, the correction the bulk sibling took and was deliberately scoped away from on this path. The embedded flag is unchanged: splitting it into two outcomes is a response-shape change this line does not take, and the finding is that the shortfall was unreported rather than that the flag is wrong. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py drives a mock index answering 500 and asserts a record at WARNING or above.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) A remote search response that is 2xx but carries no results key is accepted as an authoritative empty answer. The hit list is built with `data.get("results", [])` (cpersona/vector.py:390), and an empty list means, by this function's own stated contract, that the service answered and that answer is the result -- so the caller returns it and never runs the local scan. Measured against one locally embedded row: a transport failure fell back and returned the row, a body with an explicit empty results list stayed authoritative as designed, and a 200 body carrying only an error message returned nothing with zero log records at any level from any of the package's loggers. Every other malformed body already falls back with a warning, so the absent key is the single shape that lands silently on the authoritative side, and the same backend's embedding boundary rules the opposite way for the identical shape. The health advisory also stays unknown, because the remote branch returns before the observation call. Gated on the non-default remote search mode.
issues.pattern: if not isinstance\(data, dict\) or "results" not in data:
issues.fix_sketch: Require the key: a body without it is unusable, so return None and let the caller fall back and log, keeping the authoritative empty answer for a body that actually says results are empty.
issues.fix_note: A body that never mentions results is unusable, so the branch returns None and the caller falls back and logs. The authoritative empty answer is kept for a body that actually says results are empty, which is the distinction this function contract rests on.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The near and far vector windows are two statements issued at different times on a shared autocommit connection, so a commit landing between them breaks the disjointness the fusion depends on. Scan position is defined by an ordering over the live table, and the far window is a second read at an offset (cpersona/vector.py:1741, 1551); an insert shifts every position by one, so the row at the near window's last position reappears in the far window. Measured with the caps lowered and one row committed exactly at that seam: a row appeared on both lists, and fed through the fusion it scored two reciprocal-rank votes from a single retriever and sorted first, ahead of rows that outrank it. That contradicts the invariant asserted in the scan module, in the fusion, and in the design note, and it matters beyond ordering: the legacy quality gate rescales its threshold by a per-row maximum of three votes, which a duplicated row can now exceed. Under the alternative fusion the same duplicate is normalised and summed in two channels. The interleaving was scheduled rather than raced -- the defect is the missing snapshot, and the far scan's first database await is a real yield point -- and the setup needs the reach configured above the memory cap, which is not the default.
issues.pattern: near_rids = \{row\["_rid"\] for _score, row in top_k if "_rid" in row\}
issues.fix_sketch: Read both windows inside one read scope so they see a single snapshot, or take the far window by explicit id exclusion rather than by offset, so a shifted position cannot put the same row on both lists.
issues.fix_note: Disjointness by position is the reason the far list needs no de-duplicating pass, and it is exactly the premise a commit between the two reads breaks. The far list now drops any row the near list is already returning, keyed on the same row identity the fusion itself uses, and says so at warning level so the shifted-window case is visible rather than inferred from a strange ranking.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The autocut gap heuristic refuses to cut a cosine-ordered list unless every row carries the signal, but applies the same cut to a confidence-ordered list with no such guard (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:676-677 against the sibling test three lines below). The injected profile row has no cosine by construction, so it is scored on the strictly higher time-decay-only branch, sorts to the top, and the gap between it and the first real memory is the largest gap in the list. Measured two ways: with real scoring, a profile row at 0.8385 against four gated memories at 0.52 down to 0.45 made autocut return the profile row alone, while the same mixture keyed on cosine was returned whole; and end to end over a 60-row corpus a recall came back with the profile line as its only message, every memory that had just passed the quality gate dropped, with nothing in the response reporting it. Needs confidence scoring enabled, which is not the default.
issues.pattern: sentinels = \[r for r in results if r\.get\("id"\) == -1\]
issues.fix_sketch: Give the confidence branch the same homogeneity guard the cosine branch has, or exclude the injected profile row from the list the gap is measured over -- it is not a retrieval result and its score comes from a different branch, so it cannot be compared with the rows below it.
issues.note: The existing pin gives every row a confidence score, so the mixed-branch case it would have to see does not occur in it.
issues.fix_note: The injected profile row is removed from the list the gap is measured over and returned regardless of where the cut lands. The guard it needed was not homogeneity of the field, which the sentinel has, but that a row scored on a different branch is not a member of the comparison at all. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py pins the measured mixture that returned the profile alone, and a companion case where a real gap must still cut while the sentinel survives.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The per-user source filter is a SQL LIKE prefix predicate, and SQLite's LIKE folds ASCII case by default -- nothing in the package sets the pragma that would change it -- so a recall scoped to one principal also returns rows tagged to a different principal whose source id differs only in case. The clause is built once and reused by every retrieval arm, including the vector arm's window read and its by-id hydrate (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:2109-2113, cpersona/vector.py:814, 1641), and the escape helper neutralises only the wildcards. Measured with two rows whose source ids differ only in the case of one letter: the keyword arm, the empty-query recency arm and the raw predicate each returned both rows. This is the filter documented as preventing cross-user contamination in multi-user bridges, and neither the tool schema nor the handler docstring says the match is case-folded. It needs the optional filter plus two principal ids that collide under ASCII folding, which is why it is MEDIUM rather than higher.
issues.fix_sketch: Compare the extracted id with a case-sensitive operator (GLOB, or an explicit BINARY collation on the LIKE) once the wildcards are escaped, so the SQL authority means what the schema says. Whichever way this is settled, the index's own resolution must be settled the same way -- see bug-317, where the two currently disagree.
issues.note: Distinct from bug-317: that entry is the index's case-sensitive resolution of the same axis. They are opposite halves of one disagreement, and today the SQL side is the permissive one.
issues.fix_note: The per-user restriction is an exact prefix comparison built once in the isolation module and used by every arm, instead of a LIKE prefix spelled at four call sites. LIKE folds ASCII case unless a pragma nothing here sets, so a recall scoped to one principal returned rows tagged to another whose id differed only in case; equality compares with BINARY collation and needs no wildcard escaping. This is also the resolution the contiguous index already used, so the two arms now answer the same question. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py covers the keyword arm, the empty-query recency arm, the shared predicate itself, and a source id containing LIKE wildcards that must still match literally.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) delete_agent_data purges the database rows, the calibration state and the remote vector namespace, but not the local contiguous index (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:610-614), so the purged agent's embeddings and identifiers stay on disk. Measured: two memories were stored with distinct source ids, the index was built, and the shipped handler returned ok:true with the deleted row counts while the index file still contained the agent id, both source ids and the deleted row's embedding byte for byte. Nothing in the running server rebuilds or invalidates that file -- building it is documented as an operator action -- so the residue survives until someone runs the maintenance command, under a tool description that promises to delete all data for the agent. The precondition is that an operator built the index at all, and the artifact is documented as derived and safe to delete.
issues.fix_sketch: Add the index files to the same enumeration of derived copies the purge already walks -- deleting them is safe by the artifact's own contract, and rebuilding is an operator action either way, so removal is the conservative choice.
issues.fix_note: The purge now walks the contiguous index files alongside the calibration sidecar and the remote namespace, post-commit, dropping the index for each indexed table that actually lost rows. Removal rather than a rebuild without the agent: the module states the file is derived, never repaired and safe to delete, and rebuilding it here would move an operator-paced cost onto a delete. A delete that matched nothing leaves the file alone, so the tool cannot be used to keep the server on the live scan. The table list moved into vector_index.INDEXED_TABLES so the purge and the CLI cannot drift apart. Three tests in tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py pin it, and removing either the call or the row-count guard turns the matching ones red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The per-issuer key-set lock is held across the whole refresh, which issues up to three sequential metadata fetches plus the key-set fetch, each bounded only by the 10 s client timeout (cpersona/oauth.py:305-318, 373-419). The bearer middleware awaits verification before dispatching, so every other request carrying a token from the same issuer waits behind that lock, before authentication and before any tool runs. Reproduced through the shipped verifier with an injected fetch seam: a syntactically valid but unsigned token drove all three metadata fetches before any signature was checked, and with a key set already cached and inside its TTL, a forged token with an unknown key id past the refetch cooldown gated an in-flight fetch while a concurrent verification of a legitimate token whose key was already cached -- a call needing no network at all -- did not complete until the gate was released. The refetch cooldown bounds how often this can be provoked, not how long the lock is held during one attempt. The wall-clock size of the window depends on real connect timeouts and was not measured.
issues.fix_sketch: Serve a cached key inside the lock and release it before the network work, so only the refresh is serialised and a cache hit never waits on a fetch provoked by someone else's unverified token.
issues.fix_note: The cache is now answered before the per-issuer lock is taken, and again under it in case another request refreshed while this one waited, so the lock serialises refreshes and nothing else. Reading the cache needs no lock: every field it reads is replaced wholesale by the refresh and never mutated in place, and nothing between the reads awaits, so it sees one consistent snapshot. What this ends is a verification that needs no network at all waiting for the whole of a fetch some other caller provoked, before authentication and before any tool runs -- and the caller who provokes it need not be authenticated, since an unknown key id is the rotation signal. The refetch cooldown still bounds how often a fetch can be provoked; it never bounded how long the lock was held during one.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The pairwise-subject fail-closed check reads the metadata document that structurally never carries the field it tests. Discovery tries the URLs in order and returns at the first document with a key-set URI (cpersona/oauth.py:103-107, 415-419), the first being the spelling whose own comment in this file concedes does not carry subject_types_supported, while the discovery document that is required to declare it is never fetched. Reproduced against an issuer publishing both documents, with the public-subject requirement on: verification returned a token with a pairwise subject instead of refusing, and the fetch log shows only the first metadata URL and the key set. The comment above the refusal claims the opposite reach, that the failure is closed for the whole issuer rather than for one metadata spelling. The existing pin cannot see this because its fake issuer serves one document and injects the field into that one -- the exact spelling the code says never carries it. The consequence is that the alias ledger keys on a pairwise identifier, splitting one person's memory space per client, which is what the check exists to refuse.
issues.fix_sketch: When the requirement is on, fetch the discovery document explicitly rather than testing whichever document happened to answer first, and treat its absence as a refusal -- a gate that cannot read the field it depends on has not passed, it has abstained.
issues.fix_note: With the public-subject requirement on, discovery no longer returns at the first document that answers with a key set location: it walks on until an OpenID Connect discovery document has been read, which is the spelling that is required to carry subject_types_supported. The RFC 8414 document the walk starts with does not carry it, so the gate was being applied to a document structurally incapable of failing it while the declaring document was never fetched. With the requirement off the early return is unchanged, so discovery still costs one round trip. Deliberately NOT extended to refusing when no discovery document can be read: this module states that absence is not a pairwise declaration and a pin holds it, so turning abstention into refusal is a policy change rather than this restoration. The abstention is now logged instead, because a gate that never ran read exactly like one that passed.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The metadata and key-set fetch bounds bytes but not time: the client timeout is applied per read, so a peer that trickles a body slower than the byte cap but faster than one read timeout keeps the fetch open indefinitely (cpersona/oauth.py:490-503). Measured against a real loopback peer answering 200 chunked with a small chunk every 0.2 s and the timeout lowered to 0.5 s: the fetch returned only after 4.04 s, eight times its own configured timeout, having received 0.49% of the document cap -- the peer, not the client, chose when the transfer ended, so the docstring's claim that the request is bounded in time is false as written. The second half compounds it: the per-issuer lock is held across the fetch, and a pure cache hit for a key already held did not complete for as long as an unrelated fetch was gated. The unauthenticated reachability of the refresh (a syntactically valid but unsigned token naming a configured issuer with an unknown key id) was read in source rather than driven end to end.
issues.fix_sketch: Wrap the whole fetch in a total deadline rather than relying on a per-read timeout, so the bound belongs to the transfer and not to each chunk; the existing pin measures only the byte cap, so a time pin has to be added with it.
issues.note: The byte axis of the same function is bug-297 (fixed), which moved the bound from what is parsed to what is received; this is the time axis it did not cover. The lock-hold half is bug-338, filed separately because the fix for it is a different change.
issues.fix_note: The fetch is wrapped in a deadline over the whole call, so the bound belongs to the transfer rather than to each read. The client timeout is applied per operation, which let a peer trickling a chunk just inside it choose when the transfer ended -- measured at eight times the configured bound while delivering half a percent of the byte cap, against a docstring that promises a bounded request. It raises rather than returning the partial body: a truncation handed back as a 200 gets diagnosed by the caller as malformed JSON, which sends an operator to read the issuer document instead of the link to it. Pinned against a real loopback peer, since the property is in how the socket is read.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The calibration timestamp parser is the only one in the package that does not apply the naive-is-UTC rule: it calls fromisoformat(...).timestamp() with no tzinfo fixup (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:664-669), and .timestamp() on a naive datetime assumes system-local time. Every other reader goes through the shared helper whose docstring names this exact hazard, and the behaviour contract publishes naive-is-UTC as a promise. Measured on a host pinned to a nine-hour offset: the same instant spelled naively and with an offset parsed 32,400 s apart, and driving the consumer, two memories inserted 60 s apart -- one stamped the way the store path writes and one naive the way SQLite's own default writes -- yielded zero same-session pairs instead of one, because the comparison window is 30 minutes and the shift is nine hours. Naive stamps are routine on the episode side, where the created_at column defaults to SQLite's naive value. The end-to-end consequence, that the mislabelled pairs move the persisted gate, follows from the same comparison but was not run. Only bites on non-UTC hosts.
issues.fix_sketch: Delete this parser and call the shared UTC-aware one, which already treats a naive stamp as UTC for the documented reason that every naive value in the database comes from SQLite's own clock.
issues.fix_note: Routed through the shared _parse_timestamp_utc helper, so the naive-is-UTC rule the behaviour contract publishes has one implementation rather than two. Matters because naive stamps are routine on the episode side (SQLite's own datetime('now') writes them) and .timestamp() on a naive datetime assumes system-local time, which silently moved every pair 32,400 s on a nine-hour-offset host -- past a 30-minute adjacency window, so the calibration sat on a population it had mislabelled.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) set_recall_precision gates itself on the caller's declared session bucket and then calls calibration with no session key (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:1656), so the inner call consults the shared keyless bucket instead. Measured with a passing control in the same run: with nothing paused the call measured a threshold, applied it and wrote the sidecar; with a keyless pause armed and the caller declaring its own unpaused key, the identical call returned ok:true, precision strict, beta applied, and a calibrate block whose new_threshold is None -- the no-persist skeleton, which is itself ok:true, so the rollback guarded by that flag never fires. Nothing was measured, the sidecar was not written, and the response carries no marker the caller could branch on. That re-opens through the pause branch the failure the comment directly above the rollback describes, an un-persisted weight left applied in process memory. The follow-on, that a later unrelated calibration writes that weight to disk, was not run.
issues.fix_sketch: Thread the caller's session key into the inner calibration, and treat a skipped calibration as a reason to roll the weight back rather than as success -- a skeleton that reports no threshold has not applied the setting, whatever its ok flag says.
issues.note: The existing coverage exercises this handler only with a declared pause on another key, or with the caller itself keyless, so the keyed-caller-against-keyless-pause combination is unpinned.
issues.fix_note: Two halves. The inner calibration is now asked with the caller's own session_key, so the pause decision is made on the bucket this handler already gated itself on rather than the shared keyless one. And a skipped calibration is treated as a failure to apply: the no-persist shape is ok:true by design, so the ok flag alone could not tell 'measured and applied' from 'declined to measure', and the rollback that exists to stop an un-persisted weight living on in process memory never fired.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The import path decodes an embedding by checking only that the byte length is a whole number of float32s (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:2013-2033) and writes the bytes straight into the column, so a non-finite vector is stored durably. The store path cannot do this -- the packing seam refuses a non-finite element -- so the two paths give opposite verdicts on the same values, which was confirmed by control: packing NaN and inf both returned None while a finite vector packed, and an import line carrying a NaN vector answered ok:true with one memory imported and no errors, the row reading back as non-finite by the package's own helper. The episode twin stores an inf vector the same way. The structural gate that exists to enforce the invariant looks for calls to the packing helper, and this path packs nothing, so it has no reach here. Those rows then poison threshold calibration for the agent and mis-score on the scan paths until an operator runs a repairing health check, which is the only thing that removes them.
issues.fix_sketch: Ask the same finiteness helper the storage seam uses before accepting the decoded blob, and report the skipped rows in the import result rather than dropping them silently; widening the structural gate to any write of the embedding column, not just calls to the packer, is what would have caught this.
issues.note: The consumer of these rows is bug-312, where a single non-finite blob makes the calibrated threshold NaN. Distinct seams: this is the write, that is the read.
issues.fix_note: The import decoder now asks the storage seam's own finiteness question before it accepts a blob, so the two write paths give the same verdict on the same values, and every rejection is reported as an error line naming the record rather than returning None in silence.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The startup dimension probe reads one arbitrary row's width -- a LIMIT 1 with no ordering, divided into a dimension (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:1061-1065) -- while calibration persists the modal width its sampler settles on after dropping ragged rows. On a mixed-dimension corpus the two disagree permanently. Measured with three legacy wide rows beside twenty current ones for one agent: the probe answered 16 and calibration persisted 8, and four consecutive startup checks over an unchanged corpus returned recalibrated with dim_changed true every time, never settling, each one warning that the embedding dimension changed, backing up the sidecar, discarding every per-agent threshold and gate it held, and re-running a full calibration per agent. The selection was deterministic across every run, because the legacy rows are the oldest and a plain scan reaches them first. A homogeneous-corpus control settled after the first boot as intended.
issues.fix_sketch: Measure the same quantity on both sides: take the modal width over a sample rather than the first row's width, so the comparison that decides dim_changed asks the question calibration answered.
issues.fix_note: The startup probe now asks for the corpus's modal embedding width instead of one arbitrary row's, which is the quantity calibration persists -- so on a mixed-dimension corpus the two no longer disagree permanently and the boot stops discarding every per-agent threshold on every start. _modal_width is shared by the probe and both samplers and breaks ties deterministically (count, then the wider value); Counter.most_common broke them by row order, which is a property of the scan rather than of the corpus.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The merge copy passes read the source agent's whole table into memory before copying a row, and they do it while the process-wide write lock is held. The memory pass selects thirteen columns including the embedding and the content with no limit and no paging (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:2805-2810), and the episode pass does the same; the transaction that takes the lock is entered before all of them. Measured by instrumenting every fetch with its row count, the resident bytes of the returned rows and the lock state, over 1200 source rows carrying 1024-dimension vectors: one statement returned all 1200 rows and 5.23 MB in a single list with the write lock held, and the instrument's own control (a limited read outside the transaction) recorded 100 rows and no lock. The peer bulk path in the same file already pages at 500 with a comment saying the corpus must not be materialised. What is measured is that one read's size equals the corpus's, so it grows without bound; the out-of-memory outcome at production corpus sizes is an extrapolation from that. One sub-claim of the report is dropped: the deferred remote items list holds references to the same strings, not a second copy.
issues.pattern: FROM memories WHERE agent_id = \? AND id > \? ORDER BY id LIMIT \?
issues.fix_sketch: Page the copy passes the way the export path already does, so the resident set is bounded by the chunk rather than by the corpus, and the lock is held only for the writes.
issues.fix_note: Both copy passes read the source in keyset pages of 500 -- the bound the export path in the same file uses -- so the resident set of one read is bounded by the page rather than by the corpus. Keyset rather than one open cursor because the copy inserts into the table it is reading on the same connection.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) A move-mode merge deletes the copied source rows from the database but never removes their vectors from the source agent's remote namespace. The deletes have no remote counterpart (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:3004-3008), and the only cleanup of the source's index is the whole-namespace purge, which is gated on nothing being left at the source -- so any leftover row, including the very common case of a profile the copy skipped, leaves every moved row's vector indexed against an agent that no longer holds it. Measured with a recording remote double: the source rows were deleted, the sole remote request the entire merge made was the index push into the target namespace, and the leftover profile count of one skipped the purge. The control passed -- deleting a single memory does post a removal for it -- so the recorder does see cleanup where a path performs it. This is the same orphaned-vector class already fixed for the single-row delete paths and never for the third deleting path. The downstream consequence, that ghost vectors spend top-K slots and rehydrate to nothing, was read in source rather than measured.
issues.fix_sketch: Post a removal for exactly the ids the move deleted, in the source namespace, alongside the delete -- the ids are already carried for the delete itself, and the whole-namespace purge stays as the separate teardown for a source that ended up empty.
issues.fix_note: A move now posts a removal for exactly the ids it deleted, in the source namespace, whenever rows are left behind and the whole-namespace purge therefore does not run -- the per-row cleanup the other two deleting paths already did.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) An unreadable calibration sidecar is indistinguishable from an absent one: the loader returns None for both and logs nothing (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:972-978, and a JSON decode error is a ValueError). All three evidence-preserving guards on the startup path test that same value, so a corrupt file takes none of them, and the next save overwrites the only copy an operator could have repaired. Measured with a complete sidecar truncated by one byte: the startup check reported action initial -- the word reserved for a new install -- wrote no backup, produced no record at any level mentioning the sidecar, and left the file on disk holding empty maps, so an operator-set precision override was gone from disk with no copy anywhere. The control one branch away passed: a stale scoring version reports itself, writes a backup and logs about it, so the difference measured is the guard rather than the fixture. The alias ledger in the same package takes the opposite decision explicitly for the same class of file, refusing to start rather than starting over.
issues.fix_sketch: Separate the two answers: absent is a fresh install, unreadable is a fault -- log it at WARNING, move the unreadable file aside under a backup name before writing anything, and report it in the startup status so the operator learns of it on the boot that lost the state.
issues.fix_note: Absent and unreadable are separate answers now. An unreadable sidecar is logged at WARNING, copied aside under a backup name before anything replaces it, and reported as its own startup action instead of the word reserved for a first-ever boot.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) When the alias ledger's persist fails with anything other than an OSError, the rollback does not run and the unpersisted alias stays live in memory (cpersona/aliases.py:147-159). Reproduced by removing the attribute the persist calls unguarded, which is the platform condition the package's own permissions helper already guards for: the call raised AttributeError instead of the documented ledger error, the file was never created, and the retry took the cached fast path and returned the alias with no error, so the caller is authorised under an identity recorded nowhere. Each attempt also left a temp file beside the database with its descriptor unclosed. That is precisely the loss the module docstring says it prevents -- an alias that authorised a write but was never durably recorded is re-minted on restart and strands whatever the session stored. The OSError control rolls back correctly, so the gap is the exception class and not the rollback itself. The platform trigger is taken from the interpreter's documented surface and the package's own OS-independent classifier, not observed on that platform here.
