issues.fix_sketch: Roll back on any exception, not only OSError, and re-raise as the module's own error type so callers see the documented failure; closing the descriptor in a finally removes the leak on both paths.
issues.note: bug-322 is the other half of the same line -- why the unguarded call raises at all -- and is fixed differently (route it through the permissions helper). Both are worth keeping: one removes the trigger, this one removes the class of trigger.
issues.fix_note: The issuance rolls back on any exception rather than on OSError alone, so an unpersisted alias can no longer stay live in memory for the retry to hand out from cache. What the persist can raise is not a list worth keeping current -- the rollback is correct for every way it can fail. An exception that is not an ordinary error (cancellation, interrupt) is rolled back and re-raised as itself rather than reclassified, since telling the caller the ledger failed when it did not is its own defect. bug-322 removes this trigger; this removes the class.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Import and merge deduplicate on content only through INSERT OR IGNORE and a rowcount test, while the explicit content probe exists solely on the preview arm (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:2390-2422 and 2846-2878). The constraint that OR IGNORE resolves against is created by a best-effort upgrade step whose failure is swallowed with a warning claiming that SELECT deduplication remains -- true for the message-id axis, which does have a real probe, and false for the content axis on both write paths. Reproduced through the real upgrade ladder: with two locked rows colliding on the deduplication key, the index creation failed, was swallowed, and the ladder still stamped the newer schema version, so the step never runs again. On that database the same one-record export imported twice reported one memory imported each time and left two identical rows, with a preview in between reporting it as skipped; the merge behaved the same way, reporting one skip in preview and one merge in the real run under a skip strategy. So the tool advertised as idempotent stops being idempotent, and both paths disagree with their own previews.
issues.pattern: bug-349: the content axis, asked on BOTH arms
issues.fix_sketch: Run the same content probe on the real arms that the preview arms run, so deduplication does not depend on an index whose creation is allowed to fail; the constraint then becomes a second line of defence rather than the only one.
issues.note: The repair path for the missing index re-issues the same statement and fails the same way while a locked collider exists; that mitigation was not exercised here.
issues.fix_note: The content probe runs on the real arms of import and merge, not only on the previews, so deduplication no longer depends on an index whose creation is allowed to fail. The index is also retried on every boot, so a collision that blocked it no longer makes its absence permanent.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Two concurrent exports to the same path share one temp file, publishing a torn, mixed-agent backup while the call reports success. The temp name is derived only from the output path and the process id (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:2096), and the comment beside it addresses only the cross-process case; two coroutines in one process get the identical name, both open it truncating, and the write spans many paged-read suspension points, so they interleave and whichever reaches the rename first publishes the shared inode. Measured with 700 rows under each of two agents exported concurrently to one path: one call returned ok:true with 700 memories, the other raised FileNotFoundError out of the rename, and the published file carried a header naming one agent and a count of 700 while its body held records from both agents plus a torn line. The record split varies with scheduling; the class -- a mixed, torn, header-inconsistent backup under ok:true plus an unhandled error on the other call -- reproduced every run. The import path will later refuse that file as inconsistent, so the operator learns of it at restore time.
issues.fix_sketch: Mint the temp name with mkstemp in the destination directory, as the ledger write already does, so the name is unique per call rather than per process; the rename stays the publication step.
issues.fix_note: The export temp file is minted per call with mkstemp in the destination directory, the way the ledger write already does, so two concurrent exports to one path can no longer share an inode. The rename stays the publication step.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The alias ledger is read once when the process starts and every persist rewrites the whole file from that in-memory snapshot, with no re-read, no modification-time check and no fingerprint compare (cpersona/aliases.py:71-72, 169-190). Any write the process did not make is erased at the next issuance. Measured: with the ledger instance live, the documented manual account-linking edit was made to the file and one unrelated alias was then issued -- the operator's row was gone afterwards, with nothing raised and nothing logged. The two-process shape reproduced in the same run: two instances over one path each issued an alias and the file kept only one. The single-writer control passed. The module docstring names the operator as a legitimate second writer, so this is a documented workflow losing data silently, and the loss is exactly what the ledger exists to prevent -- after a restart the affected subject resolves to a freshly minted alias and its memory space is unreachable.
issues.fix_sketch: Re-read the file under a lock and merge before writing, refusing rather than overwriting when the on-disk state has changed since it was read; a modification-time or content fingerprint check is enough to notice, and the merge direction is unambiguous because entries are only ever added.
issues.fix_note: The one path that writes now re-reads the file before it mints, and merges: a row present in both copies resolves to the one on disk, because this process persists every row it adds in the same call, so a row of ours that disagrees with the file is somebody else s edit and never a stale read of our own. That covers both second writers the module names -- the operator relinking rows for a provider re-issue, and another server process over the same path -- without adding a refusal for a changed file. Merging before the mint rather than at the write also means a second process that already issued for the pair is adopted rather than rivalled, and the collision check for a fresh alias sees the rows only the file knows. A ledger that stopped parsing raises, as it does at startup, before anything is added in memory. Six tests in tests/test_per_subject.py pin it; removing the re-read turns four red and reversing the merge direction turns the relink test red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The private-file open follows a pre-existing symlink: it opens with create and truncate but neither exclusive-create nor no-follow (cpersona/fileperms.py:98-100), unlike its sibling which does use exclusive-create. The export writes through it at a fully predictable temp path derived from the output path and the process id, then renames that path over the output. Measured: with a symlink planted at the temp path, the export returned ok:true and the target file afterwards held the exported records including a seeded row; in a second run the rename moved the link itself, so the operator's backup was a symlink into the attacker's file. The control export with nothing planted produced a regular private file holding the corpus, so the module's normal guarantee is intact. This defeats the module's stated purpose on the very threat model its docstring names. Exploitation needs a local account with write access to the export directory and knowledge of the process id; the variant with a pre-created world-writable file, where the mode tightening fails and is swallowed by design, was not run.
issues.fix_sketch: Add the no-follow flag for the create-and-truncate case, and prefer exclusive creation for a temp file that is expected not to exist; a leftover from a crashed run should be removed deliberately rather than reused, since reuse is what makes the plant work.
issues.note: The predictable temp name is bug-350's mechanism as well -- a unique name per call removes both the collision and most of the plant window, but the open flags are the part that decides whether a plant works at all.
issues.fix_note: open_private now passes O_NOFOLLOW, so a symlink at the final component is refused instead of followed. Following one broke both halves of the module contract at once: the corpus went into a file this process did not create, and the mode tightening landed on the link target, so a file that already existed did not keep the mode it had. The pin is at the helper (tests/test_bug289_file_permissions.py, four write modes plus a control) rather than at the export path the report reached it through - minting the export temp name per call (bug-350, fixed in 2.5.12b2) had already removed the predictable name that plant needed, so a pin written against that path passes without the flag ever changing. Measured: each write mode raises ELOOP with the victim untouched at 0644, and the control still creates a new 0600 file.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) A package index document with the wrong field types escapes the update refresh instead of degrading to an unknown verdict. The decision function iterates the versions and files fields directly (cpersona/update_check.py:291-296) and is called outside the fetch's exception boundary. Measured over a stub transport: a body whose versions field is a scalar raised TypeError out of update_check.refresh, and the mirror case with a scalar files field raised as well; the exception escaped both public entry points, the maintenance tool call with refresh requested and the startup check, which is what the startup callback's own wording distinguishes as a defect in the check rather than an outage. That contradicts the module's stated rule that a schema which changed gets the same answer as an outage. Reachable only if the index serves a document violating the repository API's type contract, and the damage is confined to the update-check feature.
issues.pattern: if not isinstance\(versions, list\) or not isinstance\(raw_files, list\):
issues.fix_sketch: Type-check the two fields on entry and answer unknown when they are not lists, or widen the exception boundary to cover the decision as well as the fetch -- the module already rules that an unusable document is an unusable document whatever made it so.
issues.fix_note: The decision now checks the two fields it iterates and answers unknown when either is not a list, which is the rule the module already states for the fetch: a document whose schema changed gets the same answer as an outage. Those two are the only shapes the function took on trust -- both parse helpers already refuse a non-string. The check also fixes a case that never raised: a bare string for versions iterates as characters and produced an unlisted verdict, which reads as a development checkout rather than as an index nobody can read. Pinned in tests/test_update_check.py over both entry points and all three shapes.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The embedding-dimension check converts any failure into a clean result: the probe, the counting queries and the repair are all wrapped in a catch that logs a warning and returns no findings (cpersona/checks.py:482-484). The check is registered as critical, and the runner only synthesises a crashed-check finding for exceptions that escape it, so this catch removes the one mechanism that would have represented the failure. Measured through the real runner with an embedding client present and a connection proxy raising on the width count: the run returned no issues and a summary of zero critical, zero warn, zero info, whose health status is healthy, with the only trace a log line. A critical axis that could not be verified is reported as verified and clean.
issues.fix_sketch: Return a finding that says the check could not run, rather than an empty list, so a critical axis that failed to verify is counted as unverified instead of clean; letting the exception escape to the runner's crashed-check path would also work and needs no new shape.
issues.fix_note: Only the live embedding probe keeps a silent skip, because an unreachable backend is check_embedding_backend's finding. Every database read below it is now unguarded, so a critical check that cannot verify reaches the runner's crashed-check path instead of answering what a verified-clean corpus answers. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py, with a companion test pinning that a dead backend still skips rather than warning.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Any failure reading the schema version is reported as no finding: the read is wrapped in a bare catch that returns an empty list (cpersona/checks.py:925-929), and the check is registered as critical, so an unreadable or missing version table is indistinguishable from a current schema. Reproduced on a real database holding only a memories table -- the shape the report-only maintenance path meets, since it skips boot migrations and never initialises the schema: the version query raises no-such-table, yet the health run for that check returned no issues and a summary of all zeros, whose health status is healthy. False green on a critical axis, on an uncommon but reachable database state.
issues.fix_sketch: Report the unreadable version as its own critical finding rather than as silence -- a database whose version cannot be read is exactly the state the check exists to name.
issues.fix_note: The guard is gone: a database whose version cannot be read is the state this critical check exists to name, and the runner already turns what escapes into a crashed-check finding. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py, driving a real database that holds only a memories table (the shape the report-only maintenance path meets, since it skips boot migrations).

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The read-snapshot scope is not a snapshot when the database is in memory: that branch yields the shared write connection and returns without beginning a transaction (cpersona/database.py:124-131). Measured at the seam: a count inside the scope read one row, a commit through the shared connection landed inside the scope, and a second read in the same scope returned two -- while the file-branch control read the same value twice, so what differs is the branch and not the fixture. Driven end to end, committing one memory immediately after the export's header counts produced a file whose header claims one memory while the body carries two records, which is exactly the inconsistency the import path refuses. The interleaving was injected at the seam rather than raced, because the defect is the absent transaction. Needs an explicitly in-memory deployment, which the shipped default is not.
issues.fix_sketch: Open a deferred read transaction on the shared connection for the life of the scope and end it on exit, or state in the contract that this branch offers no isolation so callers who need one can refuse -- what cannot stand is a helper named for a snapshot that silently does not provide one.
issues.note: The shared connection is deliberate here: a second connection to an in-memory database is a different, empty database. The fix has to keep that and add the transaction, not replace the connection.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The update-index fetch bounds elapsed time but not bytes: the response is buffered and parsed with nothing between the get and the parse consulting a length or capping the read (cpersona/update_check.py:437-443). Measured against a valid but very large index document of 15.4 MB served through a stub transport: the call completed well inside the three-second deadline, returned a fully parsed structure with 1.1 million version strings, and traced 81 MB of peak allocation, 5.3x the served body. The time bound is the only bound that exists and it does not constrain memory. Exploitability is narrower than the shape suggests: the index URL is pinned, so an oversized body needs a hostile index or an intercepting proxy, and the fetch runs in a startup task nothing awaits.
issues.fix_sketch: Stream the body and abort past a cap, the way the metadata fetch on the authentication path now does, and answer unknown on refusal -- silence is already the contract for an unusable index.
issues.note: Same shape as bug-297 (fixed) and bug-298 on their own fetch paths; this is the third receive path in the package and the fix pattern is already written.
issues.fix_note: The fetch reads the body as a bounded stream and stops past MAX_INDEX_BYTES, the shape already used on the key-set fetch, and a declared Content-Length over the cap is refused before any read. The declared length is consulted only to refuse earlier, never to admit: a body that announces nothing, or lies low, still meets the running total. The cap comes from measurement rather than taste -- the URL is pinned to one package whose own index measured 60,089 bytes, while a decade-old project index measures a few megabytes -- so a mebibyte is about seventeen times todays document, and reaching it costs a notice rather than a failure because an unusable index already answers unknown.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The non-finite embedding check fetches every stored vector for both tables into one list before testing any of them (cpersona/checks.py:384-389). Measured through the real runner at two corpus sizes with 768-dimension vectors: 1,000 rows holding 3.07 MB peaked at 3.20 MB and 4,000 rows holding 12.29 MB peaked at 12.81 MB, a flat 1.04x that scales linearly with the corpus and rules out fixed overhead. The asymmetry is visible inside the same function -- the repair side is already chunked against the host-parameter limit while the read is unbounded -- and no adversary is involved, since it scales with the operator's own corpus on the default health path.
issues.fix_sketch: Page the read and test each chunk as it arrives, keeping only the offending ids -- the check's output is a list of ids, so nothing needs the blobs to be resident together.
issues.fix_note: The finiteness scan reads keyset pages of _NONFINITE_SCAN_CHUNK rows and tests each page as it arrives, keeping only the offending ids, so the peak no longer tracks the corpus. The page width is bounded by resident bytes rather than by the host-parameter limit, which is why it is a separate constant from the repair chunk beside it. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py measures the peak at both 1,000 and 4,000 rows of 768-wide vectors.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The update-cache write follows a symlink planted at its path. It hands a fixed path to the private-file open (cpersona/update_check.py:404-410), whose flags create and truncate without no-follow. Measured with a link named for the cache file pointing at an unrelated readable file: the link was followed, the target was truncated and rewritten with the update verdict, and its mode was tightened from 0644 to 0600, because the mode change lands on the descriptor and therefore on the link's target. The precondition is a database directory writable by another local account, so this is a local integrity issue rather than a remotely reachable one. The existing coverage on this path tests a corrupt cache and ordinary permission widening, not a symlink.
issues.fix_sketch: Fixing the open flags (bug-352) removes this too; until then this caller could write through a freshly created unique temp file and rename it into place, which never opens the planted name at all.
issues.note: Same root cause as bug-352, seen from the second caller of the same helper. Filed separately because the anchor is a different file and a caller-level fix is available here.
issues.fix_note: Closed by the flag change in fileperms.open_private (bug-352), which is the shared root this entry note predicted, so the anchor is that line rather than the caller. Caller-level regression in tests/test_update_check.py: a link planted at the cache filename inside the database directory is neither written through nor re-moded, with a control that the ordinary write still lands at 0600. The refusal stays swallowed by _write_cache by design, so the evidence is the untouched victim rather than a raised error.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The documentation-facts check for the calibration default reports a mismatch only where its pattern matches and never asserts that it matched anything (scripts/check-docs-facts.py:524-536). A pattern that stops matching -- through a rewording of the documented sentence or an edit to the expression -- turns the check into a silent pass, and the published claim it guards can then drift without the gate going red. Nothing in the suite covers this particular check, so the vacuity would not be caught elsewhere either. Not reproduced: this is a source reading of the check and the tests around it, not a measured failure.
issues.fix_sketch: Count the matches and fail when a document that is supposed to carry the claim yields none, so a pattern that stops finding its subject reports itself instead of passing.
issues.fix_note: The check now counts its matches across DOC_FILES and fails when the pattern found nothing, so a reworded sentence or an edited expression reports itself instead of turning the gate into a silent pass. Same doctrine the benchmark-table gate in this file already states: a comparison with nothing to compare is a failure, not a skip. Both spellings (English and Japanese) count toward the same subject, and only one page need carry it.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) A repair that fails part way through is committed rather than rolled back, because the runner converts every exception from a check into an ordinary finding (cpersona/checks.py:2584-2591) and therefore nothing escapes the transaction the fix run opened. Reproduced by seeding one row with both JSON columns invalid and arming a trigger that refuses only the second of the repair's two statements: the row was committed half repaired, with the first column rewritten and the second left invalid, while the response carried a crashed-check finding at warn severity and the log said the check crashed. The control without the trigger repaired both columns. The transaction commits on normal return, and a statement-level abort keeps the prior statements of the transaction, so the documented rollback boundary does not hold for repairs.
issues.fix_sketch: Wrap each repairing check in a savepoint and release or roll back to it around the runner, so a failed repair leaves the row as it was while the rest of the run still commits and the crashed-check finding is still reported.
issues.fix_note: Each check under fix runs inside its own savepoint, rolled back on the exception the runner converts into a crashed-check finding, so a repair that raised between its two statements leaves the row as it was while the rest of the run still commits. A re-raise was not available: one failed repair must not discard the others. The run-level savepoint is opened and never released, because RELEASE of an outermost savepoint commits and would have broken the run into per-check commits; transaction() still owns the end of the run. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py drives the injected ABORT on the second repair statement, the no-fault control, and a transaction whose caller raises after the run, which must still discard every repair.

issues.summary: (LOW) The health tool's description promises that source canonicalisation classifies at most 1000 rows per run (cpersona/server.py:1588-1589), while the configured cap defaults to 10000 and the documentation states that number independently. Measured through the served tool with 5000 mappable rows seeded: the live description advertised 1000, the configured cap read 10000, and the response reported 5000 mapped and none remaining. The consequence is a wrong expectation about convergence and about how much work one fix run does, not data corruption.
issues.fix_sketch: Render the number from the configuration constant rather than typing it, the way the same description already renders other derived lists, so it cannot drift from the value that is enforced.
issues.fix_note: The per-run bound is rendered from the enforced constant instead of typed beside it, the way the same description already renders its other derived lists, so the two cannot drift again.

issues.summary: (LOW) The health tool's description says an unknown check name is rejected rather than silently running nothing, and that every response echoes the list of checks run -- but the rejection returns an error envelope built before that list is computed (cpersona/maintenance_handlers.py:42-49), so the one path the sentence was written for is the one path without the field. Measured through the served tool with a mistyped name: the response carried ok false, the unknown names and the valid names, and no checks-run key, and the outer wrapper does not repair the omission. A caller following the documented contract either raises on the missing key or records an empty run, which is indistinguishable from a subset that legitimately executed nothing.
issues.fix_sketch: Include an empty checks-run list in the rejection, since that is both true and what the description promises; the alternative, narrowing the sentence, gives callers a contract with an exception in it.
issues.note: The fix note of the entry that introduced the rejection repeats the same claim, so that text needs correcting with the code.
issues.fix_note: The rejection now carries the empty checks_run the description promises every response echoes. Nothing ran, saying so is true, and a caller can no longer confuse a refused call with a subset that legitimately executed nothing.

issues.summary: (LOW) The deep-check argument description hand-lists six options while eight checks are registered (cpersona/server.py:1721 against cpersona/checks.py:3083-3092), and the same description string renders the report-only list from the registry, so one tool description states two contradictory option sets. Measured through the served tool: the advertised six ran and returned six names, the two undocumented ones ran fine when named explicitly and returned two, and an empty selection ran all eight -- they work, they are simply undiscoverable from the schema. An operator choosing an explicit subset from the description therefore skips two registered probes and gets a response shaped like a full run. The structural gate on this tool pins which checks can repair, not the enumerated option list, so it cannot bite on this drift.
issues.fix_sketch: Render the option list from the registry the way the report-only clause beside it already does, and add a gate pinning the rendered list against the registered names so a new check cannot ship undiscoverable.
issues.fix_note: The option list is rendered from the check registry, as the report-only clause beside it already was, and a regression test pins the advertised set against the registered names so a new check cannot ship undiscoverable.

issues.summary: (LOW) Under a pause, import and merge answer requests that could never have succeeded with a success-shaped skipped response. The pause check runs before path confinement and the file checks in one handler and before argument validation in the other (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:2290, 3099-3119), so a missing file, a path outside the confined directory, a directory, an oversized file, identical source and target agents, an unknown mode and an unknown strategy all came back ok:true with an all-zero tally; unpaused, the same seven calls returned their real errors. That is the opposite of the doctrine a sibling guard in the same file states -- that the pause check sits after pure parameter validation so invalid input still returns the real error -- and the suite pins that doctrine only for the two handlers that already follow it. The responses do carry a not-persisted flag and a reason, so they are distinguishable from a completed write, which is why this is LOW.
issues.pattern: bug-365: the gate follows the argument validation above
issues.fix_sketch: Move both pause checks after the pure validation they currently precede, so a request that is wrong stays wrong whether or not writes are paused -- a rehearsal that reads green because it was skipped is the failure this ordering causes.
issues.fix_note: Both pause gates sit after the pure validation they used to precede, so a request that is wrong stays wrong whether or not writes are paused -- a rehearsal no longer reads green because it was skipped.

issues.summary: (LOW) The queue's attribution reconcile binds one host parameter per held attribution with no chunking (cpersona/tasks.py:141-149), and the map it reads is capped at 4096 -- above the 999-variable floor that every other id list in this package is deliberately split at, with a comment naming that floor. Measured against real SQLite by lowering the connection's variable limit to that floor on the connection the queue actually uses: with 4096 attributions the statement raised too-many-SQL-variables and left every attribution in place, while at the native limit the same reconcile pruned correctly and kept only the live one. On a host with the older ceiling this therefore fails on every pass for as long as the map stays large, and the failure is swallowed by the drain's own handler, so attributions for rows deleted out of band are never forgotten. The onward chain -- the eviction dropping a live session's attribution so its queued write escapes that session's pause -- was not exercised.
issues.pattern: SELECT id FROM pending_memory_tasks WHERE id IN \(\{placeholders\}\)
issues.fix_sketch: Split the read at the same 500-per-statement bound the other id lists use and union the results; the map's own cap then stops being a statement-width decision.

issues.summary: (LOW) The by-id write handlers distinguish, in their error strings, a row that exists and belongs to another agent, a row that exists and is locked, and a row that does not exist. The lock pre-check reads the row with no agent predicate and runs before any ownership test (cpersona/admin_handlers.py:332-353, 386-393, 472-500). Measured through the real authorisation seam with a client granted one agent only: delete distinguished all three states, update distinguished not-owned from locked from missing, and lock and unlock distinguished not-owned from missing, while both foreign rows were left unchanged. The authorisation demand is on the agent_id the caller sends and never learns which agent owns the row, so these messages are the only boundary. The same file shows the intended convention elsewhere, where a single ambiguous message covers all three cases. Content does not cross; existence and lock state do, and no test pins any of these strings.
issues.fix_sketch: Collapse the three refusals into one message on these paths, as the delete result and the episode handlers already do, and put the lock check behind the ownership test so a foreign row is never inspected for it.
issues.fix_note: The by-id write handlers answer a scoped caller with one ambiguous refusal, and the ownership test runs before the lock check so a foreign row is never inspected for it. An unscoped call keeps the specific message, having no ownership predicate to hide behind.

issues.summary: (LOW) The index builder tests the canonical timestamp shape twice with predicates that disagree: the Python side asks whether each position is a digit, which is true for non-ASCII digits, while the SQL side matches an ASCII-only character class (cpersona/vector_index.py:330 against 119 and 55). Measured: a stamp with fullwidth year digits answered true in Python and false in SQL, and the real builder then raised with the message that the embedding pass returned one row while the metadata pass counted two, deleting its temp file. The row set is never shifted -- the SQL predicate is a strict subset -- but the corpus cannot be indexed at all until the offending row is found by hand, and the count mismatch is documented in the builder as the snapshot-isolation check, so the operator is pointed at a concurrent writer that does not exist. The docstring of the streaming pass asserts the two predicates are the same test, which is the claim that is false.
issues.fix_sketch: Restrict the Python test to ASCII digits so it means what the SQL class means; naming the mismatch in the count-check message as a second possible cause would also stop the misdiagnosis, but the predicates should agree first.
issues.fix_note: The Python predicate now tests ASCII digits, which is what the SQL character class means. Pinned as the invariant rather than as the fix: a parametrised test asks both SQLite and Python about the same stamps -- canonical, fullwidth, superscript, wrong separator, sub-second, empty -- and requires the same answer, so a later change to either side that reopens the gap fails. The non-ASCII stamps are written as escapes so the test file stays ASCII.

issues.summary: (LOW) archive_episode stores the episode span as the lexical minimum and maximum of the raw history timestamp strings (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:2286-2288), and byte order equals chronological order only while every stamp carries the same offset. Measured with a history whose first entry is an hour earlier but written in a different offset: the stored row came back with a start after its own end, and the same-offset control was correct. Unlike the read-side ordering defect, this value is written into the row and never recomputed -- it is what the confidence scoring and the content expansion read afterwards, so the episode is ranked and displayed at the wrong instant. The type normalisation added immediately above these lines left the comparison lexical.
issues.pattern: parseable = \[\(instant, stamp\) for stamp in timestamps
issues.fix_sketch: Choose the two ends by parsed instant and store the corresponding original strings, so the stored span names the earliest and latest moments rather than the first and last byte sequences.
issues.note: The write-side counterpart of bug-286, which is the same lexical ordering on the read side over the stored column. Distinct seams: fixing one does not correct the other, and this one persists the wrong value.
issues.fix_note: The two ends are chosen by parsed instant and the original strings are stored. Byte order equals chronological order only while every stamp carries the same offset, and this value is written into the row and never recomputed, so the episode was ranked and displayed at the wrong instant for the rest of its life. Stamps nobody can parse take no part in choosing the ends, and a history where none parse falls back to byte order rather than becoming absent. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py drives the mixed-offset history and the same-offset control.

issues.summary: (LOW) In the default warn mode, recall_with_context reports malformed context entries with a fixed note saying the entries were merged without the offending fields (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:1847-1854), which is true only when the bad field is one of the metadata fields. When the content itself is not a string, or the entry is not a mapping at all, the merge loop skips the entry entirely, and it is also skipped by the exclusion list builder and by the filter-only branch. Measured both ways: a mapping with a numeric content and a bare string entry each produced the report naming index 0 with that note, while the merged conversation carried no turn and the exclusion list handed to recall was empty. The control with a well-formed content and a bad metadata field was reported and merged, so the note is accurate only for that class. The caller renders a conversation that lost a turn while holding a report saying it was merged; nothing else in the payload discloses the drop.
issues.pattern: dropped = \[i for i in field_issues if not _ctx_content
issues.fix_sketch: Split the report by consequence: entries whose metadata was unusable were merged without those fields, entries with no usable content were dropped -- the two are different facts and the caller acts differently on each.
issues.fix_note: The report is split by consequence: entries whose metadata was unusable were merged without those fields, entries with no usable content were dropped, and a mixed batch says both. Merging an entry that carries no usable content would mean inventing content for it, so what changes is the report rather than the merge. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py covers the non-string content and non-mapping shapes and the bad-metadata control.

issues.summary: (LOW) The startup notice for a deployment that keeps no local vectors describes the risk as a remote search outage, but the guard reads only the mode string and the blob setting (cpersona/server.py:2951-2962) and never checks that a remote endpoint is configured at all. Measured with the mode set to remote, blob storage off and an embedding client whose HTTP URL is empty -- the shape an API-mode embedding configuration leaves: store answered ok:true with embedded false, the row's embedding column was NULL, and the findings surface reported nothing above the observation tier. So no vector exists locally and none is pushed remotely, permanently rather than during an outage, and no surface says the remote path was never reachable. The same state arises from a mis-cased mode string, since that setting is read unvalidated and unnormalised while its sibling settings go through a validating parser -- also measured. The boot line itself was read in source rather than executed. Reaching this needs an explicitly non-default configuration and reads stay correct through the keyword arm.
issues.fix_sketch: Ask whether the remote path is actually armed before promising it: with no local blobs and no remote endpoint the vector arm is gone, which deserves a loud refusal at boot rather than an observation, on the same reasoning the embedding-mode assertion beside it already applies.
issues.note: The unvalidated mode string is the same class as bug-321, on a different setting in the same module.
issues.fix_note: Three changes for one state. The setting is read through the choice parser its siblings use, so no third spelling survives to miss both consumers. The boot notice and the maintenance hint now ask whether the remote arm is armed before naming an outage, and say plainly when neither arm holds a vector. The severity is unchanged on purpose: escalating a static per-kind tier moves the checkup gate exit code on a deployment that boots today.

issues.summary: (LOW) The findings layer derives the embedding-backend routing key from the stamped severity alone (cpersona/findings.py:139-142), while the check stamps warn on two states that were deliberately separated: a backend that was asked and did not answer, and a configuration under which no request ever left the process. Both are therefore delivered with the key that names an unanswered backend. Measured end to end on the shipped pull channel, not only on the helper: with the misconfigured fault latched, the check emitted the misconfigured type, status and hint, and the delivered finding carried the unreachable key alongside them, so the payload contradicts its own routing key. A consumer routing on the key -- which is what the key is documented for -- is told to restart a service that was never contacted. The payload itself stays correct, and reaching the latched state is narrow because the startup assertion blocks the unsupported-mode route.
issues.fix_sketch: Derive the key from the payload's own type rather than from the severity, so the two states the check already distinguishes stay distinguished on the way out.

issues.summary: (LOW) The degraded-verification warning is rate-limited on one attribute of the verifier (cpersona/oauth.py:181, 456-460), while every other piece of refresh state is per-issuer, so all configured authorization servers share a single 60-second window. Measured with two issuers on an injected clock: a warning for the first at one moment suppressed the second's ten seconds later, and driven end to end with both issuers' fetches failing, only the first issuer's line was written while the second's identical failure produced no record at all. The same channel carries the pairwise-subject refusal, which is a permanent configuration verdict rather than a transient outage, so an unrelated issuer's flapping can hide the one explanation an operator needs for why a set of clients cannot authenticate. Diagnostics only; no behaviour changes. Nothing in the existing coverage constructs a verifier with two issuers.
issues.pattern: last = entry\.logged_at if entry is not None else self\._outage_logged_at
issues.fix_sketch: Move the last-logged stamp onto the per-issuer state beside the other refresh fields, and consider logging the configuration verdict unconditionally, since rate-limiting a permanent fact only delays the diagnosis.
issues.fix_note: The once-per-cooldown stamp moved onto the per-issuer state beside the other refresh fields, because everything else that decides whether a line is worth writing is per issuer. Shared, one authorization server flapping suppressed anothers identical failure entirely, and the same channel carries the pairwise-subject verdict, which is a permanent configuration fact and the one explanation for why a whole set of clients cannot authenticate. Still rate-limited rather than logged outright: the path is reachable from an unauthenticated request, so writing every occurrence would hand the log to whoever wants to fill it. An issuer with no cache entry -- there is none today -- falls back to the shared stamp rather than logging unbounded.

issues.summary: (LOW) The denial text for the persistence pause tools still says persistence is a process-wide switch that stops writes for every agent the process serves (cpersona/acl.py:483-490). Since the pause became keyed by session, a pause armed with a declared key stops only that key's bucket. Reproduced: a client without a wildcard grant calling pause with a declared key was denied with that sentence, while the companion assertion pinned the ground truth -- a keyed pause leaves both the shared bucket and another session unpaused -- and the tool description on the other surface states the keyed radius correctly. So the server states both readings, and an operator reading the denial may widen the client's grant far beyond what the keyed call needed. Wording only; the wildcard demand itself is intentional and no authorisation or data behaviour changes.
issues.pattern: persistence is a process-wide switch, so pausing it stops writes for
issues.fix_sketch: Restate the cause the way the tool description does -- the widest bucket, not the widest radius -- so the denial explains why a wildcard grant is demanded without asserting an effect the call does not have.

issues.summary: (LOW) The update refresh awaits a network fetch and then stores its verdict unconditionally (cpersona/update_check.py:473-479), with no check that a newer verdict landed while it was waiting. Measured by driving both real entry points against one transport that answers the startup fetch late with an older index and the explicit refresh immediately with a newer one: the refresh returned the newer version, and once the delayed response arrived the module reported the older one, in memory and in the cache file. The window is narrow -- the interleaving is only possible while the startup fetch is outstanding, which its own timeout bounds at three seconds -- and the consequence is a stale advisory version for up to the cache interval on a notice-only surface, with no effect on stored data or recall.
issues.fix_sketch: Compare the fetch time against the stored one and keep the newer verdict, so a slow response cannot overwrite a fresher answer that arrived while it was in flight.
issues.fix_note: A verdict is stored only when no fresher answer landed while this fetch was in flight, and the same check guards the cache file, which is written first and would otherwise outlive the process that declined it. The ordering key moved from when a response arrived to when its fetch was issued: stamping on arrival makes the slower answer look like the newer one, which is exactly backwards. An unparseable stamp orders as not superseded, because a stamp this module did not write can only come from a cache file and refusing on it would freeze the verdict rather than correct it.

issues.summary: (LOW) The invalid-source check decides whether its scan was exhaustive with a strict comparison against the classification cap (cpersona/checks.py:2000), so a scan that returned exactly the cap -- an exhaustive one -- is treated as truncated. Measured with the cap lowered to three and exactly three mappable offenders: the fix run repaired all three and reported none remaining, yet still answered with no repairable count, a classified field, and the hint saying to run fix again until it stops decreasing. The control one below the cap was reported correctly, so this is the boundary and not the scenario. One claimed consequence does not hold and is not carried here: driving the public health handler at the same boundary returned healthy, because the post-fix residual pass recomputes the verdict. What remains is three wrong fields in the payload of a converged run.
issues.fix_sketch: Ask for one row past the cap and classify the cap's worth, so exhaustion is answered by whether that extra row exists rather than by a count that is ambiguous exactly at the boundary.
issues.fix_note: The scan asks for one row past the cap and classifies the cap's worth, so exhaustion is answered by whether that extra row exists instead of by a count that is ambiguous at exactly the boundary. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py drives the cap lowered to three at two, three and four offenders -- three being both the boundary and where a converged fix run lands.

issues.summary: (LOW) The calibration staleness check floors the age to whole days and requires it to exceed the threshold (cpersona/checks.py:2847-2853), so a calibration one second past the 90-day threshold still reports as fresh. Measured with a matching scoring version and a sidecar stamped just past the threshold: the check answered ok at 90 days and one second and again at 90 days and nearly 24 hours, turning stale only at 91 days -- a false-freshness window a full day wide. The cost is small: the check is report-only and nothing gates on it, so the error is a delay of up to one day on a 90-day advisory.
issues.fix_sketch: Compare total elapsed seconds against the threshold in seconds and keep the floored day count for the report, so the number shown stays readable while the decision is exact.
issues.fix_note: The decision is made on elapsed seconds against the threshold in seconds; the floored day count is kept for the report so the number shown stays readable. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py drives the two ages inside the old blind window (90d 1s and 90d 23h 59m), the 91-day control, and a fresh sidecar that must stay ok.

issues.summary: (LOW) The future-timestamp check compares through SQLite's datetime function while the shared boundary is rendered with whole seconds (cpersona/checks.py:1464-1468, cpersona/utils.py:221-223), so both sides are truncated to the second and a row just past the allowance is missed. Measured with the reference instant frozen at a fractional moment: the shared policy reported the row as 300.8 seconds ahead against a 300-second allowance, while the health run for that check returned no issue at all; a control row two whole seconds past the allowance was found normally. The blind window is under one second wide and the row has to carry fractional seconds, so this is a precision gap between two paths that are supposed to agree rather than a missed class of rows.
issues.fix_sketch: Compare the stored strings against the boundary directly, or render the boundary and the compared value with the same subsecond precision, so the SQL detector and the shared verdict cannot disagree about the same row.
issues.note: Neighbouring but distinct from bug-294, which is the scoring path's clamp on a stamp already stored ahead of the clock; this is the detector that decides whether such a row is reported at all.
issues.fix_note: The boundary is rendered with its subsecond part (cpersona/utils.py) and the SQL predicate compares with strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%f', ...) on both sides, because SQLite's datetime() answers whole seconds whatever it is handed -- so the health check and the shared verdict now draw 'ahead' in the same place. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py drives a row 0.8s past the allowance against a frozen reference, the whole-second control, and a row exactly at the boundary that must stay unflagged.

issues.summary: (LOW) The NULL-embedding repair swallows every per-row exception (cpersona/checks.py:797-798) and the repaired count is added to the finding only when it is positive, so a repair that failed is indistinguishable from one that was never attempted. Measured with one NULL row, an embedding client that answers, and a proxy raising a disk error on the update: the fix run returned a finding byte-identical to the report-only run taken in the same test, and the row stayed NULL. What is lost is only the repair outcome -- the finding, its count, its critical severity and its repairable field are all still reported, and the health handler re-runs a residual pass, so the rows themselves are not hidden.
issues.fix_sketch: Count the failures alongside the successes and report them in the finding, so an operator can tell a repair that could not run from a corpus that needed none.
issues.fix_note: The re_embedded count is reported whether or not it is positive, so a fix run that repaired nothing is distinguishable from a report-only run that never attempted one; a zero under fix is an outcome. The per-row guard stays non-fatal -- one unembeddable row must not abort the pass -- but logs the row and the reason instead of discarding it. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py, with the repair WRITE raising and the row measured to be still NULL. The registry's sketch asked for a separate failure count, which would have added a response field this line does not take.

issues.summary: (LOW) The invalid-JSON check wraps both count queries in one guard that returns no findings (cpersona/checks.py:1335-1349), so a failure on the second query throws away the count the first one already produced. Measured with a control in the same run: a row with unparseable source JSON is detected normally, and with a proxy raising a locked-database error on the second count the health run returned no issues and an all-zero summary -- and no crashed-check finding could be synthesised either, because the exception never escapes. The window needs a query-level failure, which had to be injected; malformed stored JSON alone was not shown to make the count raise. The check is registered at warn rather than critical, and no data is lost -- only the finding.
issues.fix_sketch: Let the exception escape to the runner, which already turns it into a crashed-check finding, or report the counts that did succeed alongside a note that one column could not be read -- discarding both is the one answer that says nothing true.
issues.fix_note: The two counts are no longer wrapped in one guard, so a failure on the second cannot discard the corruption the first already counted, and the exception reaches the runner. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py, with the both-queries-succeed control in the same test.

issues.summary: (LOW) The maintenance command's human-readable deep output only prints a result carrying a count, a pair count, an error, or a non-ok status (cpersona/checkup.py:37-44), and the anonymous-source deep check emits none of those -- it reports recoverable and unrecoverable counts with samples. Measured end to end: a row whose source carries no identity and whose content begins with a name produced a recoverable count of one from the deep handler, while the filter returned nothing, so the non-JSON run prints no deep finding. The repair case is the same by construction, adding only another unrecognised key, and was read rather than run. The blast radius is bounded by a second measurement that passed: the ordinary health check reports the same row with a count and a hint pointing at the deep repair, so what this hides is the repairability detail and the repair result, not the row.
issues.fix_sketch: Decide interestingness from the result rather than from a fixed key list -- any non-zero numeric field, or an explicit emptiness marker on each runner -- so a new check cannot ship invisible to the human-readable output.
issues.fix_note: The human-readable filter now reads a declared set of finding-count keys (count / pairs / recoverable / unrecoverable) instead of a hand-written list, so the anonymous-source counts are printed. Not "any non-zero number in the result": the same results carry threshold, tolerance, rows_scanned and age_days, and reading those as findings would print every check on every run. A structural test asserts every registered deep check reports on one of those keys or on status, so a check added later cannot ship invisible to a non-JSON run.

issues.summary: (LOW) The health response echoes the requested check names verbatim while the runner deduplicates them into a set, so a repeated name is reported as two runs of one execution (cpersona/maintenance_handlers.py:49 against cpersona/checks.py:2578). Measured with a name passed twice against a corpus holding one offending row: the response echoed the name twice while the registry produced exactly one issue and a summary counting one warning, so the echoed list disagrees with the counts beside it. The singleton control was correct. A reporting inconsistency in one field: no rows are affected and no repair runs twice.
issues.fix_sketch: Echo the names the runner actually selected, deduplicated in the same way, so the list and the counts describe one run.
issues.fix_note: checks_run now echoes the names the runner actually selected, deduplicated the way the runner deduplicates them, so the echoed list and the counts beside it describe one run. dict.fromkeys keeps the caller order while collapsing the repeat.

issues.summary: (LOW) The apply path caps the output it returns but not the output it buffers: the child's whole merged stream is read to end of file, decoded and split into a full list before the last 40 lines are sliced off (cpersona/update_check.py:863-874, 919). Measured by driving the real apply path with one hermetic step writing 30.3 MB to standard output: it returned applied with an output tail of exactly 40 lines while tracing 107.9 MB of peak allocation, 3.6x the stream. Narrower than it looks: applying is opt-in and the steps it runs are the ordinary install commands, so producing a stream large enough to matter means controlling the package being installed, at which point code is already executing.
issues.fix_sketch: Read the stream line by line into a bounded ring of the tail length, so the cap describes what is held rather than what is returned.
issues.fix_note: The step output is read in fixed-size chunks into a ring of the tail length instead of being buffered whole and sliced afterwards, so the cap describes what is held and not only what is returned. Fixed-size reads rather than readline because a stream reader raises on a line longer than its own limit and a step that writes without newlines is exactly the case the bound is for; an unterminated run keeps its end and not its start, which is what tail means everywhere else here. The process double in the tests grew the stdout reader the real one has, since it had only ever offered communicate.

issues.summary: (LOW) The near-duplicate deep check takes every non-NULL embedding into its normalisation and similarity product with no finiteness test (cpersona/checks.py:2874-2892), and a comparison against the threshold is false for a non-finite value. Measured with two rows differing in one component, one carrying a NaN: the check returned no pairs, no error and no field naming the row it could not compare -- unlike the mixed-width branch beside it, which does say why it returned nothing -- while the finite control on the same two rows reported the pair above the threshold. Two measurements bound the damage: a third row with an infinite component did not suppress an unrelated finite pair when driven through the shipped deep handler, so the loss is confined to pairs involving the bad row, and the ordinary health check does report that row through its own non-finite probe. A report-only diagnostic silently omitting a merge candidate, not a corpus or read-path fault.
issues.pattern: non_finite = \[r\[0\] for r in rows if not vector\.stored_blob_is_finite
issues.fix_sketch: Filter the sample with the same finiteness helper the storage seam and the non-finite probe already use, and report the excluded rows the way the mixed-width branch reports its own refusal.
issues.note: Third site of the same missing guard: bug-343 writes such a blob and bug-312 lets one poison the calibrated threshold. Distinct seams, one shared helper.
issues.fix_note: The sample is filtered with the same finiteness helper the storage seam and the non-finite probe use, and the exclusion is disclosed in the field the mixed-width refusal beside it already uses. No ids are added: those rows belong to the nonfinite_embedding registry entry, which already lists them. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py, with a finite control that must gain no note and the infinite-component case that already passed, kept as a bound.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) list_memories and list_episodes clamp the caller's `limit` to 500 and 200 rows, and that ceiling is published nowhere a caller can see. `do_list_memories` passes `_clamp_limit(limit, 500)` into the LIMIT (admin_handlers.py:240) and `do_list_episodes` passes `_clamp_limit(limit, 200)` (admin_handlers.py:293), while the two published `limit` properties declare a default and no `maximum` (server.py:1185, server.py:1214) and neither tool description mentions a cap; `budget_chars` is attached only when the bug-255 CHARACTER budget bites (admin_handlers.py:265-268), never when the ROW cap does. Measured: 510 memories stored for one agent, then `do_list_memories(agent, 1000)` returned 500 rows with keys `count` and `memories` and no truncation marker of any kind. The sibling reads publish theirs -- recall / recall_with_context declare `maximum: 100` in the schema and explain the library/agent split in prose -- so these two are the only capped reads whose cap is stated on no surface. A consumer applying the ordinary "count < limit means end of data" rule stops at 500, and nothing in the response distinguishes a capped answer from a complete one.
issues.note: Split in 2.5.12b3, and open for the half that is not freeze-eligible. CLOSED HERE (adds nothing to the contract): the two bare literals became one named constant each (admin_handlers.LIST_MEMORIES_MAX_ROWS / LIST_EPISODES_MAX_ROWS), the clamp and the tool descriptions render the same value, and the sentence that read 'none is dropped' now says which bound it speaks of -- so the ceiling is discoverable where a caller reads, and the published number cannot drift from the one the handler clamps by. STILL OPEN: declaring `maximum` in the two schemas would refuse calls that succeed today, and attaching a truncation marker would add a key to a documented response; neither restores established behaviour, so both belong to the next line, where the row cap and the bug-255 character budget can be given one reporting shape instead of a marker for one and silence for the other. Documenting the cap does not make a capped answer distinguishable from a complete one at runtime, which is the half this entry stays open for.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) `session_key` is accepted with no length bound while every map keyed on it is capped by entry count rather than by bytes, so retained memory is 256 times whatever the caller chose to send. `resolve_session_key` states the absence as deliberate -- "No length limit, no format validation, no sanitization beyond strip()" (session.py:61) -- and returns the stripped string verbatim, and the schema property that publishes the parameter carries no `maxLength` (server.py:471). The resolved string then keys three process-global maps, each bounded at 256 entries: `session._pauses` (session.py:105, 203, 213), `health._told_sessions` (health.py:320) and `update_check._told_sessions` (update_check.py:569); the last two have no TTL, so their bytes are held until a 257th distinct key arrives or the process restarts. Measured: `resolve_session_key` returned a 65,536-character key unchanged with declared=True, and after 400 distinct 64 KiB keys both advisory maps held exactly 256 entries retaining 16.8 MB each; nothing in the test suite asserts a length bound. The shipped HTTP posture does not narrow it either -- CPERSONA_HTTP_BODY_LIMIT_MODE defaults to `warn` (config.py:352), so the 4 MiB body budget refuses nothing -- and the two advisory maps are populated by any `recall` that declares a key while a newer release exists or the embedding backend is degraded.
issues.pattern: No length limit, no format validation
issues.note: Deferred out of the frozen 2.5 line: the bound belongs on the published parameter as a `maxLength` refused at the boundary, and declaring one refuses calls that succeed today -- a change to the tool contract that a fix release on this line does not make. The caps that exist are not themselves the defect and count the right thing for their own purpose (which sessions have been told, which are paused); what is missing is a statement of what one key may weigh, which is a decision about the parameter rather than about the maps.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The `external_context` item schema declares all five fields as `{"type": "string"}` (server.py:969-982) and the MCP SDK validates arguments against `inputSchema` before dispatch, so a non-string `role` / `content` / `name` / `user_id` / `timestamp` is refused at the boundary -- which makes the documented default behaviour unreachable over MCP. The same tool's description promises the opposite: such a field is read as absent, the entry is merged, and the call answers with `context_field_issues` (server.py:942-944); the mode defaults to `warn` (config.py:370-371) and the handler implements it at memory_handlers.py:1847-1854. Measured against the live registered schema: an entry carrying an epoch-int timestamp raises `1735689600 is not of type 'string'`, while `do_recall_with_context` given the same entry returns the merged message plus `context_field_issues: {entries:[{index:0, fields:['timestamp']}]}`. So the warn path, the `off` path and the fail-soft readers behind them are reachable only by library callers, and the MCP caller gets an SDK error result with no `messages` key at all -- losing the recall hits that were already available, against the bug-232 rule that a failing recall still carries `messages: []`. tests/test_external_context_shape.py pins both halves at once: line 244-246 asserts every declared field is a string and line 225 asserts the mode default is `warn`.
issues.pattern: 'user' or 'assistant'; other roles filter the recall
issues.note: Deferred out of the frozen 2.5 line: reconciling the two means moving one published surface -- widening the item types so the warn mode can run at the boundary, or withdrawing the promise from the description -- and either is a change to the tool contract rather than a fix release's work. It joins the next feature line, where the three settings of the mode can be given one shape at the boundary and in the handler. Neighbouring but distinct from bug-292, which declared the three previously undeclared fields and what they mean: that work is what put the types in the schema, and this is the separate question of what the boundary should do with a value that is not one.
issues.fix_note: The five item fields state their expectation in their descriptions instead of enforcing it at the boundary, so the documented fail-soft reading, the warn default and the off setting are reachable over MCP again, and a reported entry answers with messages rather than an SDK error carrying none. Widening the schema restores documented behaviour and refuses nothing that works today.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The vector index reports one of the three row groups its query path reads exactly, so the documented staleness signal can read zero while every recall pays for thousands of rows. `_status` counts only `id > watermark AND embedding IS NOT NULL` (vector_index.py:503-521) under a comment claiming it counts "Rows the index cannot answer for and the scan reads exactly", and renders it as "N rows written since the build" (vector_index.py:543); the two hole groups -- `excluded_ids` and the bug-278 `unembedded_ids` -- are read on every query (vector.py:786, vector.py:838-845) and appear in neither that number nor `build_index`, which reports `"excluded": len(excluded)` (vector_index.py:320) although the cap is checked against the sum of both (vector_index.py:236-244). Measured: 3 embedded rows plus 5 rows with NULL embeddings below the watermark built to `excluded: 0` with `unembedded_ids == (4,5,6,7,8)`; after the embeddings were filled, `_status()` still answered `rows_since_build: 0` while the tail read returned 5 rows on every query. Filling those embeddings is exactly what `check_health(fix=True)` does, so the ordinary repair converts a named hole into a permanent per-query cost -- sized at roughly 65 ms per query at the 10,000 cap by config.py:202-220 -- that nothing an operator can query reports, while docs/operations.md:262-275 tells them `status` shows how far behind the index is.
issues.note: Deferred out of the frozen 2.5 line: the fix adds counters to the `status` and build results, which is a change to a documented response shape, and a fix release on this line does not add keys a consumer may then depend on. It belongs with the next feature line beside the same omission in the health check (`vector_index_tail_grown`, checks.py:2318-2332), which counts the same partial row set under a hint about the tail being read on every query -- so both get one definition of "behind" rather than two. The row groups and the query answers are correct; what is wrong is only what is reported about them. Re-judged against the freeze conditions in 2.5.12b3 and the deferral holds, for a reason worth recording so it is not re-opened: the tempting cheap fix is to leave the keys alone and make `rows_since_build` count all three groups, but docs/operations.md makes two claims about `status` -- that it reports how many rows have been WRITTEN SINCE the build, and that it shows how far behind the index is -- and the excluded and unembedded rows were written BEFORE it. Widening that number satisfies the second sentence by making the first false, which is a redefinition rather than a restoration. So the fix really is new counters, and it belongs with the health check's identical omission so that 'behind' gets one definition.

issues.summary: (LOW) docs/behavior-contracts.md:57-59 tells callers that `match_reason` is absent on the injected profile row, and under confidence scoring it is present. The scoring loop assigns `_confidence_score` to every row with no exclusion for the `id == -1` sentinel (memory_handlers.py:1229-1250), `_gate_score` finds that signal (memory_handlers.py:723-741), and the response loop emits `match_reason` for any row it scores (memory_handlers.py:1500-1508). Measured over a 50-row corpus plus the profile row with autocut off and the limit above the corpus size, so nothing else could remove it: with confidence on, the profile message came back as `{'content': '[Profile] ...', 'source': {'System': 'profile'}, 'confidence': {...}, 'match_reason': {'signal': 'confidence', 'score': 0.8383}}` and outscored every real hit (best 0.5215); the confidence-off control came back without the key, as the sentence says. The sentence sits inside the section describing the confidence-on configuration while section 7 of the same document (lines 203-215) states the confidence-on behaviour correctly, so the document contradicts itself and section 2 is the half the code refutes. A consumer using key presence to separate injected rows from retrieved ones reads the profile as the top-ranked hit; it stays independently identifiable by `source == {"System": "profile"}` and by carrying no `ref`, which is why this is LOW.
issues.pattern: With confidence on, the profile row is scored like any other and
issues.note: Deferred out of the frozen 2.5 line: the sentence is a published behaviour contract callers are told to branch on, and correcting what it promises for a documented configuration changes that contract rather than fixing a typo in it. It goes with the next feature line beside bug-390, the missing precondition in section 7 of the same document, so the two sections are rewritten once against one description of the behaviour instead of drifting apart again. No runtime change is warranted: the code does what section 7 already describes.
issues.fix_note: Section 3 now says the injected profile row carries match_reason under confidence and omits it only with confidence off, which is what the scoring loop and the response loop do. Rewritten together with the section 7 precondition against one description of the behaviour, which is why this was held for a pair. Regression: tests/test_docs_behavioural_claims.py measures the row carrying match_reason under confidence and quotes the sentence, so a rewrite that drops the correction is red.

issues.summary: (LOW) The profile row is suppressed entirely when the pooled row count is under 50, and docs/behavior-contracts.md:210-215 names `limit` as the only thing that cuts it. `_apply_quality_gate` drops the `id == -1` sentinel before any score branch unless `memory_count >= 50` (memory_handlers.py:795-802), and that count is the summed memories+episodes pool for the recall's isolation scope (memory_handlers.py:1357-1360), so the rule applies with confidence on as well as off. Measured: on a 30-memory pool with a query no stored row answers -- so `limit` cuts nothing -- a confidence-on recall returned `messages=[]`, while the 50-row control in the same run returned the profile, which puts the threshold rather than `limit` or scoring behind the removal. The runtime rule is canonical and intentional (docs/architecture.md:143-148, docs/configuration.md:19-20, pinned at 49-refuse / 50-accept by tests/test_docs_behavioural_claims.py:575-622); what is defective is only section 7, which promises that with confidence on profile rows "reliably surface near the top" without stating the precondition, and the response carries no counter saying the row was blocked rather than missing.
issues.pattern: The row is dropped \*\*before any scoring branch\*\*

issues.summary: (LOW) update_profile answers a refused no-op with `ok: true` and no field on the axis callers are told to branch on. `do_update_profile` returns `{"ok": True, "profiles_updated": 0, "reason": "empty profile"}` (admin_handlers.py:108) and the same shape with "empty after sanitization" for text that sanitizes away (admin_handlers.py:112), while the handler's own docstring calls that outcome a refusal (admin_handlers.py:91-93) and docs/behavior-contracts.md section 10 tells callers to branch on `ok is false` or on an `error` key -- neither of which appears. Measured: after storing a real profile, `do_update_profile(agent, " ")` and `do_update_profile(agent, "[Memory from alice] ")` both returned `{'ok': True, 'profiles_updated': 0, 'reason': 'empty after sanitization'}` with the old profile still stored, and the registered tool entry point behaves identically. The refusal is not undetectable -- `profiles_updated == 0` and `reason` are both present and already pinned by tests/test_253_silent_failures.py:58-76 -- but neither is named in the tool description, which mentions only `truncated` (server.py:1077-1086), so a caller following the published rule records a stale profile as saved and that profile keeps being injected into every recall. issues.note: Deferred out of the frozen 2.5 line: the fix is a refusal contract -- either the response gains `ok:false` / `result:'rejected'` as its sibling has, or the description names the fields a caller must read -- and both change what a documented response promises, which a fix release on this line does not do. The narrower half of the claim is what reproduced: the outcome is distinguishable to a caller that reads `profiles_updated`, so this is a gap for a caller following the published branch rule rather than an undetectable write loss.
issues.fix_note: A refused profile write now answers on the axis docs/behavior-contracts.md section 10 names: both branches (empty, and text that sanitises away) return ok:false, matching the store seam this path shares, which calls the same two inputs a rejection. The pause branch stays ok:true -- a no-persist skip is nothing going wrong, and the queue drain routes ok:false into its retry path. Nothing was added to the response: reason and profiles_updated were already there and already pinned. The bug-188 exact-dict pin in tests/test_253_silent_failures.py encoded the old verdict as a side effect of pinning the reason, and was rewritten to assert the two fields it exists for.

issues.summary: (LOW) get_queue_status returns two different shapes across a documented configuration knob: the enabled branch carries `max_retries` and `retry_delay` (tasks.py:167-172) while the disabled branch is a two-key literal `{"enabled": False, "pending": 0}` (admin_handlers.py:3215-3217). The two constants are module-level (config.py:496-497) and exist whether or not the queue runs, so nothing prevents reporting them; an operator on that deployment simply cannot read the retry configuration from the tool that advertises it, and a panel reading those keys breaks on that deployment only.
issues.note: Deferred out of the frozen 2.5 line: adding the two keys changes the observable response on the disabled branch, and a fix release on this line does not make fields appear in a shape a consumer already reads. It belongs with the next feature line beside the other asymmetries between a tool's live and inert branches (the bug-104 / bug-111 class), so one rule covers them.
