issues.fix_note: The inert branch now reports the retry state three published surfaces promise unconditionally (the tool description "pending tasks, retry config", docs/tools.md "Depth and retry state", docs/architecture.md "reports depth and retries"). The two values are module-level constants that exist whether or not a queue runs, so the fix reports what was already there rather than adding a field: both branches now answer on the same keys, and a dashboard reading them no longer breaks on the queue-disabled deployment only.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The episode-session boundary is chosen by byte order over `created_at`, so a row that spells the separator differently wins the comparison whatever instant it names. `_get_episode_boundary_ts` takes `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1` (memory_handlers.py:913-916) and SQLite compares that TEXT column byte by byte: every row this server writes carries `datetime('now')` with a space separator, but `import_memories` and `merge_memories` write the record's own value through `COALESCE(?, datetime('now'))` with no format validation (admin_handlers.py:2510-2522, admin_handlers.py:2938-2951), and 'T' (0x54) sorts above ' ' (0x20) at column 10. Measured directly in SQLite: given '2026-09-06 10:00:00' and '2026-09-06T00:00:00Z', the ORDER BY returns the second -- an instant ten hours earlier. The boundary feeds `_episode_boundary_factor` (memory_handlers.py:874-890), which multiplies `_cosine` / `_rrf_score` / `_rsf_score` at memory_handlers.py:1200-1210, so a boundary pulled backwards scores prior-session rows as current-session, and one imported stamp in the future decays every memory in the scope toward EPISODE_DECAY_FLOOR on every recall -- with nothing in the response saying which episode set it. That the import path carries a caller's own `created_at` is not hypothetical here: vector_index.py:58-59 exists because of it.
issues.pattern: ORDER BY datetime\(created_at\) DESC, created_at DESC LIMIT 1
issues.note: Deferred out of the frozen 2.5 line: the boundary is a scoring input, and changing how it is selected changes ranking -- the axis the pre-release ladder exists to keep readable -- so it joins the scoring rework on the next feature line rather than moving while this one soaks. A neighbouring seam to the open bug-286 and not the same defect: that one is MIN/MAX over `memories.timestamp` in the span statement and turns on differing UTC offsets, while this is a different statement and a different column where two stamps in the same offset still order backwards on the separator alone. Validating `created_at` at the import seam is the other half of the answer and is a decision about what the import may carry, which is a second reason this is not a spot fix.
issues.fix_note: The boundary is ordered by instant. Re-judged rather than carried forward as deferred: datetime() answers the same normalised form for both separator spellings, so on a corpus whose rows already agree the boundary does not move, and the ordering changes only where it was already wrong. Rows whose stamp cannot be read sort last instead of winning on their bytes. Validating created_at at the import seam is the other half named in this entry and is a decision about what an import may carry, so it is not made here. Regression: tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py drives the same-date pair that inverts on the separator, plus a uniformly spelled control that must be unchanged.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Calibration picks the modal embedding dimension twice, independently, so on a mixed-dimension corpus the separation threshold is placed between two different models. `_temporal_adjacency_sims` selects its positive proxy with `ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT ?` and reduces to its own modal width (admin_handlers.py:717-743); `_sample_embeddings` selects the null population with `ORDER BY RANDOM() LIMIT ?` and reduces to its own (admin_handlers.py:1246-1273); `do_calibrate_threshold` hands both to one threshold sweep (admin_handlers.py:1467-1476) with nothing constraining the two widths to agree. Measured on one agent holding 300 older 16-wide rows and 150 newest 8-wide rows at the default sample size and the `separation` method: the null sample resolved to (132, 16) while the adjacency window resolved to the 8-wide population, giving a null mean of -0.0015 against a positive mean of 0.0226 and `new_threshold: 0.2485` -- and the response and the sidecar recorded `embedding_dim: 16`, the null's width, with nothing recording that the positives came from elsewhere. A model swap is precisely when the newest rows are one model and the corpus majority another, and it is also when `ensure_calibrated_on_startup` fires, so a threshold describing neither population is written to `vector._agent_thresholds` and persisted. Distinct from the open bug-250, which is about unit-norm versus raw dot at a single width.
issues.note: Deferred out of the frozen 2.5 line: any fix decides what a threshold means on a mixed-dimension corpus -- agreeing the two samples on one width, or refusing to calibrate while two are live -- and both change the number recall gates on, so it joins the scoring rework on the next feature line rather than moving while this one soaks. The per-sample modal reduction is not itself the defect: each was added so a ragged array cannot abort calibration, and deleting either restores that crash. What is missing is a constraint between them plus a record of which width the positives came from, and the latter is also a change to the calibration response and its sidecar.
issues.fix_note: The positive proxy is now drawn at the width the null sample settled on, instead of voting on one of its own: one threshold sweep is handed both populations, so they have to describe the same model. _modal_width also breaks ties deterministically now (bug-344), so the vote itself is a property of the corpus rather than of the scan. Distinct from the open bug-250, which is about unit-norm versus raw dot at a single width.

issues.summary: (LOW) The calibration positive proxy keeps the lexicographically largest timestamps rather than the chronologically newest ones. `_temporal_adjacency_sims` -- the proxy source for the default `separation` method (config.py:559) -- selects `ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT ?` over a TEXT column (admin_handlers.py:722-726) that is caller-supplied (memory_handlers.py:143), so a client stamping in a local offset and one stamping in UTC fill the same column and the LIMIT can keep an older row while dropping a newer one. Measured: rows stamped '2026-09-06T09:00:00+09:00' (= 00:00Z), '2026-09-06T01:00:00+00:00' and '2026-09-06T02:00:00+00:00' with `ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 2` returned the +09:00 row -- the oldest -- and dropped the chronologically middle one. `_adjacency_sims_core` then re-sorts by parsed epoch and pairs consecutive rows within the window, so pairs it treats as same-session neighbours were not adjacent in the corpus, while the null population it is compared against is drawn with `ORDER BY RANDOM()`, so only one of the two is skewed. The output is a mis-placed vector similarity floor written into `vector._agent_thresholds` and persisted to the calibration sidecar, with nothing in the response distinguishing it from a correctly measured one.
issues.note: Deferred out of the frozen 2.5 line: the sample decides the threshold, so re-selecting it moves the gate every recall is filtered by -- a ranking change that joins the scoring rework on the next feature line rather than landing while this one soaks. Ordering by the parsed instant also gives up the index seek, the same trade-off the open bug-286 records at the span statement: same TEXT-versus-instant root cause, a different site, and a different consequence -- which rows are sampled rather than which span is reported. bug-287 is the third site of the family and was repaired on its own because there the ordering runs in Python over rows already in memory and costs only a parse.
issues.fix_note: The window is ordered by the parsed instant rather than the raw TEXT. `timestamp` is caller-supplied, so a client stamping an offset and one stamping UTC fill the same column and a byte-order cut kept an older row while dropping a newer one. SQLite's datetime() normalises every spelling this package writes (offset, Z, space separator, fractional seconds), measured against all of them, and answers NULL for what it cannot read -- which sorts last under DESC, and those rows were dropped by the parser downstream anyway.

issues.summary: (LOW) The API embedding path leaves an all-zero vector un-normalised and returns it as usable. `_embed_via_api` divides by the norm only when it clears the guard -- `if norm > 1e-9: vec = vec / norm` (embedding_client.py:484-487) -- and the branch that skips the division appends the vector unchanged, while wire validation refuses empty, oversized, wrong-width, non-numeric and non-finite vectors (embedding_client.py:361-408) and has no case for a norm of zero. The documented contract is that stored embeddings are unit-norm because scoring is a raw dot product (docs/getting-started.md, the contract section; the scorer at vector.py:481-506). So a backend answering with an all-zero finite vector has it accepted, marked successful, cached and persisted, and every recall scores it at exactly zero: the memory is stored and silently absent from vector results until it is re-embedded.
issues.note: Deferred out of the frozen 2.5 line: deciding what a zero-norm answer is -- a refusal at the wire validator, or a vector recorded as unusable -- changes what is stored and what is scored, and it lands on the same unit-norm invariant the open bug-250 is already holding for the next feature line, so the two belong together rather than one step apart. The guard itself is not the defect: dividing by a zero norm turns the whole vector into NaN, which is what the surrounding comment exists to prevent; what is missing is any branch that treats the un-normalised result as a failure. Detection of the resulting row is already shipped by bug-250's norm check, so the observable state is monitored -- only the acceptance is not.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) store's published schema declares `message.source` as `{"type": "object"}` (server.py:734-735) while the same schema's own description promises that a bare 'user' / 'assistant' string and a null source are normalized at the write seam (server.py:716-719, server.py:743-744). The MCP SDK validates arguments against `inputSchema` before dispatch, so both promised shapes die at the boundary and the handler is never entered, although `normalize_source` handles them (memory_handlers.py:140-142, utils.py:527-541) -- the defect bug-233 fixed one field down, on the `source.type` enum, still standing on the parent field. Measured against the live registered schema: `source: 'user'` raises "'user' is not of type 'object'" and `source: None` raises "None is not of type 'object'", while `do_store` called directly with each returns `{'ok': True, 'result': 'stored'}`, and the pinned SDK does run `jsonschema.validate` before dispatch -- so the mismatch is load-bearing and the call dies before the handler, producing an SDK error rather than a `result:'rejected'` envelope. The caller gets an explicit input-validation error rather than a silent loss and only legacy compatibility shapes are affected, which is why this is MEDIUM rather than higher. tests/test_source_normalization.py:439-446 exists to assert that the published schema lets the documented legacy calls through, and validates only the lowercase-type dict, so neither promised shape is covered.
issues.note: Deferred out of the frozen 2.5 line: the fix widens the published input schema so `message.source` admits a string and a null beside an object, and a schema change is what the current line preserves rather than makes. Withdrawing the two promises from the description instead is the alternative and carries the same weight in the other direction -- which of the two is right is a decision about how long the legacy producer shapes are supported, and that belongs with the next feature line. Whichever is taken, the test that pins the schema against the shapes the seam folds needs the bare-string and null cases: the gap in that test is what let the parent field keep the shape bug-233 removed from the child.
issues.fix_note: The parent field admits the two shapes its own description promises the write seam folds, which is the defect bug-233 removed from the child field. The schema test now covers the bare role word and the null, the gap that let the parent keep the shape.

issues.summary: (LOW) recall's `exclude_contents` schema states that entries are matched starts-with (server.py:868-869), and an entry shorter than 32 characters must in fact match exactly. `_content_excluded` applies the bug-217 floor: below `EXCLUDE_PREFIX_MIN_CHARS = 32` (utils.py:49) only a case-insensitive equality excludes anything and the prefix test is skipped (utils.py:70-76). Measured: with 'Deploy approved by the team on Friday afternoon' stored and confirmed retrievable, `exclude_contents=['deploy approved']` (15 characters) left the row in the response, while a 35-character prefix in the same run filtered it -- so the published rule holds only above a floor stated nowhere on the tool surface. The floor is deliberate and desirable and is pinned by tests/test_bug217_exclude_floor.py:44-73; what is defective is that the description carries no length qualification, and recall_with_context builds this list automatically from every external_context entry's content (memory_handlers.py:1777), so short conversational turns land under the floor in ordinary use and the caller gets back the duplication the parameter exists to prevent.
issues.note: Deferred out of the frozen 2.5 line: stating the floor where a caller reads it means changing the published parameter schema, and a schema change is what the current line preserves rather than makes. Lowering or removing the floor is not the alternative -- that restores bug-217, where a two-character acknowledgement arriving through external_context prefix-suppressed every memory starting with it, inside the retrievers and with nothing in the response reporting the exclusion. The runtime behaviour is right; only the sentence a caller sizes an exclusion list from is incomplete.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The registry verifier gives no verdict at all to a row whose `expected` is neither `present` nor `absent`, and still reports success. scripts/verify-issues.sh:97-99 preserves whatever the registry says and only defaults a MISSING value to `present`; the verdict block at :204-224 is an `if present` / `elif absent` with no else branch, so a row spelled `expected: "bogus"` increments `total` and leaves verified, stale, fixed and errors untouched. The gate whose whole purpose is to prove that every entry still describes the tree therefore cannot see the one row class it was never told about, and a typo in a single field removes that entry from the check with the run green.
issues.fix_sketch: Reject an unrecognised `expected` value where the row is parsed, counting it as an error rather than falling through, and add a case feeding the verifier a row with an invalid `expected` and asserting a non-zero exit.
issues.fix_note: The verdict block has an else branch: a row whose expected is neither present nor absent is reported and counted as an error rather than leaving the check with no verdict and the run green. Pinned with the same property bug-012 established -- Total equals the sum of the four counters, whatever the rows say -- so a row class the gate says nothing about fails the reconciliation too.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The translation drift checker searches the whole file for the source marker although its own contract calls the marker first-line metadata. scripts/check-i18n-drift.py:4-8 documents the marker as the first line of a translated page; :109 runs `MARKER.search(text)` across the entire text and never checks where the match landed. A translated page that lost its first-line marker but quotes the marker text later, in a fenced example or in copied prose, has that later occurrence's hash validated and is reported current, so a page the gate exists to prove is stamped passes unstamped.
issues.fix_sketch: Match the marker against the first line only (or assert the match offset is inside it), and add a case whose translation carries the marker in a fenced block and no first-line marker, asserting the checker reports it.
issues.fix_note: The marker is matched against the first line only, which is what this file documents it to be. A page carrying the marker text later -- in a fenced example, or in copied prose -- and nothing on its first line is now reported as missing its marker rather than validated against that later occurrence. Measured against all 25 translated pages first: every one already carries the marker on line 1, so the gate did not become stricter than the tree.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The episode index path's top-`limit` cut and its tie-break are never executed by any test. cpersona/vector.py:1440-1444 applies `heapq.nlargest(limit, ..., key=lambda i: (survivors[i][1], -i))` and re-sorts the kept indices into scan order; a line-level trace over the full suite (2047 passed) records :1441-1444 as never run, while the identical memory-scan twin at :1277 is run and is pinned by an independent oracle in tests/test_bug249_two_phase_scan.py:416. The equivalence test disables the branch by construction: tests/test_vector_index_episodes.py:154 searches with a limit of 40, wider than the fixture's surviving episode set, so `limit < len(survivors)` is always false. Inverting the tie-break to `(survivors[i][1], i)`, or dropping `sorted(keep)`, makes the index and the SQL scan resolve a cosine tie at the cut boundary the opposite way on the same corpus, and the whole suite stays green.
issues.fix_sketch: Add an episode-index equivalence case whose surviving set is larger than the requested limit, with two episodes tied on cosine at the boundary, asserting the index result equals the scan result row for row.
issues.fix_note: Two cases, over an agent that owns episodes and no memories so the cut boundary falls between two equal episode scores. The first draft reused the shared corpus and simply narrowed the limit, and both mutants survived it because memories win every tie and the episode assertions went vacuous. Measured on the rewrite: inverting the tie-break turns the first case red, and dropping the re-sort into scan order turns the second red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) `deep=true` halving the calibrated fused gate is published in the shipped tool description and never executed. cpersona/memory_handlers.py:1373 `gate = gate * 0.5` is the only thing that makes `deep` relax retrieval on an install that has run calibration or precision tuning, and a line-level trace over the full suite records it as never run. The one test that pins the claim, tests/test_docs_behavioural_claims.py:307, runs with no global fused gate and an empty per-agent table, so `gate is None` and only the `min_score * 0.5` half is exercised. Delete the line and every deployment with a calibrated gate returns exactly the same rows for `deep=true` as for a normal recall, contradicting cpersona/server.py:858 and skills/cpersona-memory/SKILL.md:233, with nothing red.
issues.fix_sketch: Add a recall case that sets a fused gate for the agent and asserts a row admitted at `deep=true` is refused at `deep=false` on the same corpus, so the halving is observed through the gate rather than through `min_score`.
issues.fix_note: A recall case sets a fused gate for the agent just above a row's measured gate score and asserts the row is refused at deep false and admitted at deep true, so the halving is observed through the gate rather than through min_score. Detection power measured: deleting the halving makes it red, which the existing pin could not do because it ran with no global gate and an empty per-agent table.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The per-agent fused gate is written by calibration and never read back through a recall in any test. cpersona/vector.py:286 `return _agent_fused_gates[agent_id]` is recorded as never executed by a line-level trace over the full suite; the `if agent_id in _agent_fused_gates` line above it runs and is always false, because every test that reaches the function has an empty table. tests/test_recall_precision.py exercises the write side and the sidecar round-trip in full, but its fixture at line 39 clears `vector._agent_fused_gates` and no test in the file drives a retrieval, so the only production reader (cpersona/memory_handlers.py:1371) is never fed a per-agent value. Replacing the body with `return _global_fused_gate`, which deletes per-agent precision from the read path so a tuned agent is filtered by the global gate or the pool-size heuristic instead, leaves the suite green.
issues.fix_sketch: Add a case that sets a per-agent precision, then drives `do_recall` for that agent and for a second untuned agent on the same corpus, asserting the two get different gates applied.
issues.fix_note: Two agents, one query, and the value each recall carries into the quality gate, plus the deep relaxation applied to it. Observed at the seam the gate is handed to rather than at the surviving rows: under the pinned mode of this suite the candidates come back unscored from the lexical cascade, which a post-fusion gate does not filter. Measured: replacing the per-agent read with the global one turns both cases red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Under the rank-sum fusion mode the episode keyword channel is called but never returns a row, so the sign it applies to bm25 is unverified. cpersona/memory_handlers.py:618-621 is recorded as never executed by a line-level trace over the full suite, while the corresponding block in the reciprocal-rank path at :486-493 runs. The negation at :621 is what turns `bm25(episodes_fts)`, where a more negative value is a better match (:2101), into a higher-is-better channel before `_minmax_norm`. Drop the minus and the normaliser scores the worst-matching episode 1.0 and the best 0.0, so the best episode can fall below the quality gate and vanish from the response; the channel can also be deleted outright, and no test goes red either way.
issues.fix_sketch: Add a rank-sum fusion case with episodes that match the query lexically, asserting the episode with the strongest bm25 outranks the weakest in the fused result.
issues.fix_note: A rank-sum case with two episodes matching the query lexically asserts the stronger bm25 outranks the weaker in the fused list, read before the quality gate so gating one row out cannot make the comparison unavailable. The vector channel is switched off for it deliberately: with it on, cosine separates the two by itself and the order is the same whichever sign the keyword channel applies. Detection power measured both ways -- dropping the negation is red with the vector arm off and green with it on.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The only test that claims to pin how the HTTP body budget is mounted never inspects the mounted object. tests/test_http_body_budget.py:173-180 fetches the mounted middleware only to borrow its `.app`, then constructs a fresh `RequestBodyBudgetMiddleware` and asserts that instance's `max_bytes` and `mode` equal the config values its `__init__` reads unconditionally: the assertion is `config == config`, true whatever arguments cpersona/server.py:2619 passes. Every other test in the file overwrites `budget.mode` and `budget.max_bytes` on the mounted instance (`_make_app`, lines 70-72), so the mount's own arguments are observed nowhere in the suite. Measured: after forcing the mounted instance to `mode="off"` and `max_bytes=10**12`, the four lines of that test body still pass, so mutating the mount to `Middleware(RequestBodyBudgetMiddleware, mode="off")` removes body accounting from the production transport with the file fully green.
issues.fix_sketch: Assert on the mounted instance itself before `_make_app` overwrites it (or read the mount's arguments from the middleware stack), so a hard-coded argument at the mount site fails the test.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The pairwise fail-closed switch is derived in production and asserted nowhere; only the class that consumes it is tested. cpersona/server.py:2049 `require_public_subject = bool(acl_config.per_subject_clients)` is the only place the pairwise-subject defence (docs/OAUTH_DESIGN.md section 12) is turned on, and it reaches the verifier at :2065. The flag appears in tests/ exactly twice, tests/test_oauth_verification.py:266 and :280, both as an explicit keyword on a directly constructed verifier; the one wiring test at :627-630 builds the verifier from an ACL file with no per-subject row and asserts only `isinstance(verifier, oauth.IdpTokenVerifier)`. Measured: building the verifier from a per-subject ACL file yields the flag set today, so it is observable and simply unobserved. Pin line 2049 to `False` and a deployment against an issuer advertising pairwise subjects verifies tokens instead of refusing them, splitting one person's memory space per client, while the refusal test still passes because it sets the flag itself.
issues.fix_sketch: Extend the wiring test to build the verifier from an ACL config that has a per-subject client and assert the constructed verifier requires public subjects.
issues.fix_note: The wiring test builds the verifier from a per-subject ACL and from a static-token one, and asserts the derived flag in both directions. Measured: pinning the production line to False turns the per-subject case red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Activating the alias ledger has neither a test nor a startup invariant, while the other half of per-subject partitioning has both. cpersona/server.py:2904-2914 is the only place `acl.activate_ledger(AliasLedger(...))` runs, and no test drives `main()` far enough to see it: tests/test_per_subject.py calls `activate_ledger` itself in its `_activate` helper at :53, the only hit in tests/ besides the reset fixture, and `main()` is otherwise drivable in tests (tests/test_254_teeth.py:114, tests/test_253_reachability.py:337). The grant table by contrast refuses to serve at both transport entries when the ACL file is set but inactive (server.py:2648 and :2823); nothing checks the corresponding `per_subject_clients and no active ledger` condition. Delete the three-line block and a fresh install denies every `@me` call from a per-subject client, while a database already holding issued aliases refuses startup against an empty known-alias set, reproducing the bug-267 incident -- the suite stays green either way.
issues.fix_sketch: Add a startup invariant refusing to serve when per-subject clients are configured and no ledger is active, and a test that drives `main()` with a per-subject ACL and asserts the ledger became active.
issues.fix_note: A test drives main() through startup with a per-subject ACL and asserts the ledger became active, in both directions. Measured: deleting the activation line turns it red. The startup invariant the entry also asks for adds a refusal to a configuration that boots today, so it is not taken here.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The operating context's Soft layer has one production wiring line and the suite is configured so that no assertion can observe it. cpersona/server.py:464 passes `instructions=operating_context.instructions_text()` into the tool registry, which is what puts the sidecar's instructions summary into the MCP `initialize` response (docs/OPERATING_CONTEXT_DESIGN.md section 4). tests/conftest.py:33 pins `CPERSONA_OPERATING_CONTEXT=off` before any import, so `server.registry` is built with `instructions=None` in every run -- measured: `server.registry.server.create_initialization_options().instructions` is `None` under the suite -- and the test that appears to cover the behaviour, tests/test_operating_context.py:124-130, builds a throwaway registry with a literal string instead. Drop the keyword and an operator with a populated sidecar gets no instructions on any transport while the Hard layer keeps working, so the sidecar still looks live, and nothing fails.
issues.fix_sketch: Add a case that sets the sidecar environment, reloads the module, and asserts the reloaded registry's initialization options carry the sidecar text -- or a source gate pinning the keyword on that constructor call.
issues.fix_note: The suite pins the sidecar off before any import, so the assertion reads the registry in a subprocess where it is on, and checks the kill switch invents nothing. Measured: dropping the keyword from the constructor turns it red.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Nothing ties a tool's declared JSON Schema properties to the `params` list its arguments are actually extracted from. cpersona/_vendored_mcp_common/mcp_utils.py:150-167 builds the handler's positional arguments from `params` alone, while each tool's `schema` dict is a separate hand-written artifact (store's is cpersona/server.py:820-825), so an entry can be dropped from one and stay advertised in the other. Every `session_key` test calls the handler directly with the keyword -- tests/test_257_session_key_stage2.py:303 and tests/test_boundary_layer.py:84, :147, :279, :350, plus one schema-shape assertion at tests/test_superauditor_findings.py:311 -- and no test dispatches a real tool call carrying the argument. Measured: schema properties and `params` keys agree for every registered tool today, so the gate is missing rather than already red. Delete `session_key` from store's params and a client that armed a keyed pause keeps sending it, the handler receives the empty default, and the write lands in the shared bucket during a pause that still reports itself as session-scoped, with the whole suite green.
issues.fix_sketch: Add a gate that iterates the registered tools and asserts each schema property has a matching `params` entry and vice versa, so a dropped extraction spec fails on the tool that declares it.
issues.note: Anchored on the extraction site rather than on one tool's params entry: the params spelling the finding names occurs 22 times in cpersona/server.py, so a pattern on it could never identify the defect. The schema/params pairs themselves live in cpersona/server.py; the missing gate would read both.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The equivalence comparator accepts a boolean where a float is expected, although its own contract says a type change surfaces immediately. tests/test_equivalence_252.py:57-62 states that everything but float leaves is compared exactly; the float branch at :64-69 admits both operands under `isinstance(..., (int, float))` and returns `math.isclose(float(a), float(b), ...)`, and Python's `bool` is a subclass of `int`. An expected `{"persisted": true}` against an observed `{"persisted": 1.0}` therefore compares equal, so the gate built to catch response regressions between two implementations cannot see a boolean-to-float change in a response field.
issues.pattern: if not isinstance\(a, \(int, float\)\) or not isinstance\(b, \(int, float\)\):
issues.fix_sketch: Reject a bool paired with a non-bool before the float branch (compare `type(a) is bool` against `type(b) is bool`), and add a case asserting `true` and `1.0` are reported unequal.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The benchmark-table gate compares dictionaries keyed by model name, so a duplicate row is discarded before the comparison runs. scripts/check-docs-facts.py:773-779 builds each table with a dict comprehension keyed on the model captured by `BENCH_ROW`, and the last row for a model silently wins; :795-809 then compares keys and values only. A published table carrying two rows for one model -- a stale measurement first, the current one second -- passes as agreement, so the conflicting row stays in the document the gate exists to check and the gate reports the two tables consistent.
issues.fix_sketch: Collect rows as a list per model and fail when a model appears more than once in one table, before comparing the two tables.
issues.fix_note: Rows are collected one at a time and a second row for the same model fails the gate before the two tables are compared, so a table publishing a stale measurement above the current one can no longer pass as agreement. Measured both shapes: the duplicate on one side, and the duplicate on both sides, which is the one a key-by-key compare cannot see at all.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The checkup CLI's `--strict` exit contract is pinned at the helper only, never end to end. cpersona/checkup.py:8-10 documents warn-level issues as exit code 1 under `--strict`, and the CLI computes that at :129; tests/test_v2437_checkup.py:316-321 covers `exit_code`'s semantics by calling it directly, and the subprocess round-trip at :384-424 exercises only the healthy and the critical cases. No test builds a warn-only database and runs the CLI with `--strict`, so rewriting line 129 to pass `strict=False` leaves the suite green while `python -m cpersona.checkup --strict` returns 0 on exactly the database state the flag exists for.
issues.fix_sketch: Add a subprocess case that seeds a warn-only database, runs the CLI with `--strict`, and asserts exit code 1 (with the non-strict run asserted 0 on the same database).
issues.fix_note: A subprocess case now seeds a warn-only database (a warn-severity registered index dropped), asserts the CLI exits 0 without --strict and 1 with it. Measured: rewriting the CLI to pass strict=False now fails that case; before, it left the whole suite green.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) Schema verification walks the registry and never the database, so an object dropped from the registry becomes invisible instead of reported. cpersona/checks.py:1132 iterates `_EXPECTED_OBJECTS` and compares each entry against `sqlite_master`; nothing compares the observed index and trigger set back against the registry. The golden test asserts only that this one-way check returns no issues on a fresh database (tests/test_v2437_checkup.py:90-94), so deleting an entry such as `idx_episodes_isolation` (defined at cpersona/checks.py:1017-1022) keeps it green -- the index still exists and is simply no longer looked at. A deployment later missing that index then gets no `schema_object_drift` issue and `--fix` has nothing to restore.
issues.fix_sketch: Add a golden test that compares the fresh database's own index and trigger names against `_EXPECTED_OBJECTS`, failing on any shipped load-bearing object the registry does not list.
issues.fix_note: A golden test now walks the fresh database's own indexes and triggers and fails on any shipped object _EXPECTED_OBJECTS does not list, which is the direction the one-way check could not run in. It found two: idx_memories_agent_channel and idx_episodes_agent_channel both ship from the migration ladder and were unwatched, so a deployment missing either got no drift issue and --fix had nothing to restore; both are now registered at warn, the severity their siblings carry. Detection power measured: deleting idx_episodes_isolation from the registry -- the mutation the finding names as staying green -- now fails tests/test_v2437_checkup.py.

issues.summary: (LOW) Mutation reporting counts a work item that produced no result and then leaves it out of the denominator, and the caller reports success regardless. scripts/mutation-diff.py:239-244 increments `counts["not_executed"]` when a work item has no worker result, while `in_scope` at :281-286 sums only killed, survived, incompetent and worker_error; the main path emits `"status": "ok"` at :497-499 whatever the classification said. Reproduced against the shipped functions: a seeded session holding one work item with no result gives `counts.not_executed = 1`, `in_scope = 0`, `survival_rate = null` and a pending count of 1, so the report's generated count omits the item entirely. The end-to-end half -- a run that exits successfully while leaving an item unexecuted -- was not reproduced, because the mutation runner is absent from this checkout and the execution helper uses `check=True` at :93-100; the accounting defect itself is measured.
issues.fix_sketch: Include `not_executed` in `in_scope` (or refuse to emit `status: ok` while it is non-zero), and add a case over a seeded session with one resultless work item asserting the report is not reported healthy.
issues.fix_note: not_executed is inside the generated count now, and a run holding one no longer reports status ok: it reports incomplete with a reason saying the figures are a lower bound. The counts table is still rendered, because what was wrong is only the word on top of it. It stays out of survival_rate by design -- the rate is over what was classified, the total over what the lane took on. The CI step only echoes the status, so nothing gates differently.

issues.summary: (LOW) `_minmax_norm`'s all-None branch, the one the documented substring-fallback path lands on, never executes in the suite. cpersona/memory_handlers.py:531-533 returns a uniform 1.0 when a channel carries no numeric score, which the docstring at :527 states as the contract for the LIKE fallback so that an exact substring match still casts a full keyword vote; a line-level trace over the full suite records :533 as never run, while its `hi <= lo` twin at :536 does run. The branch is a crash guard and a scoring decision at once and neither half is pinned: delete lines 532-533 and the next line raises `ValueError: min() arg is an empty sequence` out of recall, or return 0.0 instead of 1.0 and every exact substring match casts a zero keyword vote and is pushed under the gate. Reaching it needs the rank-sum fusion mode and a query with no term of three or more characters, so the FTS query is empty and the keyword channel comes back from the LIKE fallback with every bm25 None (:2166, :632). Both mutations leave the suite green.
issues.fix_sketch: Add a rank-sum fusion case with a two-character query that forces the LIKE fallback, asserting an exact substring match survives the gate and that the normaliser returns 1.0 for that channel.
issues.fix_note: Two cases: a direct one pinning that an all-None channel normalises to a full 1.0 vote, and a rank-sum recall with a two-character query that forces the LIKE fallback so the branch is reached end to end. Detection power measured: returning 0.0 and deleting the guard outright are both red. The end-to-end case does not pin the 1.0-against-0.0 decision -- a 0.0 vote still clears the adaptive gate on a corpus that small, and tuning a corpus until it did not would pin the gate's arithmetic instead -- which is why the scoring half is pinned directly.

issues.summary: (LOW) The comment above the lost-embedding statements says a test pins the query plan for the unary plus on `agent_id`; for the chunked form no test can bite. Measured with `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` on both statements against a 400-row seeded corpus: the range form's plan changes when the plus is removed, from `SEARCH memories USING INDEX idx_memories_lost_embedding (id>? AND id<?)` to `SEARCH memories USING INDEX idx_memories_span (agent_id=?)`, which fails tests/test_bug285_probe_bound.py:227 -- while the chunked form plans as `SEARCH memories USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)` with and without the plus and satisfies both :227 and :274 either way. A reader trusting the comment removes the plus from `_lost_embedding_chunk_sql`, or the planner's costing shifts once statistics exist, and the scattered-selection probe can walk every row of the agent per chunk -- the 3.0 s against 41 ms regression the comment cites -- with no test able to report it.
issues.pattern: bug-417: a test pins that plan for the RANGE form only
issues.fix_sketch: Give the chunked form a plan assertion that fails without the plus (a corpus and statistics where the isolation index looks selective), or narrow the comment to the range form so it stops claiming coverage that does not exist.
issues.fix_note: The comment is narrowed to the form a test actually pins, and records what was measured when trying to pin the other: on 400 rows and again on 20,000 with a skewed agent distribution and ANALYZE run, the chunked form plans identically with and without the unary plus. Adjusting a corpus until the assertion passes would pin the corpus rather than the plan, so the absence of coverage is stated where the next reader will see it.

issues.summary: (LOW) No test in either proxy file looks at a forwarded request's headers, so the bridge's only credential is unasserted. cpersona/proxy_stdio.py:176-177 builds the `Authorization: Bearer` header from `CPERSONA_AUTH_TOKEN`, which the module docstring at line 9 documents as required. Both proxy test files drive `main()` end to end and neither reads a header: the hand-written fake at tests/test_proxy_stdio.py:23 accepts a `headers` argument and discards it, and the seven mock-transport handlers in tests/test_bug253_proxy_concurrency.py all branch on the request body only. Deleting the two lines makes every forwarded message reach an authenticated remote uncredentialed and return 401, which the proxy turns into a per-request error, with both files green; the `Mcp-Session-Id` threading on the next line is unobserved for the same reason.
issues.fix_sketch: Have one mock-transport handler assert the request carries the bearer header built from the configured token, and a second assert the session id is echoed back on the following request.

issues.summary: (LOW) The mutation report loads the waiver registry and uses it without running the registry's own consistency check. scripts/mutation-diff.py:382-390 calls `active_waivers()` directly; that function accepts approved, unexpired, code-present entries and indexes them by whatever fingerprint they declare (scripts/mutation_waivers.py:210-228), while the check that a declared fingerprint matches the recomputed one exists only in `verify()` at :185-205 and is never called from here. A waiver with valid approval, date, tool version and code hash but a fingerprint belonging to a different live survivor is therefore applied to that survivor at :263-275, understating `survived_unwaived` and overstating the waived count in the report that is read as the result.
issues.fix_sketch: Run the registry verifier before computing active waivers and fail the report on a fingerprint mismatch, with a case seeding an approved waiver whose declared fingerprint belongs to another survivor.
issues.fix_note: The lane runs the registry verifier before computing active waivers and refuses to apply a registry with hard problems, of which a declared fingerprint that does not match the entry own file, definition, operator and line is one. Soft problems (expiry, tool-version drift) stay advisory, which is what they were designed to be. Pinned two ways: the ordering is asserted in the lane source, and a hard problem is measured to stop it before active_waivers is reached.

issues.summary: (LOW) `get_profile` has no test at all. cpersona/admin_handlers.py:68-75 reads the stored profile row and returns it, and docs/tools.md:24 documents the tool as returning the accumulated profile; a search of tests/ finds no reference to `get_profile` or `do_get_profile`. Replacing the return at :75 with an empty profile -- so the common read path answers empty after a successful `update_profile` -- leaves the suite green.
issues.fix_sketch: Add a round-trip case: `update_profile` a known string, then assert `get_profile` returns it for that agent and an empty profile for an agent that has none.
issues.fix_note: Round-trip coverage added in tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py: update_profile then get_profile for the same agent, plus an agent with no profile so an empty answer means absence rather than the read failing open. Measured: replacing the return in do_get_profile with an empty profile now fails 5 cases; before it left the whole suite green.

issues.summary: (LOW) The ownership guards on `update_memory` and `unlock_memory` are untested; only the lock path's guard is driven. cpersona/admin_handlers.py:393 rejects a mismatched owner on update and :500 does the same on unlock; the pattern's third match, :476, is the lock guard, which tests/test_recall_quality.py does cover. The registered contracts at cpersona/server.py:1384-1404 and :1425-1439 state that ownership is enforced when `agent_id` is supplied, and tests/test_recall_quality.py:356-401 covers update success and not-found, unlock success and lock ownership, with no wrong-agent case for either of the other two paths. Removing either guard lets one agent rewrite or unlock another agent's memory with nothing red.
issues.fix_sketch: Add two cases against a memory owned by one agent: `update_memory` with a different `agent_id` returns an error and leaves the content unchanged, and `unlock_memory` with a different `agent_id` is refused and leaves the row locked.
issues.note: The pattern matches three ownership refusals in the file (update, lock, unlock); only the lock one at :476 is exercised today, so the entry stays anchored on the shared refusal string rather than on one line.
issues.fix_note: The wrong-agent cases for update_memory and unlock_memory are driven by the bug-367 regression test, which walks all four by-id write handlers against a foreign unlocked row, a foreign locked row and a missing id, and asserts both rows are unchanged afterwards. Measured by mutation: removing either ownership guard turns it red.

issues.summary: (LOW) The bounded told-session map is asserted by size only, so its eviction order is unverified. cpersona/update_check.py:567-570 evicts the oldest insertion, and tests/test_update_check.py:487-494 checks the length bound and never which key left. Measured by mutation: with a newest-first eviction installed in place of the shipped one, the checked-in test's own body still passes, while both controls behave as expected -- on the shipped code the oldest key is evicted and the newest survives, and under the mutant the newest key is forgotten and receives a duplicate notice on its next call. The order is unspecified in docs/SESSION_IDENTITY_DESIGN.md:291-294, which promises only a bounded map whose worst case is one repeated notice, so the gap is in an unpinned property rather than a broken published contract.
issues.fix_sketch: Extend the bound test to assert which keys survive: after overflowing the cap, the first-inserted key is gone and the most recent one is still suppressed.
issues.fix_note: The bound test now asserts which keys survive rather than only how many: after overflowing the cap the first-inserted keys are gone, the most recent one is still suppressed, and the forgotten one receives its second notice. Size alone could not tell oldest-first eviction from newest-first, and the two differ in who pays the repeat -- a quiet session once, or the session that just arrived, on every call it makes.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) The OpenAI-compatible embedding path pairs vectors with input texts by list position and never reads each item's `index`. `_embed_via_api` walks `data` with `enumerate` and appends `item["embedding"]` in arrival order (cpersona/_vendored_mcp_common/embedding_client.py:470-475), then `_validate_batch` only checks the count. The API documents `index` as the position of the embedding in the input list and does not promise arrival order. Reproduced through the real client against a mock transport: a two-item response listed with `index` 1 before `index` 0 handed input 0 the vector documented for input 1, with ok=true, so the wrong vector is stored and searched for that text with no signal.
issues.fix_sketch: Read `index` from each item, refuse a response whose indices are not exactly 0..n-1 (missing, duplicated, or out of range), and place each vector by its index rather than its arrival position.
issues.note: The copy of this client that ships inside this package has diverged from the shared library it was vendored from; the defect line exists only in this package's copy, so the fix lands here.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) A backend vector holding an integer outside float range escapes the client's failure boundary as an unhandled OverflowError. `_validate_vector` converts every element with `float(value)` (cpersona/_vendored_mcp_common/embedding_client.py:387), and `embed_with_outcome` catches only `httpx.RequestError`, `httpx.HTTPStatusError`, `ValueError` and `KeyError` (lines 238-240); `float()` raises `OverflowError`, which is an `ArithmeticError`, for an int that does not fit. Reproduced through the real client against a mock transport: a JSON body whose embedding contained a 401-digit integer raised OverflowError out of `embed_with_outcome` instead of returning the documented `EmbedOutcome(attempted=True, ok=False)`, so the caller's store path aborts rather than storing the row without a vector.
issues.fix_sketch: Convert inside a try that maps OverflowError to EmbeddingResponseError (the element is not a usable number, which is the same verdict as a non-finite one), or add OverflowError to the boundary's except tuple.
issues.note: The copy of this client that ships inside this package has diverged from the shared library it was vendored from; the defect line exists only in this package's copy, so the fix lands here.

issues.summary: (MEDIUM) A failed embedding request is logged with the raw exception before the sanitised evidence is built, so an endpoint URL carrying credentials in userinfo or a query string reaches the log verbatim. `embed_with_outcome` runs `logger.warning("Embedding request failed: %s", e)` (cpersona/_vendored_mcp_common/embedding_client.py:239) and only then calls `_failure_evidence`, which strips the endpoint for the value returned to the caller (lines 416-430). httpx status and transport errors embed the request URL in their message. Reproduced through the real client against a mock transport answering 500 with the API URL configured as `https://user:PASSWORD@host/...?key=SECRET`: the returned `error` was sanitised, the WARNING record contained both the password and the query secret.
issues.fix_sketch: Log the sanitised `_failure_evidence(e)` string (or the exception's class name plus the safe endpoint) instead of the exception itself.
issues.note: The copy of this client that ships inside this package has diverged from the shared library it was vendored from; the defect line exists only in this package's copy, so the fix lands here.
issues.fix_note: The safe evidence is built first and logged, so the sanitiser the returned error already went through now covers the log line too. httpx carries the request URL inside its own message, which is how an endpoint configured with credentials in the userinfo or the query string reached a WARNING record verbatim while the value handed to the caller was clean. Regression in tests/test_2512b2_handlers.py asserts both halves plus a control that the failure is still reported at all, so a log line that simply disappeared would not pass.
